profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T12:12:07.444+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command.
Later Scholars from Tiāntái.
Gāozǔ was originally a person from the Shātuó tribe,
residing in Tàiyuán.
Upon gaining control of China,
he declared his surname to be Liú,
and thus claimed to be a descendant of Liú Bǐng (劉昞), the eighth son of Xiǎnzōng of the Eastern Hàn dynasty, who was the Prince of Huáiyáng.
The name of his state was Hàn.
Before the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, there was already the Hànjì,
so this will be recorded under Hòuhànjì.
In the twelfth year of Tiānfú (dìngwèi, 947 CE),
Hàn again used Tiānfú for its reign year,
details to be seen later.
1. Spring,
first month,
on the dìnghài day,
the hundred officials remotely bade farewell to the Jìn ruler north of the city,
north of Dàliáng city.
They welcomed the Qìdān ruler,
lying prostrate by the roadside to beg for forgiveness.
The Qìdān ruler, wearing a sable cap and sable fur,
with armor underneath,
halted his horse on a high mound,
ordered them to rise,
change their clothes,
and comforted them.
According to Ōu Shǐ (歐史),
at that time, the Jìn hundred officials welcomed the Qìdān ruler at Chìgāng.
According to Xuē Shǐ (薛史),
Ān Shūqiān (安叔千) was a descendant of the three Shātuó tribes,
and therefore accustomed to speaking Hú (胡) language.
"Are you Ān Mòzì (安沒字)?
Ān Shūqiān's appearance was imposing,
but he was illiterate,
and his actions were vulgar.
People called him
'Mòzì Bēi' (沒字碑, the 'Illiterate Stele').
You have repeatedly submitted memorials expressing loyalty,
I will not forget it."
Shūqiān bowed in thanks, cheered, and withdrew.
Cheering was a barbarian ritual,
like the dancing of the Chinese.
The Jìn ruler and the Empress Dowager and others welcomed him outside Fēngqiū Gate,
but the Qìdān ruler declined to meet them.
Kǎoyì (考異) states: Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù (漢高祖實錄) says:
"The Young Emperor led his clan to wait in the wilderness,
but the Xiélǜ (邪律) clan treated them with disdain.
The Emperor recounted past events,
stating that it was a conspiracy by ministers,
and was able to respond clearly to everything,
without showing any sign of yielding,
so the Xiélǜ clan also gave him some face."
Xiànfān Jì (陷蕃記), Xuē Shǐ Dìjì (薛史帝紀), and Wǔdài Tōnglù (五代通錄) say:
"The barbarian ruler did not meet the Emperor."
Shàodì Shílù (少帝實錄) says:
"The Emperor led his clan to await punishment in the wilderness,
and the barbarian chieftain patted his face,
sending him to stay at Fēngchán Sì (封禪寺)."
Now we follow the Xiànfān Jì.
When the Qìdān ruler entered the gate,
the people all cried out in alarm and fled.
The Qìdān ruler ascended the city tower,
and sent an interpreter to address them, saying:
"I am also a human,
do not fear!
I will surely bring you peace."
Sū (蘇) means to breathe again after one's breath has ceased;
xī (息) means one inhalation and exhalation.
Alternatively,
sū (蘇) means to breathe again.
"It was only the Hàn soldiers who led me here."
He placed the blame on Dù Wēi (杜威) and others.
He dismounted and bowed before entering the palace.
He appointed his Assistant Commissioner of Military Affairs, Liú Mì (劉密), to temporarily oversee Kāifēng Mansion affairs.
First, he replaced the capital governor to suppress the Chinese.
The Qìdān ruler went out again,
and camped at Chìgāng.
Fearing that the hearts of the people were not yet united,
he dared not reside in the city.
2. On the wùzǐ day,
Yáng Chéngxūn (楊承勳), the Defense Commissioner of Zhèngzhōu, was captured and brought to Dàliáng.
He was reproached for killing his father and rebelling against the Qìdān.
Yáng Chéngxūn imprisoned his father and surrendered to Jìn.
The matter is seen in volume 284, the first year of Kāiyùn, Prince Qí (齊王).
Soon after,
his younger brother, Yáng Chéngxìn (楊承信), General of the Right Yǔlín (羽林), was appointed Jìedùshǐ (節度使) of Pínglú,
and all of his father's old troops were given to him.
After giving him his father's old garrison,
he was again given his father's old troops.
3. Gāo Xūn (高勳) complained to the Qìdān ruler that Zhāng Yànzé (張彥澤) had killed his family members.
Zhāng Yànzé's killing of Gāo Xūn's family is seen in the previous volume, previous year.
Xūn was the one who presented the surrender memorial on behalf of Dù Wēi,
and had already been favored by the Qìdān ruler,
thus he was able to plead his case.
Zhāng Yànzé was also shackled with Fù Zhù'ér (傅住兒).
The matter of Yànzé's plunder is also seen in the previous volume, previous year.
Fù Zhù'ér
was the one supervising Yànzé's army.
Piāo (剽),
pronounced pǐmiào.
He asked:
"Should they die?"
All said,
"They should die."
The common people also submitted petitions to expose Yànzé's crimes.
On the jǐchǒu day,
Yànzé and Zhù'ér were executed in the northern market,
and Gāo Xūn was ordered to supervise the execution.
The sons and grandsons of the literati whom Yànzé had previously killed
all wore mourning clothes, carried staffs, wailed,
followed and cursed,
and struck him with their staffs.
Xūn ordered his wrists to be severed and his shackles removed,
and his heart to be cut out to offer sacrifices to the dead.
The market people scrambled to break open his skull to take out the marrow,
and cut his flesh to eat it.
4. The Qìdān sent Jǐng Yánguǎng (景延廣) back to his country.
On the gēngyín day,
he stayed at Chénqiáo.
Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志): There is Chénqiáo Town in Jùnyí County, Kāifēng Prefecture.
When he saw the guards slightly slacken,
he choked himself to death.
5. On the xīnmǎo day,
the Qìdān designated the Jìn ruler as the Marquis of Fùyì (負義侯, Marquis of Ingratitude),
and placed him in Huánglóng Fǔ (黃龍府).
Huánglóng Fǔ
is the Hélóng Chéng (和龍城) of the Mùróng clan.
Ōu Shǐ says: "From Yōuzhōu, after more than ten days' journey,
passing Píngzhōu;
exiting Yúguān,
traveling through the sandy desert,
seven or eight days to Jǐnzhōu;
then another five or six days' journey,
passing Hǎiběi Zhōu;
then more than ten days' journey,
crossing the Liáo River to Tiězhōu in Bóhǎi Kingdom;
then another seven or eight days' journey,
passing Nánhǎi Fǔ,
and finally reaching Huánglóng Fǔ."
According to the Qìdān, Huánglóng Fǔ was later renamed Lóngzhōu,
one hundred and thirty *lǐ* (里) north to Húntóng Jiāng.
Furthermore, regarding the Mùróng clan's Hélóng Chéng,
if based on the Jìn Shū and Lì Dàoyuán's Shuǐjīng Zhù,
it should be within the territory of Hàn Liáoxī Commandery.
Now the Jìn ruler was captured by the barbarians,
crossed the Liáo River and then reached Huánglóng Fǔ,
and its location is near Húntóng Jiāng,
so it is suspected that it is not the Mùróng clan's Hélóng Chéng.
"I heard that Zhòngguì (重貴) disregarded his mother's orders, leading to this.
You may seek your own convenience,
do not go with him."
The Empress Dowager said:
"Zhòngguì has always served me very respectfully.
His only failing
was violating the will of the late emperor
and severing the good relations between the two states.
Now, fortunately, I have received great kindness,
preserving my life and protecting my family.
If a mother does not follow her son,
where can I go?"
On the guǐsì day,
the Qìdān moved the Jìn ruler and his family to Fēngchán Sì,
and sent Cuī Tíngxūn (崔廷勳), the Jìedùshǐ of Dàtóng and attendant-censor.
This was an official title conferred by the Qìdān.
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: Cuī Tíngxūn was originally from Hénèi,
and was captured by the barbarians in his youth.
Whenever the Jìn ruler heard that an envoy arrived,
his whole family would be filled with worry and fear.
Fearing they would be killed.
There was no provision from outside.
Máo Jūzhèng (毛居正) says: Gōngyì (供儗),
yì (儗) has the meaning of storing and accumulating.
Gōngyì (供億) is similar to gōngyì (供儗).
Yì (億) means to estimate;
to estimate the necessary items,
and provide them according to the quantity,
to prepare for their lack.
The Empress Dowager sent someone to tell the temple monks:
"I once fed tens of thousands of monks here."
Fàn (飯),
pronounced fúwǎn.
The monks declined, saying:
"The barbarians' intentions are unfathomable,
we dare not offer food."
Alas!
Who knew that the black-robed and yellow-robed (monks and nuns) would change countenance,
and their actions
would be even worse than daring not to offer food!
Those who possess states and families,
who honor and serve Buddhism to seek blessings and benefits,
can take heed from this.
Only then did they get a little food.
On that day,
the Qìdān (Khitan) lord led his troops from Chìgāng into the palace,
entering the Jìn (Later Jin) palace.
All were guarded by Qìdān soldiers,
who did not put down their weapons day and night.
They feared a rebellion.
They hung a sheepskin on a pole in the courtyard as an apotropaic charm.
The Qìdān lord said to
his close ministers:
"From now on, there will be no need to repair armor or weapons,
no need to purchase warhorses.
Taxes will be lightened and corvée reduced.
The world will be at peace."
Easier said than done!
No sooner had these words left his mouth
than "beating the grass for grain" (a foraging tactic) followed.
Was the world truly at peace?
Kāifēng Fǔ (Kaifeng Prefecture) was demoted to Biànzhōu,
and its Yǐn (prefect) became Fángyùshǐ (Defense Commissioner).
On the *yǐwèi* day,
the Qìdān lord changed into Chinese clothing and headgear.
The hundred officials' daily routines remained as per the old system.
Historians say that the Qìdān lord still knew how to use Chinese ways to transform the barbarians.
Zhào Yánshòu and Zhāng Lì together recommended the talent of Lǐ Sōng.
At that time, Féng Dào, the Wēishèng Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Weisheng), came from Dèngzhōu to pay his respects.
The Qìdān lord had long heard of their names
and treated them both with great respect.
These two had served successive Táng (Later Tang) and Jìn dynasties,
reaching the highest positions among officials.
When their country fell, they could not die for it,
regarding their sovereign as a stranger.
What was there to respect in them?
Lǐ Sōng was appointed Tàizǐ Tàishī (Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent)
and concurrently Shūmìshǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs).
Féng Dào was given the post of Tàifù (Grand Tutor),
serving at the Shūmì Yuàn (Bureau of Military Affairs)
for consultation.
The Qìdān lord dispatched envoys
to bestow imperial edicts upon the Jìn's vassal states.
The Jìn's vassal states vied with each other to submit memorials professing allegiance,
and those summoned all hastened to arrive.
Only Shǐ Kuāngwēi, the Zhāngyì Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor of Zhangyi), held Jīngzhōu and refused the order.
Kuāngwēi
was the son of Jiàntáng.
Shǐ Jiàntáng served Jìn Wáng Kèyòng and then Zhuāngzōng,
both times earning military achievements.
The three prefectures of Qín, Jiē, and Chéng surrendered to Shǔ (Later Shu).
Shǐ Kuāngwēi did not surrender to Qìdān
because his territory was distant,
and the Qìdān's military might could not reach there.
Hé Chóngjiàn, on the other hand, surrendered to Shǔ
because his garrison bordered Shǔ.
Previously,
Dù Chóngwēi, after leading the Jìn army to surrender to Qìdān,
initially avoided the name of the Jìn lord, Chóngguì,
by dropping
"Chóng"
and using only the single name
"Wēi."
After Jìn was annihilated,
Chóngwēi immediately resumed his old name.
His ingratitude and betrayal of his lord
were merely minor points.
He drove tens of thousands of horses back to his country,
sending Chóngwēi to lead his troops to follow him south.
Upon reaching the Hé (Yellow River),
the Qìdān lord, seeing the multitude of Jìn soldiers,
feared they might revolt
and wanted to use his cavalry to herd them all into the river.
Someone remonstrated, saying:
"Many Jìn soldiers are still in other places.
If they hear that all those who surrendered are killed,
they will surely resist orders.
It is better to temporarily appease them
and then slowly devise a strategy."
The Qìdān lord then had Chóngwēi encamp his troops at Chénqiáo.
Chénqiáo was outside Chénqiáo Gate,
where there was Chénqiáo Post Station.
With no provisions from the officials,
the soldiers suffered from cold and hunger.
They all resented Chóngwēi,
gathering and weeping together.
Whenever Chóngwēi went out,
people by the roadside cursed him.
The Qìdān lord still wanted to execute the Jìn soldiers.
Zhào Yánshòu said to the Qìdān lord:
"Did Your Majesty personally brave arrows and stones to conquer the Jìn state
wishing to possess it yourself,
or to conquer it for others?"
The Qìdān lord's expression changed, and he said:
"I led my entire nation in a southern campaign,
not removing my armor for five years—
in the eighth year of Tiānfú,
Qìdān first attacked Jìn,
and by this point it had been five years.
How could it be for others?"
When Zhào Yánshòu heard the Qìdān lord's words,
he could have given up hope.
"To the south, the Jìn state has Táng (Southern Tang),
and to the west, Shǔ (Later Shu),
both constant enemies.
Does Your Majesty know this?"
He replied:
"I know."
Yánshòu said:
"The Jìn state stretches for thousands of *lǐ* from Yí and Mì in the east
to Qín and Fèng in the west,
bordering Wú (Southern Tang) and Shǔ.
It constantly garrisons troops there.
The south is hot and humid;
people from the upper country (referring to the Central Plains) cannot live there.
At that time, those in regional strongholds
referred to the Central Plains as the upper country.
Jìn, in serving Qìdān,
also called Qìdān the upper country.
Given the vastness of the Jìn state
and no troops to guard it,
Wú and Shǔ will surely join forces to invade through the void.
If this happens,
would it not be conquering it for others?"
The Qìdān lord said:
"I did not know.
What then should be done?"
Yánshòu said:
"The surrendered soldiers at Chénqiáo
can be divided and stationed along the southern border.
Then Wú and Shǔ will not be able to cause trouble."
The Qìdān lord said:
"When I was in Shàngdǎng previously,
I made a mistake in the division
and gave all the Táng soldiers to Jìn.
This incident is recorded in volume 280, Jìn Gāozǔ Tiānfú Yuánnián.
'Duàn' (斷) is pronounced 'dīng luàn fān'.
They then fought me to the north,
and it took many years of hard work
to barely defeat them.
Now that they are fortunately in my hands,
if I do not eliminate them all at this time,
how can I keep them as a future problem?"
Yánshòu said:
"When Jìn soldiers were kept in Hénán previously,
their wives and children were not held hostage,
hence this worry.
Now, if their families are all moved to the area between Héng, Dìng, Yún, and Shuò,
and they are rotated annually to guard the southern border,
what concern is there of them revolting?
This is the best plan."
The Qìdān lord was pleased and said:
"Excellent!
It is up to Your Royal Highness to handle it."
Qìdān had enfeoffed Zhào Yánshòu as Yān Wáng (King of Yan),
hence he was referred to as Your Royal Highness.
'Chǔ' (處) is pronounced 'chāng lǚ fān'.
They were then sent back to their camps in separate groups.
6 The Qìdān lord killed Lǐ Yànshēn, the Yòu Jīnwú Wèi Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General of the Right Palace Guard), and the eunuch Qín Jìmín,
because they had killed Dōngdān Wáng (King of Dongdan) on behalf of Táng Lù Wáng (Prince of Lu of Tang).
The killing of Dōngdān Wáng is recorded in volume 280, Jìn Gāozǔ Tiānfú Yuánnián,
which was the third year of Táng Lù Wáng's Qīngtài reign.
'Wéi' (為) is pronounced 'yú wěi fān'.
Wùyù had one eye missing.
He was valiant, robust, and generous.
Wùyù appears here for the first time,
setting the stage for his later establishment of a state.
'Shī' (施) is pronounced 'shì chǐ fān'.
7 On the *guǐmǎo* day,
the Jìn lord, together with Empress Dowager Lǐ, Empress Ān, Empress Féng, and his younger brother Ruì, and sons Yánxù and Yánbǎo, all moved north,
accompanied by over a hundred palace attendants and followers.
Qìdān sent three hundred cavalry to escort them;
the escorts were to protect them on their journey.
While the Jìn lord was en route,
provisions were intermittent.
At times, he and the Empress Dowager would both go without food.
None of his old officials dared to visit him.
Only Lǐ Gǔ, the Cízhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Cizhou), greeted him on the road,
and they wept together.
Gǔ said:
"I am unworthy and have failed Your Majesty."
He then offered all his wealth.
Among the scholars of the world,
those who feel they have failed someone
will surely act differently from others.
'Cí' (磁) is pronounced 'qiáng zhī fān'.
When the Jìn ruler reached Zhōngdùqiáo,
he saw Dù Chóngwēi’s camp,
and sighed:
“Oh, Heaven!
What wrong have I done,
to be broken by this rebel!”
He wept bitterly and departed.
During the time of Jìn,
everyone in the country, high and low, knew that Dù Chóngwēi was unusable.
Yet, they went against the multitude to use him, leading to the downfall of the state.
The *Shī* says:
“He sheds his tears,
but what avails his regret now?”
Now that it has come to such bitter weeping,
what good can it do?
On the *Guǐchǒu* day,
the Shǔ ruler appointed Lǐ Jìxūn, the General of the Left Guards with Rapid Cavalry, as the Pacification Commissioner of Qínzhōu.
As Hé Chóngjiàn had submitted to Shǔ,
an envoy was sent to pacify him.
On the 9th day, the Qìdān ruler appointed Liú Xī, former Grand Administrator of Yānjīng, as Grand Administrator of Xījīng.
Xuē Shǐ says: Liú Xī
was from Zhuōzhōu,
captured by the barbarians,
and rose through official ranks to Píngzhāngshì concurrent with Shìzhōng.
Kǎo Yì says: The *Shílù* writes
“Xī.”
Some say his given name was Xī.
Now we follow *Xiàn Fān Jì*.
Wū
Yù’s brother-in-law, Pān Yùlián, was made Jìdùshǐ of Hénghǎi;
Zhào Yánshòu’s son, Kuāngzàn, was made Jìdùshǐ of Hùguó.
This laid the groundwork for Zhào Kuāngzàn to return Hézhōng to Hàn later.
Shǐ Quán was made Jìdùshǐ of Zhāngyì;
Liú Yànsēng, Deputy Envoy of the Guest Bureau, was made Jìdùshǐ of Zhōngwǔ;
Hóu Yì, former Jìdùshǐ of Hùguó, was made Jìdùshǐ of Fèngxiáng.
Hóu Yì was provisionally in charge of Fèngxiángfu affairs.
Hóu Yì later also returned Fèngxiáng to Hàn.
Xī
was from Zhuōzhōu.
Soon after, Hé Chóngjiàn submitted to Shǔ,
Qínzhōu submitted to Shǔ,
and Zhāng Yànchāo had nowhere to go.
Shǐ Kuāngwēi occupied Jīngzhōu to resist Shǐ Quán.
On the 10th day, Zhào Zàilǐ, Jìnchāng Jìdùshǐ, entered the court.
He traveled from Cháng’ān to the court in Dàliáng.
Lǐ Sù, Deputy Jìdùshǐ of Jiàn, pursued and executed him,
and the military command became secure.
On the 11th day, when the Jìn ruler broke off relations with Qìdān,
the event is found in volume 283, Jìn Gāozǔ, Tiānfú 7th year.
Jìxūn had been quite involved in the plan;
when the Qìdān ruler entered Biàn,
Jìxūn entered the court,
and the Qìdān ruler interrogated him.
At that time, Féng Dào was in the hall.
Jìxūn hastily pointed at Dào and said:
“Féng Dào is the prime minister,
and he, along with Jǐng Yán’guǎng, truly conceived this plan.
My position is lowly,
how would I dare to speak!”
The Qìdān ruler said:
“This old man is not one to meddle,
do not falsely implicate him!”
Féng Dào avoided disaster by compliance;
a state that has such a prime minister, what good is he!
However, he served seven dynasties,
and was always treated with respect for his virtue and prestige,
also because he conducted himself with caution and composure,
which inspired their respect.
Jìxūn was to be sent to Huánglóngfǔ.
Zhào Zàilǐ arrived in Luòyáng.
According to the *Jiù Táng Shū Dìlǐ Zhì*: from Cháng’ān eastward to Luòyáng is 850 *lǐ*.
“The Qìdān ruler once said that the chaos of Zhuāngzōng was caused by me.
This refers to the rebellion of Huángfǔ Huī.
The event is found in volume 274, Táng Míngzōng, Tiānchéng 1st year,
which was Tóngguāng 4th year of Zhuāngzōng.
Qìdān dispatched the Qìdān general Shùyà.
Indicates a Qìdān general,
to differentiate from Hàn generals and Bóhǎi generals.
The Bóhǎi general Gāo Móhàn garrisoned Luòyáng.
Zàilǐ entered to pay his respects,
prostrating himself in the courtyard,
while Zhuàyà and others all sat cross-legged to receive him.
On the *Yǐmǎo* day,
Zàilǐ arrived in Zhèngzhōu.
According to the *Jiǔ Yù Zhì*: from Luòyáng eastward to Zhèngzhōu is 260 *lǐ*.
Greatly alarmed,
that night,
he hanged himself in the stable.
When the Qìdān ruler heard of Zàilǐ’s death,
he released Jìxūn.
Jìxūn died of worry and indignation.
Liú Xī, while in Qìdān, had served as Shūmìshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Upon arriving in Luòyáng,
he berated the Xī King, saying:
“Zhào Zàilǐ is a great minister of the Hàn house,
while you are merely a chieftain of the north.
How dare you treat him with such disrespect!”
He stood in the courtyard to rebuke him.
Because of this, the people of Luòyáng felt somewhat calmer.
The Qìdān ruler extensively received tributes from all directions,
indulged greatly in wine and revelry,
and often said to the Jìn officials:
“I know everything about the affairs of the Central Plain,
but you do not know about the affairs of my country.”
The Qìdān ruler boasted to the Jìn officials about the secrecy of his precautions.
However,
the arrival of Dōngdān
had already sown the seeds of Wūyù’s disaster in seizing the state,
which even the most foolish would know,
yet the Qìdān ruler did not.
Those who are skilled at observing states
do not look at their temporary strength or weakness, but at the general trend of their order or chaos.
Zhào Yánshòu requested provisions and fodder for the soldiers of the Upper Kingdom.
The Qìdān ruler said:
“Our country has no such custom.”
He then let his cavalry spread out in all directions,
under the pretext of grazing horses,
plundering in turns,
calling it
“beating the grass for grain.”
The able-bodied died by the sword,
the old and weak were abandoned in ditches.
From the eastern and western Gīs,
the counties under Dàliáng were the eastern Gī,
the counties under Luòyáng were the western Gī;
this was a Táng system.
According to the Táng system,
apart from the capital counties,
the other counties under the two capitals were *jī* counties.
Over several hundred *lǐ*, wealth and livestock were almost completely exhausted.
Zhèng, Huá, Cáo, Pú,
were all surrounding prefectures of Dàliáng,
by saying this,

Ōuyáng Xiū said: According to Tang (Táng) dynasty precedent, the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) would appear daily in the main hall (diàn) to see his ministers,
which was called "regular court attendance" (cháng-cān).
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month (shuò-wàng), when offering food to the imperial ancestral tombs (líng-qǐn),
out of a spirit of remembrance and longing,
if he could not preside in the front hall,
then he would hold court in the private hall (biàn-diàn) to see his ministers,
which was called "entering the inner hall" (rù-gé).
Xuānzhèng Diàn
was the front hall,
called the "yamen" (yámén),
and the yamen had guards (zhàng).
Zǐchén Diàn
was the private hall,
called the "gé" (gé).
When he did not preside in the front hall but in Zǐchén Diàn,
he would summon the guards from the main yamen to enter through the gé-gate,
and the hundred officials who were waiting for the morning court in the yamen
would then follow him in to have an audience;
therefore, it was called "entering the inner hall" (rù-gé).
However, the yamen
was for the morning court (cháo),
and its ceremony was highly esteemed;
the gé
was for informal audiences (yàn-jiàn),
and its formalities were reduced.
After the Qiánfú (Qiánfú) era,
due to disorder and a breakdown of rites,
the Son of Heaven could not see his ministers daily but only on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month,
thus the main yamen usually had no guards on ordinary days,
but on the first and fifteenth days, when entering the inner hall, there were guards.
Afterwards, this became customary,
and "entering the inner hall" (rù-gé) was regarded as important,
to the extent that even when he presided in the front hall,
it was still called "entering the inner hall" (rù-gé).
During the Five Dynasties (Wǔdài) period,
ministers had an audience in Zhōngxīng Diàn every five days,
which was a private hall;
this was a remnant of the "entering the inner hall" (rù-gé) system,
but it was called "daily attendance" (qǐ-jū).
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, he would preside in Wénmíng Diàn,
which was the front hall,
but it was ironically called "entering the inner hall" (rù-gé).
Now, according to the *Wǔdài Huìyào* (Wǔdài Huìyào), there was a "ritual for entering the inner hall" (Rùgé Yí): the Directorate of Astronomy (Sītiān) presented the hour-and-quarter tablet (kè-pái),
the Directorate of Palace Gates (Gémén) presented the "ranks aligned" tablet (bān-qí-pái),
the Emperor (Huángdì) emerged from the inner chambers wearing a robe and boots,
rode in a palanquin (niǎn) to the gate of the regular court hall (Chángcháo Diàn) where the palanquin stopped,
received the daily attendance (qǐ-jū) of the Commissioners of Military Affairs (Shūmì Shǐ) and others,
and was then led to the main court hall (Zhèngcháo Diàn).
After the Emperor was seated,
the screens were rolled up,
incense was added in the hall,
and a cry of
"Kònghè Guān bow!" was heard,
followed by the rooster's crow,
then the Gémén verified the credentials (kàn-qì),
then the Gémén Chéngzhǐ summoned the guards (huàn-zhàng),
then the Gémén Shǐ led the Jīnwǔ Jiāngjūn (Jīnwǔ Jiāngjūn) of the southern ranks to bow, after which they were separately led to their positions to exchange bows,
then the smaller guards (xì-zhàng) entered in succession,
then those holding the civil and military rank registers (wén-wǔ-bān-bù) came to their positions to exchange bows,
then the Prime Ministers (Zǎichén) of the southern ranks bowed, after which they were separately led to their positions to exchange bows,
then the Jīnwǔ Jiāngjūn reported
"Peace!" (Píng'ān),
then the civil and military officials entered.
The Messenger-in-Waiting (Tōngshì Shèrén) bowed towards the hall,
entered the sand-paved courtyard (shā-chí) wearing his boots,
bowed twice and stood still,

the Gémén Shǐ cried
"Bow!" (Bài!),
they inserted their tablets into their belts and danced,
bowed three times,

"Ten thousand blessings to Your Sacred Majesty!" (Shènggōng wànfú!);
then the Gémén Shǐ led one of the chief Prime Ministers to come forward,

danced,
knelt,
bowed three times,
and was led back to his position to exchange bows.
The Tōngshì Shèrén led the Prime Ministers to stand at the bottom of the eastern and western steps,

then those holding the civil and military rank registers of the southern ranks bowed towards the hall and exited,
then the Jīnwǔ Jiāngjūn of the southern ranks bowed towards the hall and exited,

then the Prime Ministers were led to the incense table to report their affairs, after which
the Director of the Palace Secretariat (Xuānhuī Shǐ) cried

and the southern ranks bowed towards the hall and exited;
then the Gémén Shǐ led the Attendant-in-Waiting (Dàizhì Guān) to his position to bow twice,
led him forward to report his affairs, after which
he returned to his position and bowed deeply,
the Xuānhuī Shǐ announced
"What was reported is known!" (Suǒzòu zhī!),
then he bowed twice,
danced,
knelt,
bowed three times,
the Shèrén cried
"Farewell!" (Hǎoqù!),
and the southern ranks bowed towards the hall and exited;

then the Gémén Chéngzhǐ dismissed the guards (fàng-zhàng),
then the Gémén Shǐ reported that there was nothing further in the yamen,
then a cry of
"Kònghè Guān await outside the gate!" was heard,
then the screens were lowered,
and the Emperor ascended his palanquin and returned to the inner chambers.
Furthermore, according to Ōu Shǐ: In the 9th month of the 1st year of Gānhuà (Gānhuà) of Liáng Tàizǔ (Liáng Tàizǔ), on the *xīn-sì* day,

Thus, the "entering the inner hall" (rù-gé) ceremony was established by the Liáng dynasty.
Compared to the Tang's (Táng) main yamen court assembly (zhèng-yá cháo-huì),
its ceremony was simplified and less formal,
yet the Five Dynasties (Wǔdài) called it "performing the rites" (xíng-lǐ).
The *Huìyào* (Huìyào) recorded it in detail and compiled it into a book,
which means that its ceremony was the most important one of that time.
I shall record it here for reference,
to mark the changes in court ceremonies.

Héng 恆,
read Hù Dēng 戶登.
Fearing the loss of major support,

At that time, the Khitan generals had already secretly deliberated and enthroned Wùyù as their lord.

stating that the provisions for Wùyù would be the same as for the other generals.
Wùyù resented this.
Wùyù personally controlled all the keys to the gates of Héngzhōu and the treasury's ingress and egress.
Wùyù himself managed all of it.
Yánshòu sent someone to request them,
but they were not given.
That Wùyù did not give the keys to the gates
made the situation clear.
Zhào Yánshòu, however, knew nothing of the secret preparations against him,

When the Khitan Emperor's funeral procession arrived at the capital,

leading to exhaustion,
and the unrest among the tribes.
Emperor Shǐ's return from Shòuyáng was
seen in the second month of the previous year.
The garrison soldiers, hearing that the Khitans had returned north,

The Khitans attacked them,
and the garrison soldiers panicked and dispersed.
The Khitans burned their cities and towns,
with over a hundred wolf-smoke signals raised in a single day.
Lù Diàn's Píyǎ says: "Ancient beacon fires used wolf dung,
because its smoke rises straight and dense,
and does not skew even when blown by the wind."
I say, how can today's beacons
all necessarily use wolf dung?
"These barbarians are about to flee;
they are creating a false impression."
He dispatched his trusted general Yè Rénlǔ with three thousand infantry and cavalry to respond.

On the day Dīngchǒu,
he recaptured Chéngtiān Jūn.

and nominated the commander of the fortified city, Zhāng Tínghàn, to govern the prefecture.
Tínghàn was
a native of Jìzhōu,
and the nephew of Fú Xí.
Fú Xí was
a general of Chéngdé,
who served Emperor Zhuāngzōng and Emperor Míngzōng of the Later Táng dynasty.
Someone persuaded Zhào Yánshòu, saying:

Yánshòu hesitated, unable to decide.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Yánshòu issued an order,
stating that on the first day of the coming month, he would perform a ceremony at the Dàixián Guǎn.
"Shàngshì" meant
he wished to ritually ascend to the position of provisional manager of the military and state affairs of the Southern Court.
"Shàng"
is pronounced as "shàng."

while Jìedùshǐ and those below them would bow below the steps.
Lǐ Sōng, believing that the intentions of the barbarians were different
