Leaving the civilian and military officials behind and taking palace women, eunuchs, and musicians with him,
the historian commented that Wùyù lacked foresight.
On Yǐ Sì
he departed Zhēndìng.
Hénzhōu established Zhēndìng Fǔ.
12When the emperor ascended the throne,
Lǐ Cónglǎng, Jiàngzhōu Cìshǐ, along with Qìdān general Chéng Bàqīng and others, defied the order
and had not yet surrendered.
Chéng
is a surname.
Hé Shì Xìng Yuàn:
originally descended from Chéng Bó, son of King Wén of Zhōu.
There was Chéng Sùgōng in Zhōu.
Also,
Zǐ Yù, Lìngyǐn of Chǔ, was enfeoffed in Chéng,
becoming Chéng Déchén;
his descendants also took Chéng as their surname.
The city had not fallen.
Hùguójūn, Hézhōng Fǔ;
at that time, Hézhōng had not been captured,
Bái Wénkē held the governorship.
Kē,
(qiū hé fān).
He commanded the various armies to spread out but not attack,
and explain the advantages and disadvantages to them.
On Wù Shēn,
Lǐ Cónglǎng surrendered the city.
The emperor commanded his personal generals to guard the gates,
and no soldier was allowed to enter.
Fearing they would enter the city and plunder.
13On Xīn Hài,
the emperor arrived in Shǎnzhōu,
and Zhào Huī personally led the emperor's horse into the city.
On Rén Zǐ,
he arrived at Shíháo.
Jiǔ Yù Zhì: Shíháo Zhèn is in Shǎn Xiàn, Shǎnzhōu.
People from Biàn came across Zhèng and Luò to welcome him.
This shows how they suffered from Qìdān's oppressive rule
and longed for the Hàn dynasty's revival,
though regrettably their hopes were ultimately unfulfilled!
14th day of the 6th month.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Xiāo Hàn (蕭翰) arrived at Héngzhōu (恆州),
and with Mádá (麻荅), surrounded Zhāng Lì's (張礪) residence with iron cavalry.
Lì (礪) was sick in bed at the time.
He went out to meet them,
and Hàn (翰) accused him, saying:
"Why did you tell the late emperor
that 'Hu (胡) people cannot be *jiédùshǐ* (節度使)'?
Zhāng Lì (張礪) said,
refer to volume 285, year Kaiyun (開運) 3, during the reign of Prince Qí (齊王) of Jìn (晉).
The character *shù* (數) [means]
all that is provided.
I am the *Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ* (宣武節度使),
and also the Empress's maternal uncle;
yet you, in the Central Secretariat, dared to disregard me!
Furthermore,
the late emperor left me to guard Biànzhōu (汴州)
refer to the previous volume, 3rd month of this year.
You deemed it inappropriate.
Moreover,
you slandered me and Jiělǐ (解里) to the late emperor,
saying that Jiělǐ (解里) liked to plunder people's property,
and I liked to abduct people's sons and daughters.
Today, I will surely kill you!"
He ordered him to be chained.
Lì (礪) retorted, raising his voice:
"These are all matters of great importance to the state;
I spoke the truth.
If you want to kill, then kill;
why bother chaining me!"
Mádá (麻荅), arguing that a high minister should not be executed without proper authority,
strenuously intervened to stop him,
and Hàn (翰) then released him.
That evening,
Lì (礪) died of indignation and rage.
Cuī Tíngxūn (崔廷勳) met Mádá (麻荅),
hurrying and bowing.
Rising,
he knelt and offered wine,
which Mádá (麻荅) received while sitting cross-legged.
The historian says that Zhāng Lì (張礪) was upright and defiant, and Xiāo Hàn (蕭翰) dared not kill him;
Cuī Tíngxūn (崔廷勳) was excessively obsequious, and Mádá (麻荅) did not show him proper respect.
15th day. On the *yǐmǎo* day,
the Emperor arrived at Xīn'ān (新安).
Xīn'ān (新安) County belongs to Xījīng Hénán Fǔ (西京河南府).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: it is seventy *lǐ* (里) west of the capital.
16th day. Wúyuè Zhōngxiàn Wáng Hóngzuǒ (吳越忠獻王弘佐) died.
He was twenty years old.
17th day. On the *bǐngchén* day,
the Emperor arrived at Luòyáng (洛陽)
and took up residence in the palace.
Officials from Biànzhōu (汴州) came bearing memorials to welcome him.
An imperial edict was issued, instructing that those who had received appointments from the Qìdān (契丹) should not doubt themselves;
their appointment documents were gathered and burned.
Zhào Yuǎn (趙遠) changed his name to Shàngjiāo (上交).
To avoid the Emperor's name.
*Gēng* (更) [is pronounced]
*gōnghéng* (工衡).
The Emperor ordered Guō Cóngyì (郭從義), the Defense Commissioner of Zhèngzhōu (鄭州), to first enter Dàliáng (大梁) to clear the palace,
and secretly commanded him to kill Lǐ Cóngyì (李從益) and Wáng Shū (王淑).
Shū (淑), nearing death,
said:
"My son was enthroned by the Qìdān (契丹);
what crime has he committed to die!
Why not spare him,
so that every year on Hánshí (寒食),
he might sprinkle a bowl of wheat gruel before Míngzōng's (明宗) tomb!"
The *Wǔdài Huìyào* (五代會要) says: the way for a ruler to honor ancestors
does not include Hánshí (寒食) outdoor sacrifices.
In recent times, Zhuāngzōng (莊宗) offered sacrifices outdoors every Hánshí (寒食),
which was called 'scattered' or 'broken' (*pòsàn* 破散),
thus it was habitually practiced.
Ōuyáng Xiū (歐陽修) said: with Hánshí (寒食) outdoor sacrifices and burning paper money,
how far is China from becoming barbarian!
According to the *Kāiyuán Chí* (開元敕) of the Táng (唐) dynasty:
"Visiting graves on Hánshí (寒食) is not mentioned in the ritual classics.
In recent generations, it has been passed down
and gradually become a custom.
It is appropriate to permit grave visits with sweeping rites."
This means the Táng (唐) permitted commoners to do so,
but there was no such rite for rulers.
For the founder of Hàn (漢),
treating Lǐ Cóngyì (李從益) by not killing him would have been acceptable;
killing him was excessive.
18th day. On the *wùwǔ* day,
the Emperor departed Luòyáng (洛陽).
Wèi Rénpǔ (魏仁浦), an official of the Bureau of Military Affairs, escaped from the Qìdān (契丹)
and returned, meeting the Emperor at Gǒng (鞏).
Guō Wēi (郭威) questioned him about troop numbers and past events;
Rénpǔ (仁浦) had an excellent memory and was quick-witted,
and Wēi (威) thenceforth trusted and employed him closely.
Rénpǔ (仁pǔ) was
from Wèizhōu (衞州).
19th day. On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Dòu Zhēngù (竇貞固) and other officials from Biànzhōu (汴zhou) welcomed him at Xíngyáng (滎陽).
Xíngyáng (滎陽) County belongs to Zhèngzhōu (鄭州);
it is one hundred ninety *lǐ* (里) east of Gǒng (鞏) County.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the Emperor arrived at Dàliáng (大梁).
The vassal states of Jìn (晉) successively came to surrender.
20th day. On the *bǐngyín* day,
Wúyuè Wáng Hóngzōng (吳越王弘倧) succeeded to the throne.
21st day. On the *wùchén* day,
the Emperor issued an edict granting a general amnesty.
All *jiédùshǐ* (節度使) appointed by the Qìdān (契丹),
down to their generals and officials,
were to remain in their respective posts,
without any changes.
Biànzhōu (汴州) was restored as Dōngjīng (東京)
the Qìdān (契丹) had abolished Dōngjīng (東京) and made it Biànzhōu (汴州),
see previous volume, 1st month of this year.
The Tiānfú (天福) era name was retained,
saying:
"I cannot bear to forget Jìn (晉)."
The three *jiédù* (節度) of Qīng (青), Xiāng (襄), and Rǔ (汝) were restored.
Jìn (晉) had abolished the Pínglú Jūn (平盧軍) due to Yáng Guāngyuǎn's (楊光遠) rebellion,
and the Shānnán Dōngdào (山南東道) due to Ān Cóngjìn's (安從進) rebellion.
Rǔzhōu (汝州) was never a *jiézhèn* (節鎮);
it is probably Ānzhōu (安州),
where the Ānyuǎn Jūn (安遠軍) was abolished due to Lǐ Jīnquán's (李金全) rebellion.
However, after the Qìdān (契丹) entered Biàn (汴),
they once appointed Yáng Guāngyuǎn's (楊光yuǎn) son, Chéngxìn (承信), as Pínglú Jiédùshǐ (平盧節度使).
Thus, the Hàn (漢), considering itself a successor to Jìn (晉) and having risen,
reformed the Qìdān's (契丹) administration,
not regarding it as an established decree.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Chóng (崇), the garrison commander of Běijīng (北京), was appointed Hédōng Jiédùshǐ (河東節度使)
and *Tóng Píngzhāngshì* (同平章事).
22nd day. Qìdān (契丹) Empress Dowager Shùlǜ (述律) heard that the Qìdān (契丹) ruler had enthroned himself
and was greatly enraged,
dispatching troops to resist him.
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler made Wěi Wáng (偉王) the vanguard,
and they met at Shíqiáo (石橋).
Hú Qiáo's (胡嶠) *Rùliáo Lù* (入遼錄) states: Wùyù (兀欲) and Shùlǜ (述律) battled at Shāhé Shíqiáo (沙河石橋).
It was thus the bridge of Shāhé (沙河).
To the south was Yáojiāzhōu (姚家洲),
and to the north, from Xuānhuà Guǎn (宣化館) to Xīlóu (西樓).
Lǐ Yàntāo (李彥韜), the Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry of Jìn (晉), had accompanied the Jìn (晉) ruler north
see previous volume, 1st month of this year.
The Empress Dowager made him the 排陳使 (*páichénshǐ*, commander of array formation).
Yàntāo (彥韜) surrendered to Wěi Wáng (偉王),
and the Empress Dowager's army was consequently greatly defeated.
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler imprisoned the Empress Dowager at Ābǎojī's (阿保機) tomb.
Hú Qiáo's (胡嶠) *Rùliáo Lù* (入遼錄) states: Wùyù (兀欲) imprisoned Empress Shùlǜ (述律) at Pūmǎ Shān (撲馬山),
and after traveling for three more days,
finally reached Xīlóu (西樓).
Ōu Shǐ (歐史) states: The Qìdān (契丹) established Zǔzhōu (祖州) at Ābǎojī's (阿保機) tomb.
Xiongnú Xūzhī (匈奴須知) states: Zǔzhōu (祖州) is fifty *lǐ* (里) east of Shàngjīng (上京);
Shàngjīng (上京) is Xīlóu (西樓).
Now both are recorded.
Regarding the similarities and differences of place names,
and the distances between places,
one must personally travel there to ascertain their accuracy.
He proclaimed himself Tiānshòu Huángdì (天授皇帝)
and appointed Gāo Xūn (高勳) as *Púmìshǐ* (樞密使).
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler admired Chinese customs
and used many Jìn (晉) officials,
but was dissolute in wine and women,
and treated his chieftains with disdain.
Consequently, his people did not support him,
and various tribes frequently rebelled.
He raised armies to suppress them,
thus for several years,
he had no time to raid the south.
The historian says that China, after experiencing chaos and turmoil,
was thereby able to achieve some peace and stability.
23rd day. Initially,
Qìdān (契丹) ruler Déguāng (德光) ordered Nángōng Wáng Jìhóng (南宮王繼弘), the Commander of Fèngguó (奉國)
Nángōng (南宮) County belongs to Jìzhōu (冀州).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: it is sixty-two *lǐ* (里) southwest of the prefecture.
and Zhāngdé Jiédùshǐ (彰德節度使) Gāo Tángyīng (高唐英) treated him well.
Gāo Tángyīng (高唐英) was appointed by the Qìdān (契丹),
see previous volume, 4th month of this year.
*Xiàng* (相) [is pronounced]
*xìliàng* (息亮).
Tángyīng (唐英) provided him with armor and weapons,
trusting him as a close relative.
When Tángyīng (唐英) heard that the Emperor was advancing south,
the entire garrison requested to surrender.
Before the envoy returned,
Jìhóng (繼弘) and Huī (暉) killed Tángyīng (唐英).
Jìhóng (繼弘) declared himself acting commander (*liúhòu*)
and sent an envoy to report that Tángyīng (唐英) was treacherous.
An edict appointed Jìhóng (繼弘) as the acting commander of Zhāngdé (彰德).
On the *gēngchén* day,
Huī (暉) was appointed Governor (*cìshǐ*) of Cízhōu (磁州).
When Gāo Fèngmíng (高奉明), the Ānguó Jiédùshǐ (安國節度使), heard of Tángyīng's (唐英) death,
he felt uneasy.
He requested Mádá (麻荅) to appoint Liú Duó (劉鐸), the Commander of Infantry and Cavalry, as Deputy *Jiédùshǐ* (節度使)
to manage the military affairs,
and he himself returned to Héngzhōu (恆州).
Since Xíng (邢) and Xiāng (相) could not be held,
how could Héngzhōu (恆州) stand alone!
This set the stage for the generals to drive away Mádá (麻荅).
24 Dì sent envoys to issue a proclamation to Jīngnán.
Gāo Cónghuì submitted a memorial to offer congratulations,
and also requested Yǐngzhōu.
Dì did not grant it.
When the envoy bearing special favors arrived,
he refused to accept them.
Since the Táng dynasty,
when a new ruler ascended the throne,
envoys would be dispatched to bestow special favors upon the various garrisons.
使,
shū lì fān.
25 Táng Zhǔ heard that Qìdān Zhǔ Déguāng had died,
and that Xiāo Hàn had abandoned Dàliáng and left.
He issued an edict which stated:
"I look upon the Central Plains,
the ancestral land of Our dynasty."
Táng Zhǔ claimed descent from Wú Wáng Kè,
hence he spoke thus.
朝,
zhí yáo fān.
Jīn Quán was made the Commander of the Northern Campaign.
Lǐ Jīnquán
was a Jìn general
who defected to Táng; see volume 282, Jìn Gāozǔ Tiānfú fifth year.
Upon hearing that Dì had already entered Dàliáng,
he thereupon dared not send out troops.
26 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Jiǎwǔ,
Mǎ Xīguǎng was appointed Tiāncè Shàngjiāngjūn, Wǔ'ān Jiédùshǐ, Jiāngnán Zhūdào Dūyǒng,
concurrently Zhōngshūlìng,
and enfeoffed as Chǔ Wáng.
On the occasion of his enthronement and the bestowal of special favors,
Mǎ Xīguǎng was accordingly granted his father and elder brother's official titles and ranks.
27 It was rumored that Zhào Yánshòu had died.
Guō Wēi said to Dì:
"Zhào Kuāngzàn
was appointed by Qìdān,
as seen in the previous volume, first month of this year.
It is appropriate to send an envoy to offer condolences,
and then to reinstate him and transfer his command.
Since he has no home or country to return to,
his father died among the barbarians,
so he has no home to return to;
Qìdān has gone north,
so he has no country to return to."
He was followed.
At this time, Yèdū Liúshǒu, Tiānxiong Jiédùshǐ concurrently Zhōngshūlìng Dù Chóngwēi, and Tiānpíng Jiédùshǐ concurrently Shìzhōng Lǐ Shǒuzhēn all submitted memorials pledging allegiance.
Chóngwēi furthermore requested to be transferred to another command.
Guīdé Jiédùshǐ concurrently Zhōngshūlìng Gāo Xíngzhōu entered the court.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
Chóngwēi was transferred to be Guīdé Jiédùshǐ,
and Xíngzhōu was appointed in his place.
Dù Chóngwēi soon refused the transfer,
so Gāo Xíngzhōu was ordered to attack him.
He was additionally appointed concurrently Zhōngshūlìng,
setting the stage for Lǐ Shǒuzhēn to occupy Hézhōng.
Two years later,
Yánshòu finally died in Qìdān.
History proves the baselessness of the rumor.
28 Wúyuè Wáng Hóngzōng appointed his younger brother, Táizhōu Cìshǐ Hóngchù, to jointly manage affairs in the prime minister's office.
29 Lǐ Dá made his younger brother act as interim Fúzhōu Liúhòu.
Lǐ Réndá surrendered to Táng,
and Táng bestowed upon him the name Hóngyì,
enrolling him in their registers.
When he rebelled against Táng,
and was attacked by Táng,
he sought aid from Wúyuè.
As the character Hóng offended the taboo of Wúyuè,
his name was changed to Dá.
His younger brother, formerly named Hóngtōng,
was also simply named Tōng.
Hóngzōng, by imperial prerogative, additionally appointed Dá as concurrently Shìzhōng,
and further changed his name to Rúyūn.
Soon after, Rúyūn felt regret and fear;
regret for coming,
and also fear of death.
He requested to return to Fúzhōu.
Jìn Sī pleaded on his behalf,
and Hóngzōng agreed.
30 Dù Chóngwēi considered himself to have allied with Qìdān
and wronged Zhōngguó,
as seen in volume 285, Jìn Qí Wáng Kāiyùn third year.
When the edict for his transfer of command was issued,
he again refused to accept it.
He sent his son Hóngsuì as a hostage to Mádá to seek assistance.
Zhào Yánshòu had two thousand of his personal guards from Yōuzhōu in Héngzhōu.
Zhào Yánshòu was captured and taken north by Qìdān Zhǔ Wùyù,
but his personal guards remained in Héngzhōu.
恆,
hù dēng fān.
Chóngwēi requested to use them to defend Wèi,
setting the stage for Zhāng Lián to assist Dù Chóngwēi in a strong defense.
將,
jí liàng fān.
In the intercalary month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
an edict was issued to strip Chóngwēi of his official titles and ranks,
and Gāo Xíngzhōu was appointed Commander of the Campaign,
with Zhènníng Jiédùshǐ Mùróng Yànchāo as his deputy,
to suppress Chóngwēi.
This sets the stage for Mùróng Yànchāo to use his influence to bully Gāo Xíngzhōu, and for discord among the generals.
31 On the day Xīnwèi,
Yáng Bīn, Guō Wēi, and Wáng Zhāng were all made principal envoys.
Dì ascended the throne in Tàiyuán,
appointing Yáng Bīn as acting Shūmìshǐ,
Guō Wēi as acting Shūmì Fùshǐ,
and Wáng Zhāng as acting Sānsīshǐ.
Now they were all made principal envoys.
Both public and private resources were exhausted.
The northern army and the court army combined,
more than doubling in size.
"Northern army"
refers to those who came from Tàiyuán with Dì and Shǐ Hóngzhào.
"Court army"
refers to the former Jìn court army.
Unnecessary expenses were cut to support the military,
and expenditures were sufficient.
32 On the day Gēngchén,
an edict was issued to establish ancestral temples.
Tàizǔ Gāo Huángdì and
Shìzǔ Guāngwǔ Huángdì
were to be honored for a hundred generations without relocation.
Four ancestral temples were also established,
and posthumous titles were bestowed.
Wǔdài Huìyào: Posthumously honored Gāozǔ Tuānmíng Yuán Huángdì,
with temple name Wénzǔ;
Zengzǔ Áng Gōngxī Huángdì,
with temple name Dézǔ;
Zǔ Zhuàn Zhāoxiàn Huángdì,
with temple name Yìzǔ;
Kǎo Diǎn Zhāngshèng Huángdì,
with temple name Xiǎnzǔ.
33 Mádá was greedy, cunning, cruel, and merciless.
If there were precious goods or beautiful women among the people,
he would certainly seize them.
He also captured villagers,
falsely accusing them of being bandits,
disfigured their faces,
gouged out their eyes,
severed their wrists,
and burned them to death,
hoping to intimidate the populace.
He always carried his tools with him.
"Tools"
refers to the tools for disfiguring faces, gouging eyes, severing wrists, and burning.
He hung human livers, gallbladders, hands, and feet,
and ate, drank, and lived among them,
conversing and laughing naturally.
When going in and out, he sometimes wore yellow clothes,
used imperial carriages,
and imperial attire and objects,
saying:
"These things the Hàn people consider unacceptable,
but in our country, there are no taboos."
Also, deeming the number of prime ministers insufficient,
he issued a document appointing Féng Dào to oversee the Hóngwénguǎn,
Lǐ Sōng to oversee the Shǐguǎn,
Hé Níng to oversee the Jíxián,
and Liú Xù to oversee the Zhōngshū.
His usurpation and extravagance were thus.
The division of responsibilities among prime ministers
required imperial edicts,
but Mádá carried it out with a mere document.
The historian speaks of his usurpation and extravagance.
He tolerated no one,
so the markets were undisturbed.
He often feared that Hàn people might presumptuously
leave.
He said to the gatekeepers:
"If any Hàn person is seen peeking out the gate,
immediately cut off their head and bring it to me."
Mádá sent an envoy to supervise transportation in Míngzhōu.
Míngzhōu Fángyùshǐ Xuē Huáiràng, upon hearing that Dì had entered Dàliáng,
killed the envoy
and surrendered the entire prefecture.
Dì sent Guō Cóngyì with ten thousand troops to join Huáiràng in attacking Liú Duó in Xíngzhōu,
but they did not succeed.
Liú Duó was defending for Qìdān.
Jiǔyù Zhì: From Míngzhōu northwest to Xíngzhōu is ninety *lǐ*.
Mádá sent his general Yáng Ān and former Yìwǔ Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Yīn with a thousand cavalry to attack Huáiràng in Míngzhōu.
Huáiràng defended the city,
and Ān and others let their troops plunder extensively in the border region of Xíng and Míng.
The Qìdān (契丹) troops left behind numbered less than two thousand,
referring to the troops stationed in Héngzhōu (恆州).
They gathered the rest and entered themselves.
Má Dá (麻荅) was always suspicious of the Hàn (漢) soldiers,
and moreover considered them useless.
He gradually reduced and dismissed them,
and also cut their rations to feed the Hú (胡) soldiers;
the hearts of the multitude were resentful.
Hearing that the Emperor had entered Dàliáng (大梁),
they all harbored thoughts of returning south.
The former Prefect of Yǐngzhōu (潁州), Hé Fúyùn (何福進),
and the Kònghè (控鶴) Commander, Lǐ Róng (李榮) of Tàiyuán (太原),
secretly allied with dozens of brave men in the army to plan an attack on the Qìdān (契丹).
However, fearing the Qìdān (契丹) were still strong,
they hesitated and did not act.
Just then, Yáng Gǔn (楊袞) and Yáng Ān (楊安)'s armies marched out.
Yáng Gǔn (楊袞) headed for Wèizhōu (魏州),
and Yáng Ān (楊安) attacked Míngzhōu (洺州).
Fúyùn (福進) and the others then made up their minds,
agreeing to use the striking of the Buddhist temple bell as their signal.
They agreed that when the Hàn (漢) soldiers heard the Buddhist temple bell strike,
they would all sally forth and attack the Qìdān (契丹).
However, the Buddhist temple bell struck at dawn and dusk,
and also at mealtimes,
every day;
so this must mean they had made a prior agreement before the event,
that upon hearing the Buddhist temple bell at the next day's mealtime, they would all act.
On the Xīnsì (辛巳) day,
the Qìdān (契丹) ruler Wùyù (兀欲) sent cavalry to Héngzhōu (恆州),
summoning the former Wēishèng Jiédùshǐ (威勝節度使) and concurrently Zhōngshūlìng (中書令) Féng Dào (馮道), Pīmìshǐ (樞密使) Lǐ Sōng (李崧), and Zuǒpúyè (左僕射) Hé Níng (和凝) and others,
to attend the funeral of the Qìdān (契丹) ruler Déguāng (德光) at Mùyèshān (木葉山).
Before Dào (道) and the others departed,
at mealtime,
the bell sounded.
The Hàn (漢) soldiers seized weapons from the Qìdān (契丹) gatekeepers and attacked the Qìdān (契丹),
killing over ten people,
then rushed into the prefectural office.
Lǐ Róng (李榮) first seized the armory,
summoned all the Hàn (漢) soldiers and market people,
armed them with armor and weapons,
burned the Yámén (牙門) gate,
and fought with the Qìdān (契丹).
Róng (榮) summoned the generals to unite their strength.
Bái Zàiróng (白再榮), the Hùshèng Zuǒxiāng Dōuzhǐhuīshǐ (護聖左廂都指揮使) and Ēnzhōu Tuánliànshǐ (恩州團練使),
(Ēnzhōu (恩州) at this time belonged to the territory of the Southern Hàn (南漢);
Bái Zàiróng (白再榮) held a nominal command.)
hid in another room.
A military officer used his saber to cut through the curtain,
and pulled his arm.
Bái Zàiróng (白再榮) covered himself with the curtain,
but the officer cut the curtain and pulled him out.
The generals arrived one after another;
smoke and fire rose everywhere,
and drumbeats and shouts shook the ground.
Má Dá (麻荅) and others were greatly alarmed.
They loaded their treasures and family,
and fled to secure the northern city wall.
However, the Hàn (漢) soldiers lacked unified command,
and the greedy and cunning plundered amidst the chaos,
while the timid hid.
In the eighth month,
on the Rénwǔ (壬午) day, the first day of the month,
the Qìdān (契丹) entered from the North Gate.
(This was the North Gate of the Yáchéng (牙城) in Héngzhōu (恆州).)
Over two thousand Hàn (漢) people died.
The former Prefect of Cízhōu (磁州), Lǐ Gǔ (李穀), fearing the affair would not succeed,
invited Féng Dào (馮道), Lǐ Sōng (李崧), and Hé Níng (和凝) to the battlefield to encourage the soldiers.
When the soldiers saw Dào (道) and the others arrive,
they vied to exert themselves.
But for Lǐ Gǔ (李穀)'s plan,
the Hàn (漢) army would have been in peril.
Several thousand villagers shouted outside the city,
wanting to seize the Qìdān (契ān) treasures and women.
The Qìdān (契丹) were frightened and fled north.
Má Dá (麻荅), Liú Xī (劉晞), and Cuī Tíngxūn (崔廷勳) all fled to Dìngzhōu (定州).
(Héngzhōu (恆州) is 120 *lǐ* (里) northeast to Dìngzhōu (定州).)
Zhōng (忠),
was Láng Wǔ (郎五).
Láng Wǔ (郎五) was initially stationed at Chánzhōu (澶州) but there was a military rebellion,
so the Qìdān (契丹) then made him commander of Dìngzhōu (定州).
Féng Dào (馮道) and the others went out to pacify the soldiers and civilians.
The multitude acclaimed Dào (道) as Jiédùshǐ (節度使).
Dào (道) said:
"I am but a scholar.
I should only report on affairs.
It is proper to select one of the generals to be Liúhòu (留後)."
At that time, Lǐ Róng (李榮) had the most merit.
(Lǐ Róng (李榮) had first seized the armory,
armed the soldiers, and fought with the Qìdān (契丹);
all the other generals followed him,
hence he was considered to have the most merit.)
Thus, Zàiróng (再榮) was provisionally appointed Liúhòu (留後),
and a detailed report was sent to the court,
also requesting reinforcements.
The Emperor sent the Zuǒ Fēilóng Shǐ (左飛龍使) Lǐ Yàncóng (李彥從) to lead troops to them.
(The Táng (唐) had Fēilóng Shǐ (飛龍使) and Xiǎomǎfáng Shǐ (小馬坊使);
the Liáng (梁) changed Xiǎomǎfáng (小馬坊) to Tiānjì (天驥),
the Later Táng (後唐) restored the old name;
in the first year of Chángxīng (長興),
Fēilóngyuàn (飛龍院) was changed to Zuǒ Fēilóngyuàn (左飛龍院),
and Xiǎomǎfáng (小馬坊) to Yòu Fēilóngyuàn (右飛龍院);
in the third year of Tàipíng Xīngguó (太平興國) of the Sòng (宋),
Zuǒ Yòu Tiān Jì Fāng (左、右天驥坊) was changed;
in the second year of Yōngxī (雍熙),
it was again changed to Zuǒ Yòu Qíjì Yuàn Shǐ (左、右騏驥院使).)
Bái Zàiróng (白再榮) was greedy and ignorant,
and suspicious of the generals.
Fèngguó Jūn (奉國軍)
Commander Wáng Ráo (王饒) of Huáchí (華池)
(After the Jìn (晉) moved south,
there was conflict between northern and southern armies,
and each established officials like Jūnzhǔ (軍主) and Duìzhǔ (隊主);
there was no such system after the Suí (隋) and Táng (唐).
In this book,
"Fèngguó Jūnzhǔ" (奉國軍主)
in the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn (資治通鑑) is probably adopted from old histories,
meaning merely a military commander,
not an official title.
Huáchí (華池) County in Qìngzhōu (慶州) was established by the Suí (隋);
during the Xīníng (熙寧) reign of the Sòng (宋),
Huáchí (華池) County was abolished and made into a fort town,
belonging to Héshuǐ (合水) County,
its location being southeast of Qìngzhōu (慶州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Huáchí (華池) was originally the land of Guīdé (歸德) County of the Hàn (漢),
which is Luòyuán (洛源) County.
In the second year of Rénshòu (仁壽) of the Suí (隋),
Huáchí (華池) County was also established at the old city of Kùduōhàn (庫多汗), two *lǐ* (里) northeast of the present county,
there is Huáchí (華池) water to the south,
hence the name.)
falsely claimed a foot ailment,
occupied the East Gate tower,
and heavily guarded himself.
The Sītiānjiān (司天監) Zhào Yán'ài (趙延乂), who was well-acquainted with both men,
went back and forth to explain and persuade,
and they finally reconciled.
Zàiróng (再榮), knowing that Lǐ Sōng (李崧) and Hé Níng (和凝) had long been chancellors,
and were wealthy,
(when Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖) entered Luò (洛),
Lǐ Sōng (李崧) was immediately appointed chancellor;
in the fifth year of Tiānfú (天福),
Hé Níng (和凝) became chancellor.)
Sōng (崧) and Níng (凝) each gave him their family wealth.
He also wanted to kill Sōng (崧) and Níng (凝) to silence them.
Lǐ Gǔ (李穀) went to see Zàiróng (再榮),
and reproached him, saying:
"The state has fallen, and the ruler disgraced,
yet you and your like, holding military power, did not come to rescue.
Now you have barely managed to drive away one barbarian general,
(the barbarian general
refers to Má Dá (麻荅).)
nearly three thousand townspeople have died,
(Héng (恆) was formerly Zhènzhōu (鎮州).)
You have only just escaped death,
and you immediately wish to kill the chancellors?
If the new Emperor questions you for the crime of unauthorized killing,
what will you say in response?"
Zàiróng (再榮) was frightened and stopped.
He also wanted to levy civilian wealth to supply the army;
Gǔ (穀) strongly argued against it,
and he stopped.
Zàiróng (再榮) detained all Hàn (漢) people who had served Má Dá (麻荅) to seize their wealth.
The people of Héng (恆) called him
"Bái Má Dá" (白麻荅)
because of his greed and cruelty.
(This means his greed and cruelty were like Má Dá (麻荅)'s,
only his surname was Bái (白).)
However, Zàiróng (再榮), by accumulating wealth through greed and cruelty,
eventually lost his life due to his great wealth when Guō Wēi (郭威) entered Biàn (汴).
The retribution of Heaven,
is indeed manifest.
Yáng Gǔn (楊袞) reached Xíngzhōu (邢州),
and hearing that Má Dá (麻荅) had been driven away,
immediately returned north.
Yáng Ān (楊安) also fled.
Lǐ Yīn (李殷) came with his forces to surrender.
34 On the Gēngyín (庚寅) day,
Xuē Huáiràng (薛懷讓) was appointed Ānguó Jiédùshǐ (安國節度使).
Liú Duó (劉鐸), hearing that Má Dá (麻荅) had fled,
surrendered Xíngzhōu (邢州).
Huáiràng (懷讓) feigned being an inspector,
and led his troops towards Xíngzhōu (邢州).
Duó (鐸) opened the gate to admit him.
Huáiràng (懷讓) killed Duó (鐸),
and reported it as a recovery.
The court knew but did not question it.
35 On the Xīnmǎo (辛卯) day,
Héngzhōu (恆州) Shùnguó Jūn (順國軍) was restored to Zhènzhōu Chéngdé Jūn (鎮州成德軍).
(The change of Héngzhōu (恆州) and Shùnguó Jūn (順國軍) can be found in Volume 280, under Jìn Gāozǔ (晉高祖), Tiānfú (天福) seven years.)
36 On the *yǐwèi* day,
Bái Zàiróng was made Acting Military Governor of Chéngdé.
A year later,
Hé Fújiàn was first made Defense Commissioner of Cáozhōu,
and Lǐ Róng was made Prefect of Bózhōu.
After another year,
the achievements of the two men who had expelled Mádá were finally recognized,
and they were rewarded.
This incident is similar to the affair of Mǎ Wàn and Lú Shùnmì in the second year of Tiānfú of Jìn Gāozǔ.
37 An imperial edict declared:
"Robbers, regardless of the amount stolen, shall all be put to death."
At that time, there were many robbers throughout the land,
and the imperial court was troubled by them.
Therefore, the law was made harsher,
and envoys were dispatched to hunt them down.
Sū Féngjí personally drafted an imperial decree,
which intended to say:
"All robbers and bandits,
along with their four neighboring guarantors,
shall have their entire clan executed."
The assembly thought:
"Even a robber should not have his clan executed,
let alone his neighbors and guarantors!"
Féngjí strenuously argued,
and it was only with great difficulty that the words
"entire clan"
were omitted.
As a result, Zhāng Lìngróu, an envoy for capturing robbers, killed seventeen villagers in Píngyīn.
Liú Xù said: Píngyīn
was Hánfèizǒng County in the Hàn dynasty,
became Píngyīn County in the Suí dynasty,
and was subordinate to Jìzhōu.
In the Táng dynasty, it was subordinate to Yùnzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Píngyīn County is one hundred and twenty *lǐ* northeast of Yùnzhōu.
Xiàng Ānshì’s *Jiā Shuō* says: In ancient times there were no village names;
what we now call villages
were the *bǐyě* (rural areas) of old.
Generally, places within a state or city
were called *dū*.
*Dū*
means beautiful,
implying that its people and their attire were elegant and refined.
Any place described as beautiful was called *dū*,
such as
"Zǐ Dū,"
"Dū Rénshì,"
and "the carriages are very *dū*"
(beautiful).
Areas outside the city were called *yě* (wilderness)
or *bǐ* (rustic),
meaning they were simple, unadorned, and uncultured.
As for *bǐ*,
it is like what *Lièzǐ* called
"the rustic people of Zhèng."
Therefore, the ancient saying that beautiful means *dū*
and crude means *bǐ*
is based on this meaning.
Village names already existed in the Suí dynasty.
The Táng regulations state
that a settlement in the countryside is a village,
and a village head (*cūnzhèng*) is appointed,
thus clarifying the meaning of "village."
Féngjí was a person
who was sophisticated but fond of killing.
When he was in the Hédōng headquarters,
it was when he served as the Judicial Administrator for the Hédōng Military Governor.
Féngjí killed all the prisoners in the jails and reported it.
To "clear the jails" meant
to resolve and release the detained prisoners,
but Sū Féngjí killed them all to achieve this "clearance."
As the imperial court was newly established,
the emperor entrusted all military affairs to Yáng Bīn and Guō Wēi,
and all civil administration and sundry matters to Féngjí and Sū Yǔguī.
The two chancellors made decisions
based on their personal judgment,
without adhering to old regulations;
although matters were not delayed,
promotions, demotions, and appointments
were solely according to their wishes.
The emperor relied on and trusted them,
and no one dared to speak out.
Féngjí was especially greedy and deceitful,
openly soliciting bribes
without any scruples.
When his stepmother died,
he did not observe mourning;
when his elder half-brother arrived from outside
and met his sons without informing Féngjí,
Féngjí became angry,
secretly spoke to Guō Wēi,
and had him beaten to death on another pretext.
38 The King of Chǔ, Mǎ Xīguǎng's, illegitimate younger brother, Mǎ Xīchóng, who was the Left Sīmǎ of Tiāncè,
was cunning and treacherous.
He secretly sent a letter to his elder brother, Mǎ Xī'è,
stating that Liú Yànguī had violated the late king's command.
The "late king"
refers to Mǎ Yīn, King of Chǔ.
Mǎ Yīn's dying instructions are found in volume 277, under the first year of Chángxīng of Táng Míngzōng.
This was to provoke his anger.
Xī'è
was the elder brother;
Xīguǎng
was the younger brother.
The younger brother was enthroned instead of the elder,
hence the statement.
*Cháng*
is pronounced *zhī liǎng fān*.
*Shào*
is pronounced *shī zhào fān*.
Xī'è came from Yǒngzhōu to mourn.
Ōu Shǐ says: Xī'è came from Lǎngzhōu to mourn.
The *Tōngjiàn*, in the first month of this year, when Chǔ King Mǎ Xīfàn died,
when the generals and advisors deliberated on who to enthrone,
it also stated that Xī'è was in charge of Yǒngzhōu affairs.
However, Xī'è was the Military Governor of Wǔpíng,
and the Wǔpíng Army was stationed in Lǎngzhōu.
The text below states that Xī'è requested to return to Lǎngzhōu,
and Xīguǎng wanted to divide Tán and Lǎng to govern.
Thus, Lǎngzhōu is correct,
and the previous mention of Yǒngzhōu is a mistake.
On the *yǐsì* day,
he arrived at Fūshí.
Yànguī advised Xīguǎng to send Zhōu Tínghuì, the Attendant Commander-in-Chief, and others to lead a naval force to meet him,
ordering the officers and soldiers from Yǒngzhōu to lay down their armor before entering,
housing Xī'è in Bìxiāng Palace,
and performing the mourning rites in its annex,
not allowing him to meet Xīguǎng.
Xī'è requested to return to Lǎngzhōu,
and Zhōu Tínghuì advised Xīguǎng to kill him.
Xīguǎng said:
"How can I bear to kill my elder brother?"
Perhaps Mǎ Xīguǎng was of the same ilk as Emperor Mǐn of Later Táng!
So he generously gifted Xī'è
and sent him back to Lǎngzhōu.
Xīchóng constantly spied on Xīguǎng for Xī'è,
reporting all his words and actions,
and agreed to be an internal accomplice.
History states that Xī'è's attack on Tánzhōu
was initiated by Xīchóng.
39 When the Qìdān destroyed the Jìn,
they drove twenty thousand warhorses back to their country.
This event is found in the first month of this year in the previous volume.
An edict ordered the purchase of horses from civilians in the Hénán circuits that had not been plundered.
40 An imperial decree appointed Qián Hóngzōng as Grand Marshal of the Southeast Armies, Military Governor of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng, concurrently Grand Chancellor, and King of Wúyuè.
41 Gāo Cónghuì, hearing that Dù Chóngwēi had rebelled,
dispatched several thousand naval troops to raid Xiāngzhōu,
believing that the Hàn army was busy campaigning north against Wèizhōu and had no time to relieve the south.
He also attacked Yǐngzhōu,
where the Prefect Yǐn Shí decisively defeated him.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Jīngnán Prefecture is four hundred and forty *lǐ* north of Xiāngzhōu
and three hundred and twenty *lǐ* east of Yǐngzhōu.
It was appended to Táng and Shǔ.
Gāo Cónghuì's request for Yǐngzhōu was denied,
as seen in June above.
Initially,
Jīngnán was situated between Húnán, Língnán, and Fújiàn.
This statement specifically refers to the three circuits passing through Jīngnán to offer tribute.
Since the time of King Wǔxìn Mǎ Jìxīng,
those from various circuits who passed through his territory to offer tribute
often had their goods and money plundered.
When various states sent letters of inquiry and reproach,
or even threatened with military action,
he would reluctantly return them,
never feeling ashamed.
When Cónghuì was enthroned,
Táng, Jìn, Qìdān, and Hàn successively occupied the Central Plains.
Nánhàn, Mǐn, Wú, and Shǔ all claimed imperial titles.
Cónghuì profited from their gifts
and submitted as a vassal to whomever he faced.
The various states despised him,
calling him
"Gāo Wúlái" (Gāo the Scoundrel).
A colloquial term for one who brazenly plunders and takes things without shame or remorse is *wúlái*.
42 The Táng ruler appointed Grand Tutor and concurrently Grand Chancellor Sòng Qíqiū as Military Governor of Zhènnán.
43 The Nánhàn ruler, fearing that his younger brothers and his sons would contend for the throne,
killed Qí Wáng Hóngbì, Guì Wáng Hóngdào, Dìng Wáng Hóngyì, Biàn Wáng Hóngjì, Tóng Wáng Hóngjiǎn, Yì Wáng Hóngjiàn, Ēn Wáng Hóngwěi, and Yí Wáng Hóngzhào,
executing all their male descendants
and taking their daughters into his imperial harem.
Liú Shèng cruelly slaughtered his own kin and defiled family relations;
the tyranny of Jié and Zhòu
was not as extreme as this.
He adorned himself with pearls and jewels,
and established punishments such as boiling cauldrons, iron beds, and disembowelment,
calling them
"living hells."
Once, when drunk,
he playfully placed a melon on a musician's neck to test his sword,
and severed his head.
Ōu Shǐ refers to
the entertainer as Shàng Yùlóu,
who was the musician whose head was cut off.
*Duàn*
is pronounced *duǎn*.
44 Initially,
the Dì and Lìbù Shàngshū Dòu Zhēngù had both served Jìn Gāozǔ;
they knew and respected each other deeply.
When the Dì ascended the throne,
he wanted to make Dòu Zhēngù a Xiàng.
He asked Sū Féngjí,
“Who else is fit to be a Xiàng?”
Féngjí was close to Hànlín Xuéshì Lǐ Tāo,
and so recommended him,
saying,
“Previously, Tāo requested that Zhāng Yànzé be beheaded,
a matter recorded in volume 283, Jìn Gāozǔ, Tiānfú 7th year.
I once held him in high regard;
he can be a Xiàng.”
At that time, Gāo Xíngzhōu and Mùróng Yànchāo were jointly attacking Dù Zhòngwēi in Yèdū.
The matter of sending the two generals to attack Dù Zhòngwēi first appeared in the intercalary seventh month.
Xíngzhōu wanted to delay in order to wear down the enemy.
Xíngzhōu’s daughter was Zhòngwēi’s son’s wife.
Yànchāo publicly stated,
“Because of his daughter,
Xíngzhōu is fond of the rebel and does not attack.”
Because of this, the two generals were at odds.
Mùróng Yànchāo, being a close relative of the Dì from the same lineage, not only disrespected Gāo Xíngzhōu,
but also falsely accused Xíngzhōu of delaying the enemy due to their marital ties,
hence the discord.
The Dì intended to personally lead the attack on Zhòngwēi,
but his decision was not yet firm.
Tāo submitted a memorial requesting a personal imperial campaign.
The Dì was greatly pleased,
deeming Tāo to possess the qualities of a Zǎixiàng.
In the ninth month,
on the day Jiǎxū,
Féngjí was promoted to Zuǒ Púyè concurrently Ménxià Shìláng,
Sū Yǔguī to Yòu Púyè concurrently Zhōngshū Shìláng,
Zhēngù to Sīkōng concurrently Ménxià Shìláng,
and Tāo to Hùbù Shàngshū concurrently Zhōngshū Shìláng,
all with the title Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Dòu Zhēngù was appointed Xiàng with the title Sīkōng,
but was listed after the two Púyè
because the two Sū were old Xiàngs,
while Zhēngù was a new Xiàng.
On the day Wùyín,
an edict ordered a visit to Chányuán and Wèizhōu to comfort the troops,
with Huángzǐ Chéngxùn appointed Dōngjīng Liúshǒu.
45 Féng Dào, Lǐ Sōng, and Hé Níng returned from Zhènzhōu.
Bái Zàiróng and others, having driven out the Qìdān,
allowed Féng Dào and the others to escape and return.
"Huán" (return)
is pronounced "xuān,"
or as written.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Sōng was made Tàizǐ Tàifù,
and Níng was made Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
46 On the day Gēngchén,
the Dì departed from Dàliáng.
47 Jìnchāng Jiédùshǐ Zhào Kuāngzàn
In the seventh month of this autumn,
Zhào Kuāngzàn moved from Hézhōng to Cháng'ān.
In winter,
the tenth month,
he sent envoys to surrender to Shǔ,
requesting that troops be sent out from the Zhōngnán Shān road for support.
The Zhōngnán Shān road
is the Zǐwǔ Gǔ road.
48 On the day Wùxū,
the Dì arrived at the foot of Yèdū city,
lodging in Gāo Xíngzhōu’s camp.
The ruler personally leading the army,
yet not establishing an imperial camp but lodging in the Yuánshuài’s camp,
carried the implication of entering Hán Xìn’s encampment to seize control of the army.
Gāo Xíngzhōu had no ulterior motives,
so he did not react.
“The food in the city is not yet exhausted.
A hurried attack
will only kill soldiers
and will not be easy to conquer.
It is better to delay,
and they will collapse by themselves when their food runs out.”
The Dì agreed with this.
Mùróng Yànchāo repeatedly found fault to insult Xíngzhōu.
Xíngzhōu wept and complained to the ruling officials,
scooping up dirt and feces to fill his mouth,
indicating that he suffered insults but dared not speak.
The Dì was well aware of Yànchāo’s fault,
yet he ordered the two ministers to reconcile;
he also summoned Yànchāo to his tent and reprimanded him,
but did not clearly define Yànchāo’s crime,
being swayed by affection.
Dù Zhòngwēi declared that he would surrender as soon as the imperial carriage arrived.
The Dì sent Jìshìzhōng Chén Guān to convey his intentions,
but Zhòngwēi again closed the gates and refused him.
Food in the city gradually ran out,
and many generals and soldiers surrendered.
Mùróng Yànchāo insisted on attacking the city,
and the Dì agreed.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
the Dì personally supervised the generals in attacking the city.
From Yín hour to Chén hour,
over ten thousand soldiers were wounded,
and over a thousand died.
The attack failed, and they stopped.
Yànchāo then dared not speak again.
The heavy casualties and the failure to capture the city
proved Gāo Xíngzhōu’s suggestion of prolonged attrition to be correct,
silencing Mùróng Yànchāo’s words.
Initially,
the Qìdān left 1,500 Yōuzhōu soldiers to garrison Dàliáng.
These were the ones left by Xiāo Hàn,
as seen in the fifth month above.
Someone reported that the Yōuzhōu soldiers were about to mutiny.
The Dì had them all killed beneath Fántái.
Fántái was in Dàliáng.
Dīng Dù said: Fántái was originally Shī Kuàng’s music platform.
Liáng Xiàowáng expanded it
and named it Fántái.
Xuē Shǐ said: Fántái
was Liáng Wáng’s music platform;
later, people named Fán resided near it,
and the locals called it by their surname.
Zhāng Lián led 2,000 Yōuzhōu soldiers to assist Zhòngwēi in his defense.
The matter of Zhāng Lián entering Yèdū to assist Zhòngwēi first appeared in the seventh month.
The court promised not to kill them;
Lián said:
“What crime did the soldiers of Fántái commit that they were massacred?
Now, defending this place,
we only await death.”
Because of this, the city held out for a long time.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
Nèidiàn Zhí Hán Xùn presented siege equipment.
The Dì said:
“What a city relies on
is the morale of its people.
If morale is broken,
the city has nothing to protect it.
What is the use of this!”
He finally adopted Gāo Xíngzhōu’s words.
When Dù Zhòngwēi rebelled,
Guānchá Pànguān Jīnxiāng Wáng Mǐn repeatedly wept and admonished him,
but he did not listen.
Jīnxiāng Xiàn,
in early Táng, belonged to Jìzhōu,
and later to Yǎnzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it belonged to Jìzhōu,
ninety lì southeast of the prefecture.
On the day Jiǎxū,
Mǐn was sent to present a memorial of surrender.
On the day Yǐhài,
Zhòngwēi’s son Hónglián came to pay respects;
on the day Bǐngzǐ,
his wife Shí Shì came to pay respects.
Shí Shì
was Jìn’s Sòngguó Zhǎnggōngzhǔ.
The Dì sent them back into the city.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Zhòngwēi opened the gates and surrendered.
Seven or eight tenths of the people in the city had died of starvation,
and the survivors were all emaciated and unrecognizably human.
Zhāng Lián had previously requested a sworn promise from the imperial court.
An edict promised their return to their hometowns.
But upon their surrender,
Lián and dozens of other officers were killed;
their soldiers were allowed to return north.
When they were about to leave the border,
they plundered heavily before departing.
The Yōuzhōu soldiers, about to leave the border of Wèizhōu,
were far from the Hàn army,
and felt no fear,
so they plundered extensively
and vented their anger before leaving.
"Jiàng" (general)
is pronounced "liàng."
"Xiào" (officer)
is pronounced "hùjiào."
Guō Wēi requested the execution of over a hundred of Zhòngwēi’s close generals
and the confiscation of Zhòngwēi’s family assets to reward the soldiers.
This was granted.
Zhòngwēi was made Tàifù concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng, and Chǔguó Gōng.
Whenever Zhòngwēi went out or in,
passersby often threw bricks and tiles and cursed him.
This was because, as a regional governor, he was greedy and insatiable,
and as a general, he betrayed the nation and exterminated the people.
This laid the groundwork for the future killing of Dù Zhòngwēi and the townsfolk eating his flesh.
"Gòu" (curse)
is pronounced "kǔhòu,"
or "xǔhòu."
Your subject Guāng says: The Hàn Gāozǔ killed fifteen hundred innocent people from Yōuzhōu,
which was not benevolent;
he lured Zhāng Lián and then executed him,
which was not trustworthy;
Dù Zhòngwēi’s crime was great, yet he was pardoned,
which was not just punishment.
Benevolence unites the multitude,
trustworthiness ensures orders are followed,
and punishment deters wickedness.
Losing these three,
how can one maintain the state?
That its reign would not be prolonged
Gāo Xíngzhōu, believing Mùróng Yànchāo was at Chánzhōu,
firmly declined the Yèdū post.
Chánzhōu and Wèizhōu were one hundred and fifty *lǐ* apart.
As Xíngzhōu and Yànchāo had already fallen out,
living in adjacent territories,
they certainly would not be at peace with each other.
Therefore, he vehemently declined.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
Shǐ Hóngzhào, Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ, was appointed Military Governor of Guīdé,
concurrently Grand Commander of the Palace Cavalry and Infantry.
Liú Xìn, Military Governor of Yìchéng, was appointed Military Governor of Zhōngwǔ, concurrently Deputy Grand Commander of the Palace Cavalry and Infantry.
Yànchāo was transferred to be Military Governor of Tiānpíng,
and both were given the concurrent title of *Tóng Píngzhāngshì*.
Wúyuè King Hóngzōng conducted a grand review of his navy,
and the rewards were double those of old.
Hú Jìnsī strenuously remonstrated.
Hóngzōng was enraged,
threw his brush into the water,
and said:
"My wealth is shared with the soldiers.
Why should there be limits on how much or how little?"
This laid the groundwork for Hú Jìnsī to depose Hóngzōng.
In the twelfth month,
on the *bǐngxū* day,
the Emperor departed Yèdū.
He departed from Yèdū and returned to Dàliáng.
The Lord of Shǔ dispatched Wú Chóngyùn, Chief Adjutant of Xióngwǔ.
Chief Adjutant of Xióngwǔ was
Chief Adjutant of Qínzhōu.
Yùn is
pronounced *yùn*.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Zhāng Qiánzhāo, Military Governor of Shānnán Xīdào and concurrently Grand Councilor, was appointed Commissioner for Pacification and Comfort of the Northern Advance Camp.
Hé Chóngjiàn, Military Governor of Xióngwǔ, was made his deputy.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo, during the Lùwáng Rebellion,
attacked Fèngxiáng but was defeated,
and surrendered to Shǔ.
Hé Chóngjiàn, when the Qìdān entered China, surrendered to Shǔ.
Therefore, the Lord of Shǔ used them to plan strategy for Qí and Yōng.
Chóng is
pronounced *chóng*.
They jointly led fifty thousand troops.
Qiánzhāo exited through Sànguān,
Chóngjiàn exited through Lǒngzhōu,
to attack Fèngxiáng.
Having already sent envoys to summon Hóu Yì,
they then followed up with troops to pressure him.
This was to aid Cháng'ān.
It was in response to Zhào Kuāngzàn's request.
Their banners stretched for tens of *lǐ*.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Imperial Prince Chéngxùn, Minister of Kāifēng, passed away.
Chéngxùn was filial, fraternal, loyal, and honest,
and adept in governance.
Everyone lamented his death.
The historian says that Chéngxùn's death marked the contraction of the Hàn dynasty's fortunes.
On the *guǐsì* day,
the Emperor arrived at Dàliáng.
Lǐ Rúyūn, Military Governor of Wēiwǔ, and Bāo Xiūràng, the Wúyuè garrison commander, were not in accord.
Rúyūn plotted to ambush and kill Xiūràng,
and then surrender Fúzhōu to Táng again.
Xiūràng discovered this,
led troops to attack the prefectural residence.
On that day,
Rúyūn was killed,
and his clan was exterminated.
The incident of Lǐ Rénlái occupying Fúzhōu was first mentioned in volume 285, Jìn Qíwáng Kāiyùn 2nd year.
The historian says that treacherous and deceitful individuals eventually die at the hands of others.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
Imperial Prince Chéngxùn was posthumously granted the title of Prince of Wèi.
Hóu Yì requested to surrender to Shǔ.
He sent Wú Chóngyùn back west with military registers and grain accounts,
and together with Zhào Kuāngzàn, they submitted a memorial requesting the dispatch of troops to pacify Guānzhōng.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
Bāo Xiūràng sent Lǐ Rúyūn's head to Qiántáng.
Wúyuè King Hóngzōng appointed Wú Chéng of Shānyīn, the Chancellor, to manage the affairs of Wēiwǔ Military Governorship.
Wúyuè King Hóngzōng,
by nature firm and severe,
resented that during the time of his father, the King Zhōngxiàn Hóngzuǒ, generals were indulged
and governance was not decided by himself.
According to Xuē Shǐ: Wúyuè King Qián Liú, during Xú Wǎn's rebellion,
sent his son Yuánguàn as a hostage to Xuānzhōu,
and kept Hú Jìnsī, Dài Yùn, and others by his side.
When Yuánguàn succeeded to the throne,
he employed Jìnsī as a great general.
After Yuánguàn died and Hóngzuǒ ascended,
Jìnsī, considering himself an old general,
was greatly respected and honored.
But when Zōng ascended,
he somewhat slighted and insulted him,
which Jìnsī could not tolerate.
He executed three magistrates in Hángzhōu and Yuèzhōu for abusing the law.
"Wǔ"
should be
"wǔ" (meaning 'to wield' or 'play with').
Hú Jìnsī, Commander of the Palace Guards, relied on his meritorious service in enthroning the king
and interfered in government affairs.
Hóngzōng disliked him
and wished to appoint him to a prefecture,
intending to strip him of his military authority and send him away.
When Jìnsī proposed plans or discussed matters,
Hóngzōng frequently reprimanded him directly.
Jìnsī returned home,
set up a shrine for King Zhōngxiàn,
let down his hair, and wept bitterly.
Shù is
pronounced *shuò*.
Zhé is
pronounced *zhé*.
Pī is
pronounced *pī*.
An official reported that Jìnsī had purchased nearly a thousand *jīn* of meat.
Hóngzōng asked Jìnsī:
"How much meat does a large ox yield?"
He replied:
"No more than three hundred *jīn*."
Hóngzōng said:
"Then the official is lying."
He ordered an investigation into the official's crime.
Jìnsī bowed and praised the king's discernment.
Hóngzōng asked:
"How do you know the details so well?"
Jìnsī answered timidly:
"Before I joined the army,
I also engaged in this business."
Jìnsī felt that Hóngzōng knew of his past profession
and thus humiliated him,
which increased his resentment and anger.
This is why Chǔ Suíliáng warned Táng Tàizōng not to press Zhāng Xuánsù too hard.
See July above.
It means he again wished to surrender to Táng.
Jìnsī felt increasingly uneasy.
Hóngzōng and Hé Chéngxùn, Commander of the Palace Guards, conspired to expel Jìnsī.
He also consulted Shuǐqiū Zhāojuàn, Commander of the Palace Supervisors.
According to Xuē Shǐ: Wúyuè King Liú's mother was Lady Shuǐqiū,
so Zhāojuàn was probably a maternal relative.
Zhāojuàn advised against it, suggesting tolerance.
Hóngzōng hesitated and could not make a decision.
Chéngxùn, fearing the plot would be exposed,
instead reported the plan to Jìnsī.
As the ancients said,
"Hesitation is the bane of action."
Hóngzōng's indecision
caused Hé Chéngxùn to become fearful and develop ulterior motives.
Xiè is
pronounced *xiè*.
On the last day of *gēngxū*,
Hóngzōng hosted a night banquet for his generals and officials.
Jìnsī suspected that Hóngzōng was plotting against him.
He conspired with his associates to rebel,
leading a hundred of his personal soldiers,
dressed in military attire and armed, into the Tiāncètáng to see the king.
He said:
"This old servant is innocent,
why does Your Majesty plot against him?"
Hóngzōng shouted at him but he did not retreat.
Those on his left and right holding weapons were all enraged.
Hóngzōng was suddenly startled and had no time to speak.
If he had taken advantage of the anger of his attendants
to suppress the rebellion with legitimacy,
what would he have to fear from Hú Jìnsī?
Therefore, it is important for a person to have courage and decisiveness.
Jìnsī locked the gate,
falsely proclaimed a royal decree,
and announced to all that
"the king suddenly suffered from a stroke
and has abdicated the throne to Hóngtì, who holds the concurrent title of *Tóngcān Xiàngfǔ Shì*."
Jìnsī then led the generals to welcome Hóngtì from his private residence,
and also summoned Chancellor Yuán Dézhāo.
When Dézhāo arrived,
he stood outside the curtain and did not bow,
saying:
"I shall wait until I see the new lord."
Jìnsī quickly stepped out and lifted the curtain,
and only then did Dézhāo bow.
Jìnsī claimed it was Hóngzōng's decree,
and by royal prerogative, appointed Hóngtì Military Governor of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng, concurrently *Shìzhōng*.
Hóngtì said:
"Only if you can ensure my brother's safety
will I dare to accept the mandate.
Otherwise,
I must yield the path to the worthy."
Jìnsī agreed to this.
Hóngtì then began to attend to affairs.
Jìnsī killed Shuǐqiū Zhāojuàn and Lù Guāngxuàn, a palace attendant.
A palace attendant
was an official of Wúyuè stationed at the king's side.
He was Hóngzōng's maternal uncle.
Jìnsī's wife said:
"Others might be killed,
but Zhāojuàn
was a gentleman.
How could you harm him?"
The historian says that some women possess greater wisdom than men.
In the 60th year of this reign,
the Lord of Táng appointed Yǔlín Grand General Wáng Yánzhèng as Ānhuà Jìedùshǐ and King of Póyáng,
to鎮 Ráo Zhōu.
The Táng likely established the Ānhuà Army in Ráo Zhōu.
Wáng Yánzhèng's surrender to Táng is mentioned in Volume 284, second year of Kāiyùn of Jìn Qíwáng,
which was the third year of Bǎodà of Southern Táng.
First year of Qiányòu (wùshēn, 948)
1 In spring,
first month,
on the day yǐmǎo,
there was a general amnesty
and the reign title was changed.
2 The Emperor was troubled by Zhào Kuāngzàn and Hóu Yì forming a bandit group with the Shǔ army.
Coincidentally, the Huíhú came to offer tribute,
complaining that they were blocked by the Dǎngxiàng.
Since Táng Chángxīng,
Dǎngxiàng tribes in the western route had been plundering envoys and tribute from foreign lands.
Although Táng sent troops to suppress them,
they could not be stopped.
"Dǎng"
is pronounced "dǐláng" (底朗) in fanqiè.
An imperial edict ordered Left Guard Grand General Wáng Jǐngchóng and General Qí Zàngzhēn to lead several thousand Imperial Guards there,
and thus to manage the affairs of Guānxī.
This was under the pretext of escorting the Huíhú envoys to dispatch troops,
but was actually to manage Guānyòu.
Lǐ Shù, the Judgement Officer of Jìnchāng Jìedù,
had long served under Zhào Yánshòu,
who had him assist Kuāngzàn.
When Kuāngzàn was about to enter Shǔ,
Shù advised:
"When the King of Yàn entered the court,
was it what he desired?
This refers to Zhào Yánshòu being imprisoned by the Qìdān and entering the north.
We are currently focused on attracting and appeasing.
If you apologize and return to court,
you will surely maintain wealth and honor.
Entering Shǔ is not a complete plan.
'A hoofprint puddle cannot hold a foot-long carp.'
This is a saying of Liú Yào.
"Cén"
is pronounced "chúzhēn" (耡針) in fanqiè.
A "hoofprint puddle"
refers to a depression made by a horse's hoof,
where water collects.
It cannot hold a foot-long carp;
this is an analogy that Shǔ is a small state
and cannot accommodate Zhào Kuāngzàn.
Kuāngzàn then sent Shù to present a memorial requesting to enter court.
Before Jǐngchóng and others departed, Shù arrived.
The Emperor asked Shù:
"Why did Kuāngzàn attach himself to Shǔ?"
He replied:
"Kuāngzàn, feeling that he himself had received a barbarian official position,
believed he had previously received the order of Qìdān Lord Yélǜ Déguāng to garrison Hézhōng Fǔ.
His father
refers to Zhào Yánshòu.
Therefore, he attached himself to Shǔ to seek temporary escape.
Your servant believes that the state must certainly comfort and pacify him,
so he sent me to beg for mercy."
The Emperor said:
"Kuāngzàn and his father
are originally our people,
but unfortunately fell into the hands of the barbarians.
Now Yánshòu is trapped,
Zhào Yánshòu was imprisoned by the Qìdān, as seen in May of last year.
I will permit him to enter court."
Hóu Yì also requested to attend the Shèngshòu Festival on the fourth day of the second month to offer longevity wishes.
Wǔdài Huìyào states: The Emperor was born on the fourth day of the second month in the second year of Táng Qiánníng.
The Emperor summoned him into his private chambers
and commanded him:
"The intentions of Kuāngzàn and Yì
are both still unknown.
When you arrive there,
if he has already entered court,
then do not question him;
if he is still delaying and observing,
you should act according to expediency."
3 On the day jǐwèi,
the Emperor changed his name to Gǎo.
4 Féng Dào, formerly Wēishèng Jìedùshǐ, was appointed Grand Preceptor.
5 On the day rénxū,
Wúyuè King Hóngchù moved the former King Hóngzōng to a private residence in Yījǐn Jūn.
He was moved to his private residence in Lín'ān.
He secretly warned him:
"If there are any unusual dispositions,
they are not my intention.
You should resist them to the death."
6 Since the death of Wèi Wáng Chéngxùn, the Emperor
had been excessively grieved.
On the day jiǎzǐ,
he began to be unwell.
7 Zhào Kuāngzàn did not wait for Lǐ Shù's return message,
and had already left Cháng'ān.
On the day bǐngzǐ,
he had an audience.
When Wáng Jǐngchóng and others arrived in Cháng'ān,
they heard that the Shǔ army had already entered Qín Chuān.
From Dàsànguān northward to Qí and Yōng,
straddling the north and south banks of the Wèichuān,
there was a fertile plain extending for a thousand li,
called Qín Chuān.
They dispatched over a thousand men from the local command and Zhào Kuāngzàn's personal guards to jointly resist them.
"Local command"
refers to the Jìnchāng command.
They intended to tattoo their faces,
subtly revealing the imperial will.
Military officer Zhào Sīwǎn
was the first to request to tattoo his own face to lead his subordinates,
tattooing his face with his military designation,
so that he would have nowhere to flee.
"Xiào" (校)
is pronounced "hùjiào" (戶教) in fanqiè.
"Shuài" (帥)
is read as "shuài" (率).
Qí Zàngzhēn secretly said:
"Sīwǎn is fierce and difficult to control;
it is better to kill him."
Jǐngchóng did not listen.
Sīwǎn
was from Wèizhōu.
This laid the groundwork for Zhào Sīwǎn to seize Cháng'ān and rebel.
When Lǐ Tíngguī of Shǔ was about to reach Cháng'ān,
he heard that Zhào Kuāngzàn had already entered court
and intended to retreat.
Wáng Jǐngchóng intercepted him
and defeated Tíngguī at Zǐwǔ Gǔ.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo arrived at Bǎojī,
but the generals' deliberations were not harmonious,
and they held their troops without advancing.
Hóu Yì, hearing that Tíngguī was returning west,
closed his fortifications to resist the Shǔ army.
Qiánzhāo, finding himself isolated,
led his troops to retreat by night.
Jǐngchóng led the armies of Fèngxiáng, Lǒng, Bīn, Jīng, Fū, and Fāng to pursue and defeat the Shǔ army at Sànguān,
capturing four hundred generals and soldiers.
The two armies of Lǐ Tíngguī and Zhāng Qiánzhāo
were both dispatched by the Lord of Shǔ in December of the previous year.
"Shuài" (帥)
is read as "shuài" (率).
"Fū" (鄜)
has the sound "fū".
"Bài" (敗)
is pronounced "bǔmài" (補邁) in fanqiè.
8 On the day dīngchǒu,
the Emperor's illness worsened critically.
Yáng Bīn, fearing Liú Xìn, the Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Jìedùshǐ of Zhōngwǔ,
immediately dispatched him to his garrison.
Liú Xìn, being a close cousin, commanded the Imperial Guards,
which is why Yáng Bīn feared him and sent him to garrison Xǔzhōu.
He left weeping tears like rain.
"Weeping tears like rain"
means crying profusely.
The Emperor summoned Sū Féngjí, Yáng Bīn, Shǐ Hóngzhào, and Guō Wēi to receive his dying wishes,
saying:
"My breath is faint;
I cannot speak much.
Chéngyòu is young and weak;
future matters are entrusted to you, my lords."
He further said:
"Guard well against Zhòngwēi."
This referred to executing Dù Zhòngwēi.
He passed away in Wànsuì Diàn,
aged fifty-four.
Xuē Shǐ states: When Liáng received the abdication,
Dàliáng Wànsuì Táng was renamed Wànsuì Diàn.
On the day gēngchén,
an imperial edict was issued,
stating:
"Zhòngwēi and his son,
taking advantage of Our minor illness,
slandered and incited the populace."
His sons Hóngzhāng, Hónglián, and Hóngcàn were all executed.
Jìn Gōngzhǔ and all relatives, both within and outside the court,
were completely absolved.
Jìn Gōngzhǔ
was of the Shí clan,
Dù Zhòngwēi's wife.
The townspeople vied to eat his flesh,
and the officials could not stop them;
in a short while, it was all gone.
In the second month,
on xīnsì, the first day of the month,
the imperial son, Left Guard Grand General and Grand Palace Dotestator Chéngyòu, was enthroned as King of Zhōu,
and concurrently Grand Councillor.
After a short while,
the mourning was announced,
and the imperial will was proclaimed,
ordering the King of Zhōu to ascend the throne.
He was eighteen years old at the time.
9 Shǔ’s Hán Bǎozhēn and Páng Fúchéng led their troops back from Lǒngzhōu.
Hán Bǎozhēn was also sent by the Shǔ ruler in the twelfth month of the previous year.
Upon their return,
“從宣翻” (note on pronunciation).
Also, as written.
On this day,
Bǎozhēn and others arrived at Qínzhōu,
divided their troops to guard all the gates and thoroughfares,
and then rebuilt and entered Shǔ.
10 On the *dīnghài* day,
the Empress was honored as Empress Dowager.
11 The imperial court knew that Bái Zàiróng, the acting military commissioner of Chéngdé, was not a talent for generalship,
so on the *gēngyín* day,
they replaced him with Liú Zàimíng, formerly the acting military commissioner of Jiànxióng.
12 On the *guǐsì* day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
The amnesty was granted thirteen days after the emperor's ascension.
13 Hé Chéngxùn, the commander of the inner palace guards of Wúyuè, again requested the execution of Hú Jìnsī and his faction.
Wúyuè Wáng Hóngchù detested his duplicity
and feared inviting disaster,
so on the *yǐwèi* day,
he apprehended Chéngxùn
and executed him.
Jìnsī repeatedly requested the killing of the deposed king, Hóngzōng, to eliminate future troubles,
but Hóngchù did not permit it.
Jìnsī falsely used the king's command to secretly order Xuē Wēn to harm him.
Wēn said:
"On the day I received my orders,
I did not hear this instruction,
so I dare not act rashly."
Jìnsī then secretly sent two of his confederates, Fāng Ān, at night to climb over the wall and enter.
Hóngzōng shut his door and resisted them,
shouting loudly for help;
Wēn heard this,
led his troops in,
and killed Ān and his accomplice in the courtyard.
He then reported to Hóngchù,
traveling from Lín'ān to Qiántáng to report the incident.
Hóngchù said:
"Saving my brother
is your accomplishment."
Hóngchù feared and was wary of Jìnsī,
and he condescended to him.
Jìnsī also felt internal anxiety and fear,
and before long,
a carbuncle erupted on his back, and he died.
Hóngzōng was thus preserved.
14 An imperial edict appointed Wáng Jǐngchóng to concurrently serve as the Phoenix Inspection Commissioner.
Jǐngchóng led his troops to Fèngxiáng,
but Hóu Yì had not yet departed.
Jǐngchóng used the imperial guards to divide and defend the various gates.
Someone advised Jǐngchóng to kill Yì,
but Jǐngchóng had received a secret imperial edict from the former emperor.
“密旨” (secret edict)
refers to the command from Gāozǔ to act expediently in his sleeping chambers,
as seen above.
“朝” (court),
pronounced *zhí yáo fān* (note on pronunciation);
the same below.
He hesitated, unsure whether to execute him,
as he was uncertain about unauthorized killing.
Yì heard of this,
left without informing Jǐngchóng.
Jǐngchóng regretted it
and blamed himself.
On the *wùxū* day,
Yì had an audience with the emperor.
Yǐndì asked:
"Why did you summon the Shǔ army?"
He replied:
"Your minister wished to lure them in and kill them."
The Emperor smiled.
15 Shǔ’s Zhāng Qiánzhāo regretted his lack of accomplishments,
so on the *guǐmǎo* day,
upon reaching Xīngzhōu,
he died of shame and indignation.
He returned from Sànguān to Xīngzhōu.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo probably did not know whether it was feasible,
nor did he gauge the advantages and disadvantages,
but was a person who was eager to seek achievement.
Observing his attack on Wáng Dū in Dìngzhōu
and on Lù Wáng in Fèngxiáng,
it is clear that his eagerness to win led to defeat.
“恚” (anger), *yú bì fān* (note on pronunciation).
16 Shǐ Hóngzhào, the Grand Commander of the Palace Cavalry and Infantry, and Concurrent Chancellor, suffered the loss of his mother.
Within a few days,
he resumed court attendance.

Qiányòu First Year (Wùshēn, 948)
1 In the third month,
on the *bǐngchén* day,
Shǐ Hóngzhào was reinstated in office
and given the concurrent title of *Shìzhōng*.
2 Hóu Yì was rich in wealth
and heavily bribed the ruling officials and Shǐ Hóngzhào and others,

“執政” (ruling officials)
refers to Sū Féngjí, Yáng Bīn, and others,
all prominent officials of that time.
“譽” (praise), pronounced *yú*.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
Yì was appointed concurrently as Grand Chancellor
and acting Mayor of Kāifēng.
“行” (acting)
means performing the duties of the Mayor,

3 Guǎngjìn

"Wèi
is Dàmíng."

To change the name of Jìn,
therefore Guǎngjìn and Jìnchāng were renamed.
4 Hóu Yì severely slandered Wáng Jǐngchóng at court,
saying that he was arrogant and tyrannical.
Hóu Yì, because Wáng Jǐngchóng had attempted to kill him,

hence he slandered him.
“橫” (tyrannical), *hù mèng fān* (note on pronunciation).
Jǐngchóng, knowing the situation had changed,
felt uneasy internally
and resented the imperial court.
He resented the court for not upholding the late emperor's dying wishes,

He summoned Zhào Kuāngzàn’s personal guards to the capital.
Zhào Sīwǎn and others were very fearful.

On the way, Sīwǎn said to his confederate Cháng Yànqīng:

He's dead,
what should we do?"
Yànqīng said:
"Act expediently when the moment comes,

On the *guǐyǒu* day,
they arrived in Cháng'ān.
Ān Yǒuguī, the deputy military commissioner of Yǒngxīng, and Qióu Shǒuwēn, the inspection commissioner, came out to welcome Wáng Yì
and hosted a banquet at the guest pavilion.
All prefectures and garrisons had guest pavilions,
used for welcoming, sending off, and banquets.
"The 'Moat and Stockade Commissioner' has already arranged lodging in the east of the city."
The Moat and Stockade Commissioner
was in charge of construction, dredging, and arranging temporary camps.
Zhào Sīwǎn’s troops had previously garrisoned Cháng'ān with Zhào Kuāngzàn,
hence their families were in the city.
Yǒuguī and others assented.
At that time, Sīwǎn and others had no armor or weapons.
Upon entering the West Gate,
there was a provincial officer sitting by the gate.
Sīwǎn immediately seized his sword and killed him.
His followers then made a great clamor,
wielding white staffs,
and killed more than ten gatekeepers.
They dispatched their confederates to guard all the gates.
Sīwǎn entered the prefecture office,
opened the arsenal, and distributed armor and weapons to them.
Yǒuguī and others all fled.
Sīwǎn then occupied the city,
assembled the young men in the city,
gathering over four thousand people.
They repaired the city walls and moats
and mended the battlements.
Within ten days,
all equipment for battle and defense was ready.
Wáng Jǐngchóng subtly prompted the officials and people of Fèngxiáng to petition for Jǐngchóng to manage the military and prefectural affairs.
The imperial court was troubled by this,
so on the *jiǎxū* day,
they transferred Wáng Shǒu'ēn, the military commissioner of Jìngnàn, to be the military commissioner of Yǒngxīng,
intending to control Zhào Sīwǎn.
“難” (Nàn), pronounced *nǎi dàn fān* (note on pronunciation).
They wanted to use this to control Wáng Jǐngchóng.
Jǐngchóng was appointed acting military commissioner of Bīnzhōu,

The entertainer Jìng Biāntíng (靖邊庭) from Guózhōu (虢州) killed the Military Commissioner Tián Lìngfāng (田令方),
and drove away and plundered the people of the prefecture,
then fled to Zhào Sīwǎn (趙思綰).
Jìng (靖)
is a surname.
The names of entertainers often take the same meaning as a surname,
which is why they are used to jest.
The *Hé Shì Xìng Yuàn* (何氏姓苑) says: The Jìng (靖) surname
is descended from Jìng Guó Jūn (靖郭君) of Qí (齊).
The *Fēng Sú Tōng* (風俗通) says: The Jìng (靖) surname
is descended from Dān Jìng Gōng (單靖公).
Guózhōu (虢州) is over a hundred *li* northwest of Tóngguān (潼關).
All his followers dispersed.
5 At first,
the Qìdān (契丹) ruler returned north,
reaching Dìngzhōu (定州).
The Qìdān (契丹) ruler Déguāng (德光) returned north
and died in Shāhú Lín (殺胡林).
This refers to Wùyù (兀欲) returning north to Dìngzhōu (定州).
The former Military Commissioner Sūn Fāngjiǎn (孫方簡) was transferred to be the Military Commissioner of Dàtóng (大同).
In the third year of Kāiyùn (開運) of Qí Wáng (齊王) of Jìn (晉),
the Qìdān (契丹) ruler Déguāng (德光) appointed Sūn Fāngjiǎn (孫方簡) as the Military Commissioner of Yìwǔ (義武).
*Kǎo Yì* (考異) says: The *Shílù* (實錄) writes
"Fāngjiǎn" (方簡)
as
"Fāngjiàn" (方諫).
According to custom, Fāngjiǎn (方簡) avoided the taboo name of the Zhōu (周) dynasty
and changed his name to Fāngjiàn (方諫);
the *Shílù* (實錄) is incorrect.
Fearing that if he entered the court he would be detained by the Qìdān (契丹),
he delayed and did not accept the appointment,
leading three thousand of his followers to hold the old fort in Lángshān (狼山).
Sūn Fāngjiǎn (孫方簡) and his brothers held Lángshān (狼山),
seen in volume 285, Jìn (晉) Kāiyùn (開運) third year.
Shuài (帥)
is read as lǜ (率);
the same applies below.
The Qìdān (契丹) attacked them
but could not overcome them.
Soon after,
he sent an envoy to request surrender,
and the Emperor restored his old office
to defend against the Qìdān (契丹).
He was again made Military Commissioner of Yìwǔ (義武).
Yélǜ Zhōng (邪律忠) heard that Yèdū (鄴都) had been pacified.
Last year, in the eleventh month,
Dù Chóngwēi (杜重威) surrendered,
and Yèdū (鄴都) was pacified.
The event is seen in the previous volume.
An imperial edict appointed Liú Zàimíng (劉在明), acting military governor of Chéngdé (成德), as the Deputy Commander of Horse and Foot Soldiers for Yōuzhōu (幽州) Circuit,
ordering him to dispatch troops to manage Dìngzhōu (定州).
Before he could depart,
Zhōng (忠) and Mádá (麻荅) and others burned and plundered Dìngzhōu (定州),
driving all its people away and abandoning the city to go north.
Dìngzhōu (定州) is only separated from Zhènzhōu (鎮州) to the east
by Qízhōu (祁州).
The Qìdān (契丹) heard that Zhènzhōu (鎮州) was about to dispatch troops,
