He returned to occupy Dìngzhōu (定州) and also memorialized to appoint his brother Xíngyǒu (行友) as the Prefect of Yìzhōu (易州)
and Fāngyù (方遇) as the Prefect of Tàizhōu (泰州).
Whenever the Qìdān (契丹) invaded,
the brothers rushed to the rescue.
"Bēnmìng" (奔命) means to rush to relieve an emergency.
Thus, all the prefectures and counties in the late Jìn (晉) dynasty that had fallen to the Qìdān (契丹)
were again taken by the Hàn (漢).
On the day *bǐngzǐ* (丙子),
Liú Zàimíng (劉在明) was appointed Military Commissioner of Chéngdé (成德).
When Mádá (麻荅) reached his country,
the Qìdān (契丹) ruler reprimanded him for losing the defense.
Mádá (麻荅) refused to submit,
saying:
"It was due to the court's conscription of Hàn (漢) officials that chaos ensued."
This refers to the conscription of Féng Dào (馮道) and others.
The event is seen in the previous volume, previous year.
6 Sū Féngjí (蘇逢吉) and others served as chancellors,
often moving and appointing officials;
Yáng Bīn (楊邠) considered this a wasteful expenditure of state funds,
and often suppressed what they memorialized,
which displeased Féngjí (逢吉) and others.
Lǐ Tāo (李濤), Grand Academician of the Central Secretariat, concurrently Minister of Revenue, and concurrently Grand Councillor, submitted a memorial stating:
"Currently, Guānxī (關西) is in turmoil,
and external defense is urgent.
The two Privy Councilors are both meritorious ministers who assisted the founding,
their offices are noble but their families are not yet wealthy;
it is fitting to grant them important and critical great garrisons."
Lǐ Tāo's (李濤) memorial
was based on Sū Féngjí's (蘇逢吉) intentions.
The two Privy Councilors
refer to Yáng Bīn (楊邠) and Guō Wēi (郭威).
"It is easy to make decisions;
Féngjí (逢吉) and Yǔguī (禹珪) have been serving since the previous emperor's time,
and both can be entrusted."
When Yáng Bīn (楊邠) and Guō Wēi (郭威) heard this,
they tearfully complained to the Empress Dowager,
stating:
"We followed the late emperor through difficult times,
and now the Son of Heaven listens to others' words
and wishes to cast us out.
Moreover, Guānxī (關西) currently has troubles,"
referring to Qí (岐) and Yōng (雍) raising troops in rebellion.
"He disregards the state.
If we are truly unfit for office,
we beg to remain until after the imperial funeral."
The Empress Dowager was enraged
and reprimanded the Emperor,
saying:
"How can you listen to others' words and drive away the meritorious old ministers of the state!"
The Emperor said:
"These are the words of the chancellors."
He then interrogated and reprimanded the chancellors.
Tāo (濤) said:
"This memorial was made solely by me;
no one else was involved."
On the day *dīngchǒu* (丁丑),
Tāo (濤) was dismissed from his political office
and ordered to return to his private residence.
This laid the groundwork for the future conflict between the generals and chancellors.
7 On this day,
the four garrisons of Bīn (邠), Jīng (涇), Tóng (同), and Huá (華)
The commander of Bīn (邠) was Wáng Shǒu'ēn (王守恩),
the commander of Jīng (涇) was Shǐ Kuāngwēi (史匡威),
the commander of Tóng (同) was Zhāng Yànwēi (張彥威),
and the commander of Huá (華) was Hù Cóngkē (扈從珂).
Huá (華) is pronounced *hù huà fān*.
Zhào Sīwǎn (趙思綰) occupied Yǒngxīng (永興),
and Wáng Jǐngchóng (王景崇) occupied Fèngxiáng (鳳翔).
Initially,
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) was fearful when he heard of Dù Chóngwēi's (杜重威) death.
Dù Chóngwēi's (杜重威) death is seen in the first month of this year in the previous volume.
He considered himself to have been a senior general in the Jìn (晉) dynasty
with military achievements.
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn (李守貞) defeated the Qìdān (契丹) at Mǎjiā Kǒu (馬家口) and captured Qīngzhōu (青州),
and also defeated the Qìdān (契丹) at Yángchéng (陽城);
his achievements were not minor.
He won the hearts of his soldiers.
The Hàn (漢) dynasty was newly established,
the Son of Heaven was young and had just ascended,
and the ruling officials were all recent appointees,
so he harbored intentions of disrespecting the court.
Therefore, he recruited fugitives,
nurtured loyal followers,
repaired city fortifications,
and maintained weapons and armor,
day and night without rest.
He sent messengers through secret paths to send wax-sealed letters to ally with the Qìdān (契丹),
but they were repeatedly captured by border officials.
Zhào Xiūjǐ (趙修己) from Jùnyí (浚儀),
who was skilled in divination,
The *Jiù Táng Shū Dìlǐ Zhì* (舊唐書地理志) says: Jùnyí (浚儀) was an old county,
established by the Suí (隋) dynasty,
located thirty *li* north of the present county;
in the fourth year of Wǔdé (武德) of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
the county was moved into the northern *luóchéng* (羅城) of the prefecture;
in the first year of Zhēnguān (貞觀),
it was moved one *li* west of the prefecture;
later it was governed under the outer wall.
He was appointed Supervisor of Households,
and accumulated experience from successive garrison transfers.
In the early Kāiyùn (開運) era of Jìn (晉),
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn (李守貞) was garrisoned at Yìchéng (義成),
and later moved to Tàiníng (泰寧), Tiānpíng (天平), and Guīdé (歸德),
until he was garrisoned at Hùguó (護國) and caused rebellion.
"The timing is not right,
do not act rashly!"
He repeatedly and earnestly remonstrated with him, but
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) did not listen,
so he claimed illness and returned to his hometown.
The monk Zǒnglún (總倫) flattered Shǒuzhēn (守貞) with his arts,
saying that he would certainly become the Son of Heaven,
and Shǒuzhēn (守貞) believed him.
He also once gathered his generals and aides for a banquet,
and drew his bow, pointing at a tiger drawing licking its palm, saying:
"I have extraordinary fortune,
and I will hit its tongue."
He fired an arrow and hit it,
and everyone around congratulated him.
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) became even more conceited.
At that time, Zhào Sīwǎn (趙思綰) occupied Cháng'ān (長安)
and presented a memorial offering imperial robes to Shǒuzhēn (守貞).
Shǒuzhēn (守貞) believed that Heaven and man were in accord,
and thus proclaimed himself Prince of Qín (秦).
He sent his valiant general Wáng Jìxūn (王繼勳) from Pínglù (平陸)
to occupy Tóngguān (潼關).
The *Jiù Táng Shū Dìlǐ Zhì* (舊唐書地理志) says: Pínglù (平陸) County of Shǎnzhōu (陝州)
was Héběi (河北) County of the Suí (隋) dynasty.
In the third year of Tiānbǎo (天寶) of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
Lǐ Qíwù (李齊物), Prefect of Shǎn Jùn (陝郡), opened the Three Gates,
and a *jǐ* (戟) was found beneath the stones,
with the large blade bearing the seal script characters
"Pínglù" (平陸);
it was thus renamed Pínglù (平陸) County.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) says: Pínglù (平陸) County is five *li* north of Shǎnzhōu (陝州).
Tóngzhōu is closest to Hézhōng;
Hézhōng Fǔ is only sixty *lǐ* west of Tóngzhōu.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* of Zhōu Tàizǔ writes
"Yànchéng,"
probably to avoid the taboo name of the Zhōu Ancestor;
Xuē Shǐ followed this.
Now we follow the expanded edition.
A memorial was submitted requesting preparations be made in advance.
An imperial edict commanded Luó Jīnshān, the Commander of Cavalry in Huázhōu, to lead his troops to garrison Tóngzhōu;
thus, when Shǒuzhēn rose in rebellion,
Tóngzhōu was not annexed by him.
Jīnshān
was from Yúnzhōu.
8. Lǐ Yíyīn, the Military Commissioner of Dìngnàn, dispatched troops to garrison the border,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"Three years ago,
the Qiāng tribe
Yèmó
*Lóngkān Shǒujìng* says: *Yè*,
pronounced *yè*.
*Mó*,
pronounced *mó*. Request to attack them."
Qìngzhōu reported:
"Request additional troops for defense."
This was to guard against the Qiāng.
This year was not favorable for initiating military action,
so an edict was issued to stop them.
9. In summer,
fourth month,
on the *Xīnsì* day,
Wáng Yù, the Supervisor of Shǎnzhōu, reported the recapture of Tóngguān.
10. The Emperor consulted with his attendants,
considering that the Empress Dowager was angry at Lǐ Táo for causing estrangement,
and wished to further promote the two Grand Counselors,
to show that it was not the Emperor's intention.
The attendants also resented the dominance of the two Sū,
and wished to seize their power,
so they jointly urged this.
The two Grand Counselors were
Yáng Bīn and Guō Wēi.
The two Sū were
Fēngjí and Yǔguī.
On the *Rénwǔ* day,
an edict appointed Yáng Bīn, Grand Counselor, as Junior Minister of the Department of the Central Secretariat and Minister of Personnel, concurrently Grand Chancellor,
with his position as Grand Counselor remaining as before;
Guō Wēi, Vice Grand Counselor, was appointed Grand Counselor;
Wáng Zhāng, Commissioner of Finance, was also given the concurrent title of Grand Chancellor.
For all appointments made by the Central Secretariat
and all matters reported by various departments,
the Emperor entrusted Bīn with discretion.
From then on, the three Grand Chancellors stood with folded hands.
The three Grand Chancellors were
Dòu Zhēngù, Sū Fēngjí, and Sū Yǔguī.
Any matter not yet approved or disapproved by Bīn
no one dared to implement,
thus leading to stagnation.
Whenever the three Grand Chancellors proposed candidates for office,
if it was not in accordance with Bīn's wishes,
even for minor officials, they would not be granted the position.
Bīn had always disliked scholars,
often saying:
"The state's granaries being full
and its armaments strong
are the urgent priorities.
As for literature and rituals,
why bother with them!"
He already resented the two Sū for ostracizing him,
because they had Lǐ Táo submit a memorial
requesting the two Grand Counselors be sent out as regional commanders.
He was criticized by the public,
and wished to rectify this abuse.
Consequently, appointments became difficult,
and scholars and officials often went from the founding of the Hàn to its demise without receiving a single appointment.
These "scholars and officials"
refer to those in office, both inside and outside the capital.
"Appointment"
refers to an appointment in the Hàn court.
"Hereditary privilege"
refers to the system of *rènzǐ*.
"Officials of various departments entering service"
refers to those outside the main official ranks.
People at the time also blamed the two Sū's unfairness for this.
11. Guō Cóngyì, Military Commissioner of Zhènníng, was appointed Commander of the Yǒngxìng Campaign,
leading the Imperial Guards to attack Zhào Sīwǎn.
On the *Wùzǐ* day,
Bái Wénkē, Military Commissioner of Bǎoyì, was appointed Commander of the Hézhōng Campaign,
and Wáng Jùn, Director of the Imperial Guests Department, was appointed Supervisor.
On the *Xīnmǎo* day,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn's official titles and ranks were stripped,
and Wénkē and others were ordered to muster troops to attack him.
On the *Yǐwèi* day,
Shàng Hóngqiān, Military Commissioner of Níngjiāng and Commander of the Imperial Guard Infantry, was appointed Field Commander of the Western Campaign.
Níngjiāng Army was in Kuízhōu,
which at the time belonged to Shǔ territory,
so Shàng Hóngqiān held a remote command.
12. Wáng Jǐngchóng procrastinated and did not proceed to Bīnzhōu.
He reviewed and assembled able-bodied men from Fèngxiáng,
falsely claiming to attack Zhào Sīwǎn,
and also sent a dispatch to Bīnzhōu to muster troops.
Wáng Jǐngchóng wished to combine the forces of Qí and Bīn to launch his undertaking.
13. The Khitan ruler went to Liáoyáng.
The Hàn Liáodōng Commandery had Liáoyáng County,
where the Dàliáng River met the Liáo River.
The Khitan established Liáoyáng Fǔ there.
Oū Shǐ says: From Huánglóng Fǔ, travel northwest 1300 *lǐ* to Liáoyáng Fǔ.
Note:
Liáoyáng Fǔ was
the Eastern Capital of the Khitan,
formerly Bóhǎi territory,
2510 *lǐ* from Yānjīng.
There was a man named Chánnúlì,
the brother-in-law of the Khitan ruler.
Hearing that the Jìn ruler had an unmarried daughter,
he went to the Jìn ruler to request her;
the Jìn ruler declined, citing her youth.
A few days later,
the Khitan ruler sent men to swiftly take the daughter and leave,
giving her to Chánnú.
14. Wáng Jǐngchóng sent a letter to Xú Yàn, the Prefect of Fèngzhōu in Shǔ,
requesting the establishment of mutual markets.
On the *Rénxū* day,
the Shǔ ruler had Yàn reply to the letter, inviting him.
15. The Khitan ruler kept Xú Táifú, the Jìn Hanlin Academician, in Yōuzhōu.
Xú Táifú had accompanied the Khitan ruler north, as seen in the previous volume, previous year.
16. In the fifth month,
on the *Yǐhài* day,
Huázhōu reported that the river had burst its banks at Yúchí.
Yúchí
is a place name;
after the river burst,
it was called Yúchíkǒu.
17. In the sixth month,
on the *Wùyín* day (the first day of the month),
there was a solar eclipse.
18. On the *Xīnsì* day,
Liú Cí, Commander of the Left Wing of the Fèngguó Army, was appointed Commander of Cavalry and Infantry for the Hézhōng Campaign.
19. On the *Yǐyǒu* day,
Wáng Jǐngchóng sent an envoy to request surrender to Shǔ,
and also accepted official titles from Lǐ Shǒuzhēn.
20. Gāo Cónghuì, having broken ties with Hàn,
as seen in the previous volume, Tiānfú 12th year,
and with his territory impoverished,
then sent an envoy to submit a memorial expressing regret,
begging to resume tribute;
an edict was issued to send an envoy to comfort and pacify him.
21. Shàng Hóngqiān, Field Commander of the Western Campaign, attacked Cháng'ān,
was severely wounded, and died.
22. In autumn,
seventh month,
Lǐ Gǔ, Minister of Works, was appointed Commissioner of Transport for the Southwest Campaign.
This sets the stage for Lǐ Gǔ being favored and trusted by the Zhōu court.
23. On the *Gēngshēn* day,
Guō Wēi, Grand Counselor, was given the concurrent title of Grand Chancellor.
24. Zhāng Yè, Grand Minister of Public Works and Junior Minister of the Department of the Central Secretariat, concurrently Grand Chancellor of Shǔ,
was by nature extravagant and arrogant.
He forcibly purchased people's land and residences.
Using his power and influence to intimidate people,
people, fearing his power and influence,
had no choice but to engage in transactions with him;
this was known as "forcible purchase."
He set up prisons
and imprisoned debtors, sometimes for years,
to the extent that some died from illness in prison.
Sū Lín says: *Yǔ*,
means illness.
When prisoners fall ill,
the legal term is *yǔ*.
Rú Chún says: The law states: a prisoner who dies of hunger or cold is called *yǔ*.
Pronounced as *yǒngzhǔ*.
He enjoyed sword fighting.
Once, he and the monk Guīxìn visited a skilled swordsman.
Sūn Hànsháo, Commander of the Right Kuāngshèng Army, had a grudge against Yè.
He secretly accused Yè and Jìzhāo of plotting rebellion;
Lǐ Hào, Hanlin Academician, and Ān Sīqiān, Commander of the Fèngshèng Kònghè Cavalry and Infantry, further slandered them.
On the *Jiǎzǐ* day,
Yè entered court.
The Shǔ ruler ordered strongmen to kill him in the Imperial Hall,
issued an edict exposing his crimes,
and confiscated his property.
Wáng Chǔhuí, Grand Counselor, Military Commissioner of Bǎoníng, and concurrently Grand Mentor,
also wielded exclusive power and was avaricious.
Wáng Chǔhuí, with his title of Military Commissioner and Grand Mentor,
was not in Lángzhōu.
Gifts and tributes from all directions
were first presented to Chǔhuí,
then to the imperial treasury.
"All directions" here
refers only to the borders of Shǔ.
His son, Dédgūn,
was also arrogant and domineering.
After Zhāng Yè's death,
the Shǔ ruler could not bear to kill Chǔhuí,
allowing him to return to his private residence;
Chǔhuí, in fear, resigned his position,
and was made Military Commissioner of Wǔdé and concurrently Grand Minister of the Central Secretariat.
Wáng Chǔhuí also did not get to go to Zǐzhōu.
The Shǔ ruler wished to appoint Gāo Yánzhāo, the supervisor of the Pǔfēng Treasury, and Wáng Zhāoyuǎn, the supervisor of the Tea and Wine Treasury, as枢密使 (Shūmìshǐ).
The supervisors of the Pǔfēng and Tea and Wine Treasuries
were both offices established by Shǔ.
So, he appointed them as tōngzòushǐ
and put them in charge of the Privy Council affairs.
The office of tōngzòushǐ
was also established by Shǔ.
Wáng Zhāoyuǎn, a native of Chéngdū,
as a young Buddhist acolyte, followed his master into the palace.
Shǔ Gāozǔ loved his quick wit and intelligence,
and ordered him to serve the Shǔ ruler personally.
By this time,
the Shǔ ruler entrusted him with state affairs.
The gold and silk in the palace treasuries
were at his disposal,
without needing to be accounted for.
On the 25th day, wùchén,
Guō Cóngyì was appointed as the Jiédùshǐ of Yǒngxīng,
and Bái Wénkē concurrently took charge of the Hànhfǔ affairs in Hézhōng.
At this time, Guō Cóngyì was campaigning in Cháng'ān,
so he was appointed Jiédùshǐ of Yǒngxīng there;
Bái Wénkē was campaigning in Hézhōng,
so he was made to take charge of the Hànhfǔ affairs there.
On the 26th day, the Shǔ ruler appointed Lǐ Hào, the Hàlín Chéngzhǐ and Shàngshū Zuǒchéng, as Ménxià Shìláng concurrently Hùbù Shàngshū,
and Xú Guāngpǔ, the Hàlín Xuéshì and Bīngbù Shìláng, as Zhōngshū Shìláng concurrently Lǐbù Shàngshū,
both with the title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
On the 27th day, Shǔ Ān Sīqiān plotted to remove all the old generals,
and further slandered Zhào Tíngyǐn, the Wèishèng Dūzhīhuǐshǐ and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng, of plotting rebellion,
intending to take his position.
That night,
he dispatched troops to surround Zhào Tíngyǐn's residence.
It happened that Lǐ Tíngguī, the Jiédùshǐ of Shānnánxīdào, came to court,
and strongly argued that Tíngyǐn was innocent.
Thus, he was spared.
Tíngyǐn then claimed illness,
and firmly requested to resign from his military post.
On the day jiǎxū,
the Shǔ ruler granted his request.
Historians say that the Shǔ ruler used the new to displace the old.
On the 28th day, Zhào Huī, the Jiédùshǐ of Fèngxiáng, arrived in Cháng'ān.
On the day yǐhài,
he reported that Wáng Jǐngchóng's rebellious intentions were becoming increasingly clear,
and requested to advance troops to attack him.
Initially,
when Gāozǔ was stationed in Hédōng,
his imperial younger brother Chóng served as the Mǎbù Dūzhīhuǐshǐ,
and vied for power with Guō Wēi, the Fānhàn Dōukǒumùguān,
leading to a rift.
When Wēi came to power,
Chóng became anxious.
Zhèng Gǒng, the Jiédù Pàn'guān,
advised Chóng to make plans for his own safety,
and Chóng followed his advice.
Gǒng was a native of Qīngzhōu.
In the eighth month,
on the day gēngchén,
Chóng reported that he would recruit four divisions of soldiers.
From then on, he selected and recruited brave warriors,
took in fugitives,
repaired armor and weapons,
filled the treasuries,
and stopped remitting financial contributions to the court.
All this was done under the pretext of preparing against the Qìdān.
Many of the imperial edicts
were not complied with.
At this time,
Liú Chóng was acting defiantly.
However, once Guō Wēi was established,
and the empire became Zhōu,
if Hédōng had not been prepared in advance,
it would likely not have been able to hold out.
Since the three garrisons of Hézhōng, Yǒngxīng, and Fèngxiáng defied orders,
the court successively dispatched generals to suppress them.
Cháng Sī, the Jiédùshǐ of Zhāoyì, was stationed at Tóngguān;
Bái Wénkē was stationed at Tóngzhōu;
Zhào Huī was stationed at Xiányáng.
Cháng Sī and Bái Wénkē dared not approach Hézhōng,
and Zhào Huī dared not approach Fèngxiáng.
The two disliked each other like fire and water,
and from spring to autumn,
they relied on each other and were unwilling to engage in battle.
The emperor was troubled by this,
and wished to send a high-ranking official to supervise.
On the day rénwǔ,
Guō Wēi was appointed as the Xīmiàn Jūnqián Zhāowèi Ānfǔshǐ.
The Kǎoyì states: Xuē Shǐ's record of Zhōu Tàizǔ:
"On the thirteenth day of the seventh month,
he was granted the title Tóng Píngzhāngshì,
and immediately dispatched on a western expedition,
under the pretext of 'comfort and pacification'.
He departed on the sixth day of the eighth month,
leaving the capital."
According to the Veritable Records of Hàn Yǐndì and Zhōu Tàizǔ,
"In the seventh month,
he was granted the title Píngzhāngshì."
The imperial decree contained no mention of a western expedition.
It was not until the day rénwǔ of the eighth month
that he received the order to go on campaign.
This is likely an error in Xuē Shǐ.
When Wēi was about to depart,
he asked Grand Preceptor Féng Dào for strategy.
Dào said:
"Shǒuzhēn considers himself an old general,
and is supported by his soldiers.
I wish you would not begrudge official resources,
but give them to the soldiers,
then you will take away what he relies on."
Wēi followed this advice.
Guō Wēi, a hero from the ranks,
asked for strategy from the old and conservative Féng Dào.
Observing Dào's answer and Wēi's adoption of it,
it is true that people's talents and insights may not always align with the Way,
but when it comes to assessing circumstances and responding to events,
one cannot lightly dismiss them.
This laid the groundwork for Guō Wēi to gain the empire.
An imperial edict ordered Bái Wénkē to hurry to Hézhōng,
and Zhào Huī to hurry to Fèngxiáng.
On the 31st day, jiǎshēn,
the Shǔ ruler appointed Zhào Tíngyǐn as Tàifù,
granted him the title Sòng Wáng,
and for major state affairs,
consultations would be held at his residence.
On the 32nd day, wùzǐ,
Shǔ renamed Fèngxiáng to Qíyáng Jūn,
because the territory of Fèngxiáng was south of Qíshān.
On the day jǐchǒu,
Wáng Jǐngchóng was appointed Qíyáng Jiédùshǐ and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
On the 33rd day, yǐwèi,
Qián Hóngshù was appointed Dōngnán Bīngmǎ Dūyuánshuài, Zhènhǎi-Zhèndōng Jiédùshǐ concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng, and Wúyuè Guówáng.
On the 34th day, Guō Wēi discussed the attack with his generals.
The generals wished to first capture Cháng'ān and Fèngxiáng.
Hù Cóngkē, the Jiédùshǐ of Zhènguó,
said:
"Now the three rebels are allied,
recognizing Shǒuzhēn as their leader.
If Shǒuzhēn falls,
then the two garrisons will collapse on their own.
If we abandon the near to attack the distant,
and by any chance Wáng and Zhào block us in front,
and Shǒuzhēn harasses us from behind,
this is a dangerous path."
Wēi approved of this.
Thereupon, Wēi from Shǎnzhōu,
Bái Wénkē and Liú Cí, the Jiédùshǐ of Níngjiāng and Shìwèi Bùjūn Dūzhīhuǐshǐ, from Tóngzhōu,
and Cháng Sī from Tóngguān,
attacked Hézhōng from three directions.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Shǎnzhōu north to Hézhōng is 237 lǐ.
From Tóngzhōu east to Hézhōng is 60 lǐ.
From Tóngguān across the river to Hézhōng is over 100 lǐ.
Shǎn,
read as shǎn.
Wēi shared hardships and joys with his soldiers,
and would reward even small achievements.
He would personally attend to even minor injuries.
Regardless of whether a soldier was worthy or unworthy,
if they had something to report or suggest,
he would receive it with gentle words and demeanor.
He did not get angry at disobedience,
nor did he reprimand for minor faults.
Because of this, the generals and soldiers all turned their hearts to Wēi.
Initially,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn believed that the imperial army had all once been under his command,
and had received his favors.
Moreover, the soldiers were traditionally arrogant
and found the strict Hàn laws difficult,
so he thought that when they arrived, they would knock on the city gates and welcome him,
and he could just wait for them.
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn was accustomed to the affairs of Fèngxiáng and Tàiyuán,
and based his expectations on Yáng Sīquán's anticipation of the Hàn army.
However, all of them had forgotten Shǒuzhēn's old favors.
On the day jǐhài,
when they arrived at the city walls,
they raised flags, beat drums,
and shouted curses enthusiastically.
Shǒuzhēn watched them, his face losing color.
Bái Wénkē captured the Xīguān City,
and built a stockade west of the river.
The Xīguān City of Hézhōng was west of the river,
serving to protect the Pújīn pontoon bridge.
Wēi built a stockade west of the city.
Cháng Sī and Guō Wēi,
presumably, built stockades close to the city.
Wēi, deeming Cháng Sī lacked leadership ability, first sent him back to his garrison.
The generals wanted to attack the city quickly.
Wēi said:
"Shǒuzhēn is a veteran general from the previous dynasty,
skilled in fighting and generous,
having repeatedly achieved military successes.
Moreover, the city faces the great river,
its towers and battlements are strong and complete,
it is not easy to take lightly.
Furthermore, if they fight from behind the city walls,
and we attack from below,
how is that different from leading our soldiers into boiling water or fire?
Valor has its ebbs and flows,
attacks have their urgency and slowness,
timing has its suitability,
and affairs have their priority;
it is better to first establish a long siege and hold them,
cutting off their escape routes.
We will wash our weapons and graze our horses,
sitting idly while food is transported to us,
well-fed and with ample provisions.
Once there is no food in the city,
and the public treasury and private wealth are all exhausted,
then we will advance with ladders and battering rams to pressure them,
and send out urgent messages to solicit their surrender.
Their generals and soldiers,
trying to escape death,
will not even be able to protect their own fathers and sons,
let alone a rabble of a crowd!
Sīwǎn and Jǐngchóng
need only be engaged by a detachment of troops;
they are not to be worried about."
Thereupon, he mobilized over twenty thousand laborers from various prefectures,
and had Bái Wénkē and others lead them
to dig long moats,
build connecting fortifications,
and arrange their formations to besiege the city.
Wēi further said to his generals:
"Shǒuzhēn previously feared Gāozǔ,
and dared not act defiantly;
'Xiàng'
refers to former times.
'Chīzhāng'
means like an owl spreading its wings,
wishing to fly high and far.
His achievements are not yet apparent,
and he holds me in low regard,
hence his rebellion.
It is proper to control him with stillness."
Thereupon, he lowered his banners and muffled his drums,
only setting up fire-posts along the river,
extending for dozens of *lǐ*,
and rotating infantrymen to guard them.
He dispatched the naval forces to moor their boats by the bank,
and any enemy attempting to sneak past
were all captured.
At this, Shǒuzhēn was like a fish caught in a net.
The Military Governor of Wǔdé of Shǔ and concurrently Minister of the Central Secretariat, Wáng Chǔhuí, requested retirement.
On the *Xīnchǒu* day,
he retired as Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
The Southern Hàn ruler
Since the Central Kingdom adopted "Hàn" as its dynastic name,
the Hàn in Lingnan
is written as "Southern Hàn" to distinguish it.
(The place) Xuānhuà
was a territory of Fāngxiàn county in Hàn.
During the Jìn dynasty, Jìnxīng Commandery was established.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery
and established Xuānhuà County and Jìnxīng County.
The Táng dynasty made Xuānhuà the seat of Yōngzhōu,
and Jìnxīng also belonged to Yōngzhōu.
The King of Chǔ, Mǎ Xīguǎng, did not permit it.
The Southern Hàn ruler was angry,
and asked Yǔnzhāng:
"Can Duke Mǎ still plan strategies for the southern lands?"
He replied:
"The Mǎ brothers
are busy striving for their own ruin and have no time,
how can they harm us!"
The Southern Hàn ruler said:
"Indeed.
Xīguǎng is cowardly and stingy,
and his soldiers have long forgotten how to fight.
This is the opportune moment for us to advance and conquer."
This was the origin of the Southern Hàn raising an army to attack Chǔ.
Mǎ Xī'è, the Military Governor of Wǔpíng, requested to maintain separate tributary relations with the court from King Xīguǎng of Chǔ,
seeking additional official titles and ranks from the imperial court,
wishing to make Tán and Lǎng like two separate states.
He heavily bribed the powerful officials
to reject his request.
In the ninth month,
on the *Rénzǐ* day,
an imperial edict was bestowed upon Xī'è and King Xīguǎng of Chǔ,
instructing them
that "brothers should live in harmony,
and all tribute from Xī'è
should be reported via Xīguǎng."
Xī'è did not comply.
The Shǔ army reinforced Wáng Jǐngchóng's forces at Sànguān.
Zhào Huī dispatched the Commander Lǐ Yàncóng to launch a surprise attack,
defeating them.
(The *Kǎoyì* says: The Veritable Records state,
"On the *Wùchén* day,
the Commissioner of Military Affairs, Guō [Huì], reported: 'Commander Lǐ Yàncóng led troops to ambush the Sichuan bandits
at Dàsànguān,
killing over three thousand bandits,
the rest abandoned their armor and fled.' "
The Veritable Records of Hàn Yǐndì state,
"In the ninth month,
Lǐ Yàncóng defeated the Shǔ army at Sànguān."
However, the Veritable Records of the Later Shǔ ruler make no mention of it.
The Shǔ Veritable Records state,
"In the tenth month,
Ān Sīqiān defeated the Hàn army at Shíjiā Zhúlín,
and then burned and destroyed Bǎojī.
In the twelfth month,
he again defeated the Hàn army at Yùnǚtán."
However, the Hàn Veritable Records make no mention of it.
Probably, both countries only reported their victories and concealed their defeats.
However, the Hàn Veritable Records state that the government army was less than ten thousand men,
while the Shǔ army was several times that,
meaning twenty to thirty thousand men.
This was not a minor engagement,
how could it be entirely unrecorded?
Killing three thousand people was not a minor defeat,
how could they immediately launch another campaign in the tenth month?
Perhaps in the ninth month, it was merely a small sally by a Shǔ border general,
who was defeated by Hàn,
and the Hàn general exaggerated it in his report.
Furthermore, the Shǔ Veritable Records,
in the tenth month, only state
"Sīqiān retreated to Fèngzhōu,"
not
"returned to Xīngyuán."
In the twelfth month, it states
"Sīqiān advanced from Xīngyuán to Fèngzhōu."
Perhaps the tenth month entry was abbreviated.
The Shǔ ruler, finding that Zhāng Yè and Wáng Chǔhuí monopolized government affairs,
leading to many obstructions,
on the *Jǐwèi* day,
first established a petition box,
later renamed the Suggestion Box.
Wáng Jǐngchóng killed over seventy members of Hóu Yì's family,
resenting Hóu Yì for slandering him at court.
(Hóu Yì) escaped.
On the *Gēngshēn* day,
Rénjǔ was appointed Prefect of Xízhōu.
Rénjǔ's son Yán'guǎng
was still in swaddling clothes.
His wet nurse, Lady Liú, exchanged him with her own son.
When choosing a wet nurse,
one must select someone with a newborn child,
and she is allowed to bring her child,
thus enabling the exchange.
Begging for food, they reached Dàliáng
and returned to Hóu Yì's home.
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn repeatedly sent out troops attempting to break through the long siege,
but all were defeated and returned;
he sent people carrying wax pills to seek help from Táng, Shǔ, and Qìdān,
but all were captured by the patrols.
Food in the city was almost exhausted,
and the number of people starving to death increased daily.
Shǒuzhēn's worry was evident on his face.
He summoned Zǒnglún and questioned him.
Zǒnglún flattered Shǒuzhēn three months earlier.
*Jié*
(pronunciation) *qù jí fān*.
"(Your) Great King is destined to be the Son of Heaven,
no one can take it from you.
However, this region currently suffers from a disaster.
When the destruction is almost complete,
and only one man and one horse remain,
that will be the time for the Great King to rise like a magpie."
Zhuāngzǐ said: A magpie builds its nest precariously on a high city wall,
atop a high branch.
When the city crumbles and the nest breaks,
it rises with the wind.
Therefore, a noble person in the world,
if the time is right, acts righteously;
if the time is wrong, he rises like a magpie.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Wáng Jǐngchóng sent his son Déràng,
and Zhào Sīwǎn sent his son Huáiyì,
to see the Shǔ ruler in Chéngdū.
On the day of Wùyín,
Wáng Jǐngchóng dispatched troops out of the west gate.
Zhào Huī attacked and defeated them,
then captured Xīguān City.
Wáng Jǐngchóng retreated to defend the main city;
Zhào Huī
dug trenches and surrounded it,
challenging them to battle repeatedly,
but they did not come out.
Zhào Huī secretly sent over a thousand men, donned in armor and bearing weapons,
displaying the banners of Shǔ,
to descend along the southern mountains,
ordering all his armies to declare loudly:
"The Shǔ army has arrived!"
Wáng Jǐngchóng indeed sent several thousand soldiers out to meet them.
Zhào Huī set up an ambush and attacked,
annihilating them all.
From then on, Wáng Jǐngchóng no longer dared to sally forth.
The Shǔ lord sent Ān Sīqiān, Jìedùshǐ of Shānnánxīdào, to lead troops to relieve Fèngxiáng.
Wú Zhāoyì, Zuǒ Púshè and concurrently Ménxià Shìláng, Tóng Píngzhāngshì, submitted a memorial remonstrating, saying:
"Your subject humbly observes that Emperor Zhuāngzōng's ambition coveted the west,
and the former Shǔ lord's intention was to travel north.
'Ambition coveted the west'
refers to Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Hòutáng being covetous of Shǔ's wealth and thus attacking it.
'The former Shǔ lord'
refers to Wáng Yǎn.
'Intention was to travel north'
refers to his eagerness to visit Qínzhōu.
Both events are found in the 'Annals of Zhuāngzōng'.
'Shàng'
is pronounced 'cháng' (翻).
Both presented memorials of remonstrance,
but were utterly unheeded;
what was achieved?
These two dynasties alone
can serve as a warning."
He did not listen, and further dispatched Hán Bǎozhēn, Jìedùshǐ of Xióngwǔ, to lead troops out of Qiānyáng to divide the Hàn army's strength.
Qiānyáng County belonged to Lǒngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it is sixty-seven *lǐ* east of the prefecture.
'Qiān'
is pronounced 'kǔ jiān' (翻).
Wáng Jǐngchóng sent Lǐ Yànshùn, former Jìedùshǐ of Yìchéng, of Suānzǎo, and others to intercept the Shǔ army.
Suānzǎo was
an ancient county,
which belonged to Biànzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it is ninety *lǐ* northeast of the prefecture.
On the day of Bǐngshēn,
Ān Sīqiān encamped at the right border.
'Right border'
was probably the western border of Bǎojī,
the place where Hàn and Shǔ divided their territories.
Sīqiān sent Shēn Guì, Cìshǐ of Méizhōu, with two thousand troops to head towards Móbi,
setting up an ambush in the bamboo forest.
On the morning of Dīngyǒu,
Shēn Guì, with several hundred soldiers, advanced to Bǎojī and formed ranks.
The Hàn army pursued them,
encountered the ambush and were defeated.
The Shǔ army pursued the fleeing enemy,
and captured Bǎojī Fort.
When the Shǔ army departed,
the Hàn army re-entered Bǎojī.
On the day of Jǐhài,
Sīqiān advanced to encamp by the Wèishuǐ.
The Wèishuǐ flows north of Bǎojī County.
Sīqiān feared them,
and said to his troops:
"Our provisions are few and the enemy is strong;
we should make other plans for the future."
On the day of Xīnchǒu,
he retreated to encamp at Fèngzhōu,
and soon returned to Xīngyuán.
Xīngyuán was
Ān Sīqiān's original commandery.
He was a native of Lùzhōu.
Gāo Cónghuì, Jìedùshǐ of Jīngnán and King Wénxiàn of Nánpíng,
fell critically ill.
He appointed his son Gāo Bǎoróng, Jìedù Fùshǐ, to manage all military affairs, both internal and external.
On the day of Guǐmǎo,
Gāo Cónghuì died;
he was fifty-eight years old.
Gāo Bǎoróng was
Gāo Cónghuì's third son.
History does not mention the reason for his succession.
Gāo Yǔnquán, Jìedùshǐ of Zhāngwǔ, had a grudge against Lǐ Yíyīn, Jìedùshǐ of Dìngnán.
From Yánzhōu north to Xiàzhōu is three hundred eighty *lǐ*.
The two commanderies bordered each other,
so disputes easily arose.
'Nán'
is pronounced 'nǎi dàn' (翻).
Gāo Yǔnquán dispatched troops to encamp on the border between Yán and Dān.
Hearing that the imperial army had surrounded Hézhōng,
he then retreated.
On the day of Jiǎchén,
Gāo Yǔnquán reported the situation,
and Lǐ Yíyīn also defended himself.
The imperial court mediated their reconciliation.
Earlier,
when Gāo Zǔ entered Dàliáng,
FÉng Dào, Tàishī, and Lǐ Sōng, Tàizǐ Tàifù, were both in Zhēndìng.
This event is mentioned in the previous volume under Tiānfú 13th year.
Lǐ Sōng's residence was bestowed upon Sū Féngjí.
Sū Féngjí took possession of all the buried treasures in Lǐ Sōng's residence and his detached property in Luòyáng.
When Lǐ Sōng returned to court,
he considered his position isolated and precarious.
During the Shí Jìn era,
Emperor Gāo Zǔ of Hàn already harbored a grudge against Lǐ Sōng;
after ascending the throne,
Lǐ Sōng first returned to court,
hence he harbored inner fear.
He was always cautious and humble,
often feigning illness and secluding himself.
However, his two younger brothers, Lǐ Yǔ and Lǐ Yí,
together with Sū Féngjí's sons and younger brothers, were all court officials.
They occasionally uttered resentful words when drunk,
saying
"They took our residence and family assets."
Sū Féngjí consequently disliked them.
Not long after,
Lǐ Sōng offered the title deeds of his residences in both capitals to Sū Féngjí,
but Sū Féngjí became even more displeased.
Táo Gǔ, Hànlín Xuéshì,
who had previously been recommended by Lǐ Sōng,
then further slandered him.
The Hàn laws were already strict,
and Shǐ Hóngzhào, Shìwèi Dūzhīhuīshǐ, was particularly cruel.
He favored and trusted Xiè Huī, Kǒngmùguān.
Anyone who entered the military prison
was subjected to torture at Xiè Huī's will,
and none failed to falsely implicate themselves.
When the three rebels joined forces,
'Three rebels'
refers to Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, Wáng Jǐngchóng, and Zhào Sīwǎn.
The common people sometimes spread alarming rumors.
Shǐ Hóngzhào commanded the capital's forbidden army
and patrolled the capital city.
'Bù'
means 'to divide'.
'Luó'

Guō Cóngyì sent someone to lure him.
Initially,
when Sīwǎn was young,
he sought to become a servant to the retired Zuǒ Xiāowèi Shàngjiàngjūn Lǐ Sù.
Sù did not accept him,
saying:
"This man's eyes are wild and his words are outrageous;
he will surely become a rebel in the future."
Sù's wife, Lady Zhāng,
was the daughter of Zhāng Quányì.
Zhāng Quányì, when garrisoned in Luò,
achieved fame between the Liáng and Táng dynasties.
"If you reject him now,
he will cause trouble later."
So she generously gave him gold and silk.
When Sīwǎn occupied Cháng'ān,
Sù lived in leisure in the city.
Sīwǎn frequently went to see him,
bowing and prostrating himself with the same old courtesy.
In the twelfth year of Tiānfú,
Zhào Zàilǐ traveled from Cháng'ān to the Qìdān court.
His subordinate generals who remained in Cháng'ān revolted,
and Lǐ Sù suppressed and executed them,
indicating his prestige must have been significant.
Zhào Sīwǎn also cherished the kindness he received in the past,
so even though he was a usurper,
his respect for Sù was like a slave serving his master.
數,
read suò jué fān.
"This fellow comes too often
and will defile me."
He wanted to commit suicide.
His wife said:
"Why not persuade him to return to the state!"
The history indicates Lǐ Sù's wife was intelligent.
Sù then, with his Pànguān Chéng Ràngnéng, persuaded Sīwǎn, saying:
"You originally had no ill will toward the state,
but merely feared punishment.
Now the state is deploying troops on three fronts,
none of which have achieved success yet.
The three fronts refer to
Guō Wēi attacking Hézhōng,
Zhào Huī attacking Fèngxiáng,
and Guō Cóngyì attacking Sīwǎn.
The court will surely be pleased,
and you can certainly retain wealth and honor.
How can you just sit and await death?"
Sīwǎn followed his advice,
sending an envoy to the court to request surrender.
On Yǐchǒu,
Sīwǎn was appointed Huázhōu Liúhòu,
designated as Zhèngguó Jūn Liúhòu.
He was ordered to proceed directly to his post.
He was not allowed to enter the court,
which was to calm his restless heart.
12 The Wúyuè Nèiyá Dūzhǐhuīshǐ Dǒu Tāo
was a member of Hú Jìnsī's faction.
Kǎoyì says: In Wúyuè Bèishǐ and Shíguó Jìnián,
Tāo's surname is always
金
next to
斗.
According to Hé Shì Xìngyuàn and Yuánhé Xìngzuǎn,
this surname does not exist.
Now, according to the dictionary: 鈄,
pronounced tā kǒu, tú kǒu èr qiē,
both say it is a surname.
I note that Guǎngyùn says the surname Dǒu comes from Xìngyuàn.
His confession implicated Chancellor Hóngyì.
Wúyuè King Hóngchù did not want to pursue the investigation thoroughly,
and demoted Tāo to Chǔzhōu.
13 In the sixth month,
on Guǐyǒu, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
14 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Jiǎchén,
Zhào Sīwǎn cast off his armor and left the city to receive the edict.
Guō Cóngyì guarded his south gate with troops,
then sent him back into the city.
Sīwǎn requested his personal guards and weapons,
and Cóngyì also provided them;
Sīwǎn procrastinated,
collecting wealth,
and changed his departure date three times.
Cóngyì and others suspected him,
and secretly reported to Guō Wēi,
requesting permission to act against him,
which Wēi granted.
On Rénzǐ,
Cóngyì and Dūjiān, Nányuàn Xuānhuīshǐ Wáng Jùn,
it should be
Xuānhuī Nányuànshǐ,
positioned themselves in the government residence.
They summoned Sīwǎn for a farewell drink,
and then seized him,
along with Cháng Yànqīng and his father, brothers, and three hundred of his retainers,
all of whom were executed in the marketplace.
15 On Jiǎyín,
Guō Wēi attacked Hézhōng,
capturing its outer wall.
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn gathered his remaining forces
and retreated to defend the inner city.
His generals requested an immediate assault,
but Wēi said:
"When a bird is cornered, it will peck;
how much more so an army!
Catching fish in dried-up water,
what need is there for haste?"
On Rénxū,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, with his wife and son Chóngxūn and others, set themselves on fire.
Wēi entered the city,
capturing his son Chóngyù and others, and his appointed officials, Chancellor Jìng, Sūn Yuàn, Pìshūshǐ Liú Ruì, Guóshī Zǒnglún and others,
and sent them to Dàliáng,
where they were torn limb from limb in the marketplace.
Jìng
is the surname;
is his given name.
圉,
read tū tóng fān,
the same as 嵞.
Shuōwén says
禹會諸侯於塗山之
塗
is written as
嵞.
磔,
pronounced zhú gé fān.
Referring to Zhào Xiūjǐ, who frequently admonished Lǐ Shǒuzhēn.
In the flourishing Táng, there were Tiānwén Bóshì and Tiānwénshēng,
all belonging to the Sītiānjiān;
those awaiting orders in the Hànlín Yuàn were called Hànlín Tiānwén.
Wēi reviewed Shǒuzhēn's documents,
and found letters of communication from powerful court officials and regional governors with Shǒuzhēn,
whose words and intentions were rebellious.
He intended to present them,
but Mìshū Láng Yúcì Wáng Pǔ advised:
"Demons emerge in contention at night,
but vanish by themselves when they see the sun.
I wish that all of them be burned,
to pacify the wavering hearts."
Wēi followed his advice.
Wáng Pǔ's advancement in Zhōu
came from this statement.
When Guō Wēi campaigned in the west,
he gained Lǐ Gǔ and Wáng Pǔ from outside,
and Fàn Zhì from inside.
How could this be achieved by a mere stubborn military man of the time!
16 After the three rebellions were quelled,
Fèngxiáng was still not pacified at this time.
Due to the emperor's arrogance and indulgence, this is generally recounted.
He was intimate with his attendants.
The Fēilóng Envoy, Háqiū Hòu Kuāngzàn,
and the Chájiǔ Envoy, Tàiyuán Guō Yǔnmíng, gained favor through flattery.
The emperor liked to engage in riddles and vulgar jokes with them.
Sòucí
means hidden words.
Hǎo
is read as Hū Dào Fān.
Sòu
is read as Suǒ Jiū Fān.
The emperor took no notice.
On Guǐhài,
Tài Cháng Qīng Zhāng Zhāo submitted a memorial, saying:
"It is advisable to draw close to Confucian officials
and study the classics and teachings."
He did not listen.
Zhāo
was originally Zhāo Yuǎn,
changed to avoid the given name of Gāozǔ.
17 On Wùchén,
Guō Cóngyì, the Military Commissioner of Yǒngxīng, was granted the additional title of Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
Hù Cóngkē, the Military Commissioner of Zhènguó, was transferred to be the Military Commissioner of Hùguó.
Liú Cí, the Grand Usher of Horse and Foot Soldiers for the Héchōng Campaign Army, was made the Military Commissioner of Zhènguó.
18 The Lord of Táng again promoted Wèi Cén.
Wèi Cén had been demoted for a crime, as seen in Volume 286, Gāozǔ's Tiānfú 12th year,
which was the 5th year of Bǎodà for the Lord of Táng.
He participated in national politics.
Both relied on imperial favor and were frivolous.
Although they were not allied with Cén,
all the people of the country detested them.
Fàn Chōngmǐn, the Yúanwàiláng of the Ministry of Revenue,
was of a stern and upright character.
He instructed Wáng Jiànfēng, the Grand Usher of Tiānwēi, to submit a memorial
criticizing all the officials in power
and requesting the promotion of upright individuals.
The Lord of Táng considered Jiànfēng a military official commanding troops
who should not interfere in national politics,
and was furious.
He exiled Jiànfēng to Chízhōu.
Before he arrived,
he was killed.
Chōngmǐn was executed in the marketplace.
When the Lord of Táng heard that Héchōng had been defeated,
he appointed Zhū Yuán as Jìabù Yuánwàiláng
and Lǐ Píng, a Dàizhào of the Wénlǐyuàn, as Shàngshū Yuánwàiláng.
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn had sent Zhū Yuán and Lǐ Píng to Táng last year in November.
The Wénlǐyuàn
was established by Southern Táng.
The Shàngshū Yuánwàiláng had no specific bureau,
but was established among the Láng and Yuánwài officials of the twenty-four departments.
19 Wúyuè Wáng Hóngchù appointed Chancellor Hóngyì to oversee Míngzhōu.
He removed Hóngyì due to the affair of Dǒu Tāo.
20 Wáng Shǒu'ēn, the Commissioner of Xījīng and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì,
was greedy and despicable,
dedicated solely to accumulating wealth.
Funeral carriages could not leave the city without paying a fee.
Even those who emptied latrines and begged for a living
were not exempt from taxes and levies.
Shū
is read as Xù Lǚ Fān.
Shūcè
means taking people's "tiger vessels" (chamber pots),
emptying the filth,
and washing them with water.
When a rich family was marrying a wife,
Shǒu'ēn went with several actors as guests,
obtained several ingots of silver, and returned.
"Bīn"
is sometimes written as
"Hè".
Tǐng
is read as Tú Dǐng Fān.
In the eighth month,
on Jiǎshēn,
Guō Wēi returned from Héchōng,
passing through Luòyáng.
Shǒu'ēn, relying on his combined position as general and chancellor,
(meaning Commissioner, Military Commissioner, and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì,
which refers to a position combining general and chancellor)
angered Wēi,
who considered it an insult.
He feigned taking a bath
and did not meet him.
Immediately, using a "tóuzi," he ordered Bái Wénkē, the Military Commissioner of Bǎoyì and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì, to replace Shǒu'ēn as Commissioner.
Shěn Kuò said: "After the Latter Táng Zhuāngzōng reinstated the Privy Council,
Guō Chóngtāo and Ān Zhònghuǐ successively served there,
beginning the separation of political affairs.
Decrees not directly issued by the Central Secretariat were called 'xuān,'
like imperial edicts from the Central Secretariat.
For minor matters, 'tóuzi' were issued,
resembling 'tángtiē'."
Shǒu'ēn was still waiting in the guest chamber.
Kècì
is what is now called the guest seat.
He sat in the guest chamber awaiting an audience.
"The new Commissioner has already taken office at the yámen."
Shǒu'ēn was greatly astonished,
and returned in disarray,
finding his hundreds of family members already expelled from the yámen
and in the main thoroughfare.
The imperial court did not question this,
and appointed Wénkē concurrently as Shìzhōng,
serving as Commissioner of Xījīng.
Ōuyáng Xiū remarked: "From ancient times, countries that suffered chaos and downfall
first destroyed their legal systems
and then chaos followed.
This is the natural course of events,
and the period of the Five Dynasties exemplifies this.
Both Wénkē and Shǒu'ēn were high officials of Hàn,
yet Zhou Tàizǔ, with a single 'tóuzi' from the Privy Council, replaced them
as if changing guardsmen.
At that time, Tàizǔ did not yet harbor ambitions to usurp the throne,
but his actions were such
because it had become a habitual practice.
Thus, Wénkē dared not disobey,
and Shǒu'ēn dared not resist.
Since Tàizǔ carried this out without hesitation,
and the Hàn court's monarch and ministers also ignored it,
was this not the ultimate breakdown of discipline and order, leading to such a state!
I recall that at the beginning of Táng Mǐndì's reign,
Zhū Hóngzhāo and Féng Yūn, using 'xuān' from the Privy Council, replaced various regional commanders,
which led to the rebellion of Lù Wáng.
Although the outcomes differed,
the heavy power of the Privy Council had a precedent.
One must not neglect the subtle and always guard against its gradual development.
How can one not be cautious!"
21 When Shǒu'ēn arrived in Dàliáng,
fearing punishment,
he made extensive contributions and heavily bribed influential officials.
The imperial court also considered that Shǒu'ēn had been the first to bring Lùzhōu back to Hàn,
(as seen in Volume 286, Tiānfú 12th year),
and therefore only executed a few of his close associates.
22 Mǎ Xī'è mobilized all able-bodied men from Lǎngzhōu to form a local militia,
establishing the army named Jìngjiāng Jūn.
Zàohào
means creating a military title.
He was about to attack Tánzhōu,
but his wife, Lady Yuàn, admonished him, saying:
(The surname Yuàn: Zǐ Wén, son of Shang Wǔdì, was enfeoffed in Yuàn
and thus took it as his surname.
According to the Zuǒ Zhuàn,
there was a great official from Qí named Yuàn Héjì.
Zhào Míngchéng's Jīnshí Lù contains a stele for Yuàn Zhèn, a Colonial Officer of Jīngzhōu during the Hàn Dynasty,
which states: His ancestors came from Yuàn Bǎihé,
who was a Music Master of Jìn,
and whose family for generations managed the ceremonial rites of the court.
There was also Yuàn Zǐyuán,
who was truly capable of managing the principles of Yin and Yang.
According to the Xìngshì Zhì,
all say that the Yuàn clan descended from Yuàn Héjì.
Now, this stele mentions Yuàn Bǎihé and Zǐyuán,
who are not found in either the Zuǒ Zhuàn or the Guóyǔ,
so I record it to inform those who know.)
"Brothers attacking each other,
victory or defeat, will both be laughed at by others."
He did not listen,
and led his troops towards Chángshā.
Mǎ Xīguǎng heard of this and said:
"Lǎngzhōu
is my brother.
I cannot contend with him;
I should just yield the kingdom to him."
Liú Yànfù and Lǐ Hónggāo strongly argued against it.
So, Wáng Yūn, the Prefect of Yuèzhōu, was appointed General Commander of the War Fleet.
Yànfù was made Supervising Commander of his army.
On Jǐchǒu,
Xī'è was decisively defeated at Púshè Zhōu,
and 300 of his warships were captured.
Yūn pursued Xī'è,
about to catch him,
when Xīguǎng sent an envoy to recall him, saying:
"Do not harm my brother!"
Yūn led his troops back.
Yūn
was Huán's son.
Xī'è fled back in a light boat from Chìshā Hú.
(Chìshā Hú is west of Dòngtíng Hú
and connects with Dòngtíng Hú.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù says: The Lǐshuǐ River meets the waters of Chìshā Hú;
the lake water connects north to the river and flows south into the Lǐshuǐ.)
"Calamity is about to arrive.
I cannot bear to see it."
He jumped into a well and died.
On the 23rd day, Wùxū,
Guō Wēi arrived at Dàliáng.
He entered to have an audience.
The Emperor consoled him,
bestowing upon him gold, silk, clothes, a jade belt, and a saddled horse.
He declined, saying:
"Your servant received the mandate a year ago.
Last July,
I was ordered to lead Guō Wēi on a western expedition.
By now, it has been more than a year."
'Qī'
is read as 'jī'.
"What merit have I?
Moreover, your servant leads troops outside.
All those who stabilize the capital, provide for its needs, and ensure the troops are well-fed
are due to the efforts of the high ministers who remain in the court.
How dare your servant alone accept this reward!
Please bestow it upon all of them."
They also discussed promoting him to
a regional commander.
He declined, saying:
"Yáng Bīn's position is above mine,
yet he has not received territory and enfeoffment."
At that time, Yáng Bīn was the Pīmì Shǐ,
his position was above Guō Wēi's,
and he had never commanded a Jiézhèn.
"Shǐ Hóngzhào cannot be used as a comparison."
Guō Wēi himself said that his duty was close and confidential,
that he was a minister of the curtain and tent.
Shǐ Hóngzhào commanded the Imperial Guard,
which is why he held a Jíezhèn,
so he could not be compared.
On the day Rén'yín,
the nine individuals—the chancellors, Pīmì, Xuānhuī, Sānsī, and Shìwèishǐ—were all rewarded
equally with Wēi.
At that time, there were three chancellors:
Dòu Zhēnggù, Sū Féngjí, and Sū Yǔguī.
The Pīmì Shǐ was
Yáng Bīn.
The Xuānhuī Shǐ were
Wáng Jùn
and Wú Qiányù.
The Sānsī Shǐ was
Wáng Zhāng.
The Shìwèishǐ was
Shǐ Hóngzhào.
In total, there were eight people.
The remaining one is unknown.
Perhaps Guō Wēi himself was included to make nine?
He declined, saying:
"Formulating strategies and plans
comes from the imperial court;
dispatching troops and supplying provisions
relies on the regional commands;
enduring exposure and fighting battles
falls to the generals and soldiers.
Yet, the merit is attributed solely to your servant.
How can your servant bear this!"
On the day Yǐsì,
Wēi was additionally appointed concurrent Shìzhōng,
and Shǐ Hóngzhào concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng.
On the day Xīnhài,
Dòu Zhēnggù was additionally appointed Sītú,
Sū Féngjí Sīkōng,
Sū Yǔguī Zuǒ Púyè,
and Yáng Bīn Yòu Púyè.
The high ministers deliberated,
believing that the widespread bestowal of grace upon court officials
might cause regional commanders to feel overlooked.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
Gāo Xíngzhōu, the Tiānxíong Jiéduhǐ, was additionally appointed Shǒu Tàishī;
Ān Shěnqí, the Shānnán Dōngdào Jiéduhǐ, Shǒu Tàifù;
Fú Yànqīng, the Tàiníng Jiéduhǐ, Shǒu Tàibǎo;
Liú Chóng, the Hédōng Jiéduhǐ, concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng.
On the day Jǐwèi,
Liú Xìn, the Zhōngwǔ Jiéduhǐ, Mùróng Yànchāo, the Tiānpíng Jiéduhǐ, and Liú Zhū, the Pínglú Jiéduhǐ, were all additionally appointed concurrent Shìzhōng.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
Féng Huī, the Shuòfāng Jiéduhǐ, and Lǐ Yíyīn, the Dìngnán Jiéduhǐ,
were additionally appointed concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Rénshēn,
Sūn Fāngjiǎn, the Yìwǔ Jiéduhǐ, and Liú Yūn, the Wǔníng Jiéduhǐ, were additionally appointed Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Wúyuè Wáng Hóngchù was additionally appointed Shàngshū Lìng,
and Chǔ Wáng Xīguǎng Tàiwèi.
On the day Bǐngxū,
Gāo Bǎoróng, the Jīngnán Jiéduhǐ, was additionally appointed concurrent Shìzhōng.
Commentators believed:
"Guō Wēi not claiming all the merit for himself, but distributing it among others,
is indeed admirable.
However, for the state's noble titles,
to extend throughout the realm because one person achieved merit,
is this not excessive!"
Wúyuè Wáng Hóngchù recruited people who could reclaim wasteland,
exempting them from taxes.
Consequently, there was no abandoned land within his territory.
Someone requested to investigate overlooked adult males among the populace to increase revenue.
'Yídīng'
refers to people who had reached adulthood but were omitted from household registers
and had not borne taxes or corvée.
Hóngchù had him beaten at the national gate.
All the people of the state were pleased.
Mǎ Xīzhān, the Chǔ Jìngjiāng Jiéduhǐ, seeing his elder brothers Xī'è and Xīguǎng fighting,
repeatedly sent envoys to advise them to stop,
but they did not listen.
Knowing that the clan would ultimately be destroyed,
a carbuncle erupted on his back.
On the day Dīnghài,
he died.
The Qìdān invaded Héběi,
killing and plundering wherever they went.
The Jiéduhǐ and Cìshǐ each barricaded themselves in their cities.
Their cavalry reached Bèizhōu and the northern border of Yèdū.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Thirty *lǐ* south of Bèizhōu
is the northern border of Yèdū.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Pīmì Shǐ Guō Wēi was dispatched to lead the various generals to resist them,
with Xuānhuī Shǐ Wáng Jùn supervising his army.
This was to lay the groundwork for Wáng Jùn to assist Guō Wēi in raising an army and marching on the capital.
In the eleventh month,
when the Qìdān heard that the Hàn army had crossed the river,
they withdrew.
On the day Xīnhài,
Guō Wēi's army reached Yèdū,
ordering Wáng Jùn to divide his forces and head towards Zhèn and Dìng.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Wēi arrived at Xíngzhōu.
The Táng army crossed the Huái River
and attacked Zhèngyáng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Yǐngzhōu Yǐngshàng Xiàn has Zhèngyáng Zhèn,
which is on the Huái ferry.
Bái Fújìn, a general from Yǐngzhōu, attacked
and defeated them.
Yáng Bīn's governance was harsh and meticulous.
Initially,
Zhōu Càn from Xíngzhōu was a general of the Imperial Guard.
Having been dismissed from his post with no one to rely on,
he followed Wáng Jǐngchóng on the western expedition.
When Jǐngchóng rebelled,
Zhōu Càn became his chief strategist.
Bīn reported:
"All former officials
like to stir up regional vassals."
'Qiánzīguān'
refers to officials whose positions were all granted by previous dynasties.
'Xǐ'
is read as 'xǔ jǐ fān'.
"Soon, they gather from all directions,
blocking the chancellors' horses daily to seek official positions."
On the day Xīnmǎo,
Bīn again reported:
"Former officials should be divided to live in the two capitals,
awaiting vacancies to fill."
Many were left drifting without a place.
Bīn further reported:
"All who travel on the roads
must be issued *guòsuǒ*."
The system of the Prosperous Táng had twenty-six passes throughout the realm.
Those crossing a pass obtained a *guòsuǒ* from the Sīmén Lángzhōng,
similar to using passes in the Hàn dynasty.
Sòng Bái said: Ancient writings on silk were called *xū*,
and carved wood was called *qì*.
These two objects were collectively called *guòsuǒ*.
Public sentiment was greatly disturbed,
so it was stopped.
Zhào Huī urgently attacked Fèngxiáng.
Zhōu Càn said to Wáng Jǐngchóng:
"You previously were closely allied with Pú and Yōng."
'Pú'
refers to Lǐ Shǒuzhēn,
'Yōng'
refers to Zhào Sīwǎn.
'Yōng'
is read as 'yōng'.
"The Shu children are not to be relied upon."
Wáng Jǐngchóng sought aid from Shu,
but the Shu troops did not arrive,
hence the remark "not to be relied upon."
Jǐngchóng said:
"Good.
I will think about it further."
A few days later,
the outer assault grew more urgent.
Jǐng Chóng (景崇) said to his followers,
"The situation is desperate.
I wish to make a desperate move."
He then said to his generals, Gōngsūn Niǎn (公孫輦) and Zhāng Sīliàn (張思練),
"Zhào Huī's (趙暉) elite troops
are mostly north of the city.
Tomorrow, before the fifth watch,
you two shall burn the east gate and feign surrender,
but do not let the bandits enter.
Zhōu Càn (周璨) and I will take the Yá Bīng (牙兵) and burst out of the north gate to attack Huī's army.
Even if we do not succeed and die,
it is better than doing nothing."
They all said,
"Excellent."
On Guǐsì (癸巳) day,
before dawn,
Niǎn (輦) and Sīliàn (思練) burned the east gate and requested surrender.
Fires also erupted from the government offices and the Yá (牙) (military headquarters).
The two generals sent men to spy,
and Jǐng Chóng (景崇) had already set himself on fire with his family.
Càn (璨) also surrendered.
On Dīngyǒu (丁酉) day,
Wáng Wàngǎn (王萬敢), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Mìzhōu (密州), attacked and
devastated the Díshuǐ (荻水) post in Hǎizhōu (海州) of Táng (唐).
According to the Jīnrén Jiāngyù Tú (金人疆域圖), Díshuǐ (荻水) post was in Gànyú Xiàn (贛榆縣) of Hǎizhōu (海州).
In this month,
the Lord of Nán Hàn (南漢) went to Yīngzhōu (英州).
Nán Hàn (南漢) established Yīngzhōu (英州) on the land of Zhēnyáng Xiàn (湞陽縣) in Guǎngzhōu (廣州) which belonged to Táng (唐).
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) states: Guǎngzhōu (廣州) is four hundred twenty *lǐ* (里) north of Yīngzhōu (英州).
In this year,
Liú Cóngxiào's (留從效) elder brother, Cóngyuàn (從願), the Fùshǐ (副使) of Nánzhōu (南州), assassinated Dǒng Sī'ān (董思安), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Quánzhōu (泉州) under Táng (唐), and replaced him.
In the second year of Kāiyùn (開運) of Qí Wáng (齊王) of Jìn (晉),
Táng (唐) renamed Zhāngzhōu (漳州) to Nánzhōu (南州),
and appointed Dǒng Sī'ān (董思安) as Cìshǐ (刺史).
This was the third year of Bǎodà (保大) of Táng (唐).
The matter is recorded in Volume 284.
Qīngyuán Jūn (清源軍) was established in Quánzhōu (泉州),
and Cóngxiào (從效) was made Jiédǔshǐ (節度使).
Chapter by Zhāng Xíchēn (章錫琛), collated by Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐)
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
by imperial decree
Later Study Tiāntái
Qiányòu (乾祐) 3rd Year (Gēngxū (庚戌), 950)
1. Spring,
1st month,
on Dīngwèi (丁未) day,
Zhào Huī (趙暉), the Jiédǔshǐ (節度使) of Fèngxiáng (鳳翔), was additionally appointed Shìzhōng (侍中).
2. Wáng Wàngǎn (王萬敢), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Mìzhōu (密州), requested more troops to attack Táng (唐).
Wáng Wàngǎn (王萬敢) had already devastated the Díshuǐ (荻水) post last year,
and now requested more troops to attack it.
Guō Qióng (郭瓊) led the imperial guards and Qízhōu (齊州) troops to the scene.
Due to Wáng Wàngǎn's (王萬敢) request for troops,
Guō Qióng (郭瓊) was sent to lead them.
En route, he passed through Qīngzhōu (青州),
and consequently replaced Liú Shū (劉銖).
Shuài (帥)
is pronounced as *lǜ* (率).
3. Guō Wēi (郭威) requested to lead troops to the northern border with Qìdān (契丹),
but an imperial edict forbade it.
4. On Bǐngyín (丙寅) day,
envoys were dispatched to Hézhōng (河中) and Fèngxiáng (鳳翔) to collect and bury the remains of those who died in battle and of starvation.
At that time, a monk had already gathered two hundred thousand.
5. When the Táng (唐) ruler heard that the Hàn (漢) army had pacified all three rebels,
he finally dismissed Lǐ Jīnquán (李金全) as the Běimiàn Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ (北面行營招討使).
Táng (唐) appointed Lǐ Jīnquán (李金quán) as seen in the first year of volume 287.
6. Liú Yànzhēn (劉彥貞), the Qīnghuái Jiédǔshǐ (清淮節度使) of Táng (唐), heavily extorted people's wealth to bribe powerful nobles.
The powerful nobles competed to praise him.
Having been in Shòuzhōu (壽州) for many years,
fearing replacement,
he wished to secure his position through an urgent warning.
He falsely reported that the Hàn (漢) army was about to launch a large-scale southern expedition.
In the 2nd month,
the Táng (唐) ruler appointed Yān Wáng (燕王) Hóngjì (弘冀), the Liúshǒu (留守) of Dōngdū (東都), as the Dàdūdū (大都督) of Rùnzhōu (潤州) and Xuānzhōu (宣州),
garrisoned at Rùnzhōu (潤州).
Zhōu Zōng (周宗), the Níngguó Jiédǔshǐ (寧國節度使), was made Dōngdū Liúshǒu (東都留守).
Because the Hàn (漢) army was making a large-scale move,
and Hóngjì (弘冀) was young,
it was feared he could not manage and defend effectively.
Zhōu Zōng (周宗) had assisted the Táng (唐) ancestor in establishing the dynasty
and was a veteran of high standing,
hence he was transferred to garrison Yángzhōu (揚州).
7. The court wished to relocate the Fānzhèn (藩鎮).
Taking advantage of their request to attend the Jiāqìng Jié (嘉慶節) to offer birthday felicitations,
the Wǔdài Huìyào (五代會要) states: The Emperor designated the 9th day of the 3rd month as Jiāqìng Jié (嘉慶節).
Hóng Mài's (洪邁) Suíbǐ (隨筆) says: In the first year of Emperor Mùzōng's (穆宗) reign in Táng (唐),
an imperial edict stated:
"On the 6th day of the 7th month,
which is the day of Our birth,
officials of all ranks and imperial ladies should proceed to Guāngshùn Mén (光順門) to present their names and offer congratulations.
We shall meet the officials inside the gate."
The next day,
another edict ordered that the reception ceremony for congratulations be suspended.
Previously,
Zuǒchéng (左丞) Wéi Shòu (韋綬) had proposed its implementation,
but the prime ministers believed that ancient times had no custom of receiving birthday congratulations,
and petitioned for its abolition.
However, the congratulatory ceremony was resumed the following year.
The system of birthday festivals
began with Míng Huáng (明皇), who ordered banquets throughout the realm
and a three-day holiday.
The matter of receiving congratulations
has been in use from Chángqìng (長慶) until now.
Shàng (上)
is pronounced as *shàng* (上) (sháng).
8. On Jiǎshēn (甲申) day,
Guō Wēi (郭威) returned from his northern campaign.
Guō Wēi (郭威) had campaigned north in the 10th month of winter last year,
and now he returned.
Xíng (行)
is pronounced as *háng* (下孟翻).
Huán (還)
is pronounced as *huán* (從宣翻),
and also *hái* (如字).
9. Some people from Fúzhōu (福州) went to Jiànzhōu (建州) to report to Zhā Wénhuī (查文徽), the Yǒng'ān Liúhòu (永安留後) of Táng (唐),
saying that the Wúyuè (吳越) troops had abandoned the city and left,
requesting Wénhuī (文徽) to be their commander.
Wénhuī (文徽) believed it,
and dispatched Chén Huì (陳誨), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Jiànzhōu (劍州), to lead a naval force down the Mǐnjiāng (閩江).
Xuē Shǐ (薛史) says: In the 3rd year of Lǐ Jǐng's (李景) Bǎodà (保大) era,
Yánpíng (延平) was made Jiànzhōu (劍州),
and Jiànpǔ (劍浦) of Jiànzhōu (建州) and Shāxiàn (沙縣) of Tīngzhōu (汀州) were subordinated to it.
Jiànxī (劍溪) connects to Jiànxī (建溪) upstream and reaches Fútáng (福唐) downstream,
also known as Mǐnjiāng (閩江).
Xià (下)
is pronounced as *xià* (戶嫁翻).
Jiàng (將)
is pronounced as *jiàng* (即亮翻).
There was heavy rain,
and the water level rose.
Huì (誨) traveled seven hundred *lǐ* (里) overnight,
reached the city,
defeated the Fúzhōu (福州) troops,
and captured their general Mǎ Xiānjìn (馬先進) and others.
On Gēngyín (庚寅) day,
Wénhuī (文徽) arrived at Fúzhōu (福州).
Wú Chéng (吳程), who was overseeing the Wēiwǔ Jūn (威武軍) for Wúyuè (吳越), deceptively sent several hundred men to welcome him.
Wúyuè (吳越) had not yet appointed Wú Chéng (吳程) as Wēiwǔ Jiédǔshǐ (威武節度使),
but first ordered him to oversee Wēiwǔ Jūn (威武軍) affairs.
"The Mǐn (閩) people are often deceitful and
cannot be trusted.
It is advisable to set up a camp and plan slowly."
Wénhuī (文én huī) said,
"Hesitation breeds trouble;
it is better to seize the opportunity and occupy the city."
Thereupon, he led his troops directly forward.
Huì (誨) arranged his troops and beat the drums,
stopping by the riverbank.
Wénhuī (文徽) made no preparations.
Chéng (程) led his troops out to attack,
and the Táng (唐) army was utterly defeated.
Wénhuī (文徽) fell from his horse
and was captured by the Fú (福) people.
Ten thousand soldiers died.
Huì (誨) returned to Jiànzhōu (劍州) with his entire army.
Chéng (程) sent Wénhuī (文徽) to Qiántáng (錢唐).
Wúyuè (吳越) King Hóngchù (弘俶) presented him to the Five Temples and then released him.
10. On Dīnghài (丁亥) day,
Rǔzhōu (汝州) reported that the Fángyùshǐ (防禦使) Liú Shěnjiāo (劉審交) had died.
Officials and common people went to the imperial court to petition,
stating that Shěnjiāo (審交) had governed with benevolence,
and requested permission to bury him in Rǔzhōu (汝州)
so they could attend to his grave.
An imperial edict granted permission.
The people of the prefecture gathered together, wept, and buried him,
establishing a shrine for him
and offering sacrifices seasonally.
Tàishī (太師) Féng Dào (馮道) said,
"I once served as a subordinate to Lord Liú (劉君)."
According to Ōu Shǐ (歐史),
Liú Shěnjiāo (劉審交) was a man from Yān (燕).
When Liú Shǒuguāng (劉守光) usurped the title,
he appointed Shěnjiāo (審交) as Bīngbù Shàngshū (兵部尚書).
Féng Dào (馮道) served Shǒuguāng (守光) as a Cānjūn (參軍).
He must have been a subordinate at that time.
"He did not surpass others
by being able to reduce their taxes
or abolish their corvée labor.
He merely acted with a public, honest, compassionate, and loving heart.
This is also something everyone can do,
but others did not do it, and Lord Liú (劉君) alone did,
which is why the people of Rǔ (汝) loved him so much.
If all the Èrqiānshí (二千石) (governors) in the realm emulated his actions,
what fear would there be of not gaining the people's affection as Lord Liú (劉君) did!"
The Fángyùshǐ (防禦使) of various prefectures during the Five Dynasties were not quite equivalent to the Èrqiānshí (二千石) of the Hàn (漢) commandery governors.
Later generations simply referred to them as such because they governed cities and defended territories.
11. On Jiǎwǔ (甲午) day,
Dù Jiànhuī (杜建徽), the Chéngxiàng (丞相) of Wúyuè (吳越), Zhaohua Jiédǔshǐ (昭化節度使), and Tóngpíngzhāngshì (同平章事), died.
On the 12th day, *yǐwèi*,
Zhào Kuāngzàn, formerly the Military Commissioner of Yǒngxīng, was made Supreme General of the Left Swift Cavalry Guard.
Zhào Kuāngzàn entered the court from Cháng'ān,
as recorded in Volume 287, in the first year of Gāozǔ Qiányòu.
In the 3rd month, on the
*bǐngwǔ* day,
the Jiāqìng Festival,

Gāo Xíngzhōu, Defender of Yèdū; Mùróng Yànchāo, Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng; Fú Yànqīng, Military Commissioner of Tàiníng; Cháng Sī, Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì; Yáng Xìn, Military Commissioner of Ānyuǎn; Xuē Huáiràng, Military Commissioner of Ānguó; Wǔ Xíngdé, Military Commissioner of Chéngdé; Guō Jǐn, Military Commissioner of Zhāngdé; and Wáng Ráo, acting Military Commissioner of Bǎodà, all came to court.
They were permitted to attend the Jiāqìng Festival to offer congratulations on the Emperor's birthday,
which is why they all came to court.
On the 14th day, *jiǎyín*,
an edict was issued to construct ancestral temples at Gāozǔ's Chánglíng and Shìzǔ's Yuánlíng,
for seasonal sacrifices.
The relevant officials, deeming the cost too high,
suspended the matter.
Up until the state's collapse,
the two imperial tombs never received a single offering.
In the 11th month of this year,
Guō Wēi entered Dàliáng;
in the 12th month,
the generals and soldiers elevated him.
Since the edict for seasonal sacrifices
had been suspended and not implemented by the officials,
it was naturally the case that
no offerings were made between the 6th and 7th months.
On the 15th day, *rénxū*,
Gāo Xíngzhōu was transferred to be Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng,
and Fú Yànqīng was transferred to be Military Commissioner of Pínglú;
on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Mùróng Yànchāo was transferred to be Military Commissioner of Tàiníng.
Zhē Chóngruǎn, Military Commissioner of Yǒng'ān, brought his entire clan to court.
Zhē Chóngruǎn entered the court from Fǔzhōu.
In summer,
4th month,
on the 1st day, *wùchén*,
Xuē Huáiràng was transferred to be Military Commissioner of Kuāngguó;
on the *gēngwǔ* day,
Zhē Chóngruǎn was transferred to be Military Commissioner of Wǔshèng.
According to the *Wǔdài Huìyào*,
in the 3rd month of the 2nd year of Guǎngshùn of the Zhōu dynasty,
Dèngzhōu Wēishèngjūn was first renamed Wǔshèngjūn,
to avoid the personal name of Zhōu Tàizǔ.
The historians recorded it using the later revised name of the commandery.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Yáng Xìn was transferred to be Military Commissioner of Bǎodà;
Liú Cí, Military Commissioner of Zhènguó, was transferred to be Military Commissioner of Ānguó;
Wáng Lìngwēn, Military Commissioner of Yǒngqīng, was transferred to be Military Commissioner of Ānyuǎn.
During the rebellion of Lǐ Shǒuzhēn,
Wáng Ráo secretly communicated with him.
Wáng Ráo secretly used Fūzhōu to communicate with Hézhōng.
Everyone believed that Ráo would certainly be given a *sàndì* (a minor, uninfluential post);
a *sàndì* is an official post with a "sàn" character in its name.
*Sàn*,
pronounced *sì* or *tàn*.
However, he formed strong ties with Shǐ Hóngzhào,
and was promoted to Military Commissioner of Hùguó,
which astonished those who heard of it.
They were astonished that not only was he exempted from punishment,
but he also obtained a major governorship.
Yáng Bīn requested to resign as Grand Councillor (Shūmìshǐ),
and the Emperor sent an imperial envoy to persuade him to stay.
Wú Qiányù, the Commissioner of the Northern Bureau of the Xuanhui Academy, who was nearby, said:
Wú Qiányù was probably next to Yáng Bīn at that time.
"The Grand Councillor is a crucial position,
difficult to hold for long.
Successors should take turns in this role,
so it is right for you, Excellency, to resign."
When the Emperor heard this,
he was displeased.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Qiányù was made Defender of Zhèngzhōu.
The court, considering that the Qìdān had recently invaded
and were rampaging through Héběi,
and that the various regional governors were merely defending themselves
without offering resistance (this matter is found in the previous volume, 10th month of the previous year),
sent Guō Wēi to supervise the generals in preparing against the Qìdān.
Shǐ Hóngzhào wanted Wēi to retain his position as Grand Councillor,
but Sū Féngjí believed there was no precedent for it,
meaning there was no precedent for someone holding the title of Grand Councillor while serving as a regional governor.
However, Shǐ Hóngzhào argued,
"If he holds the title of Grand Councillor, he can act expediently as he sees fit.
The various armies will fear and obey him,
and his orders will be carried out."
The Emperor ultimately followed Hóngzhào's suggestion.
Hóngzhào resented Féngjí's differing opinion.
Féngjí said,
"To control the outer regions from within [the court] is proper.
But now, to reverse it and control the inner court from the outer regions,
how can that be acceptable!"
On the *rénwǔ* day,
an edict was issued making Wēi Defender of Yèdū and Military Commissioner of Tiānxíong,
with his title of Grand Councillor remaining as before.
An edict was also sent to Héběi, stating that
all military provisions, money, and grain
should be subject to Guō Wēi's written orders.
The next day,
prominent court officials gathered for a banquet at Dòu Zhēnggù's residence.
Hóngzhào raised a large goblet and offered it to Wēi,
saying in a loud voice,
"Yesterday's court debate,
how different it was!
Today, I drink for my younger brother."
Shǐ Hóngzhào called Guō Wēi "younger brother."
The character "為" (wéi) is pronounced "yúwěi" here.
"This is a matter of the state,
why concern yourself with it!"
Hóngzhào then raised his voice again and said,
"To stabilize the state
depends on long spears and great swords;
what use are 'hairy awls'?"
Wáng Zhāng said,
"Without 'hairy awls,'
how can revenues be generated?"
"Hairy awls"
refers to writing brushes;
they are made of bundled hair
and shaped like an awl.
Wáng Zhāng was the Commissioner of the Three Bureaus,
in charge of finances,
hence his remark.
On the 20th day, *guǐwèi*,
the Yǒng'ān Army was abolished.
Fǔzhōu was again subordinated to Hédōng.
On the 21st day, *rénchén*,
Guō Róng, General of the Left Gate Guard, was made Prefect of Guìzhōu and Commander-in-Chief of the Tiānxíong Garrison.
Guìzhōu was then under the Southern Hàn.
Sòng Bái said: Guìzhōu
was formerly the land of Xī'ōu and Luòyuè.
Although Qín established Guìlín Commandery,
the names Ōu and Luò persisted.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn changed Guìlín to Yùlín Commandery.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng made Yùlín Commandery into Guìzhōu.
Later, Yùlín and Níngpǔ from Guìzhōu were detached to form Dìngzhōu,
which was soon renamed Nándìngzhōu.
Suí changed Nándìngzhōu to Yǐnzhōu.
Táng changed it to Guìzhōu.
The Hàn dynasty appointed Guō Róng as a titular Prefect,
while his actual position was a general in the Tiānxíong garrison.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shìzōng Shílù* states:
"He was the eldest son of Emperor Tàizǔ,
his mother was Empress Shèngmù Chái.
He was born on the 24th day, *bǐngwǔ*, of the 9th month in the 18th year of Tiānyòu of Táng,
in a villa in Xíngtái."
Xuē Shǐ's *Shìzōng Jì* states:
"He was Tàizǔ's adopted son,
the nephew of Empress Shèngmù.
His original surname was Chái.
His father, Shǒulǐ,
was the Crown Prince's Junior Protector,
who had retired.
When the Emperor was not yet a youth,
he attended Empress Shèngmù
and was by Tàizǔ's side.
As Tàizǔ had no sons at the time,
he adopted him as his own son."
Now, it is universally known that Shìzōng was a son of the Chái clan,
and is called Chái Shìzōng.
Yet the *Shìzōng Shílù* claims he was Tàizǔ's eldest son,
which is a great falsehood.
His father, Shǒulǐ,
was Guō Wēi's wife's elder brother.
Wēi adopted him as a son when he had no children of his own.
Guō Róng first appears here.
In the 5th month,
on the *jǐhài* day,
Zhē Déyǐ, Commander-in-Chief of the Barbarian and Han Cavalry and Infantry of Fǔzhōu,
was made Commissioner of Militias for his prefecture.
Previously, the Yǒng'ān Army was established in Fǔzhōu
to favor Zhē Chóngruǎn.
Now that Chóngruǎn had transferred his governorship,
his son Déyǐ was guarding Fǔzhōu,
but his rank was not yet high enough,
and Fǔzhōu was merely a single city on the frontier.
Therefore, he was demoted to Commissioner of Militias.
Later, it was again made a military governorship
to favor the Zhē clan.
He was Chóngruǎn's son.
In the 23rd year, *gēngzǐ*,
Guō Wēi took his leave,
and addressed the Emperor, saying:
"The Empress Dowager has been with the late Emperor for a long time,
and has experienced many affairs of the world.
Your Majesty is in the prime of your youth;
when matters arise, you should seek her instruction and act accordingly.
Keep loyal and upright people close,
and distance yourself from slanderous and wicked individuals.
Between good and evil,
it is essential to discern clearly.
Sū Féngjí, Yáng Bīn, and Shǐ Hóngzhào are all old officials of the late Emperor;
they are devoted and serve the state.
I wish Your Majesty would trust and employ them wholeheartedly;
there will surely be no failures.
Guō Wēi spoke to this extent,
perhaps already knowing that the Emperor trusted his close attendants and alienated his meritorious old officials.
Your servant wishes to exert his humble and meager abilities,
so as not to betray the trust placed in him."
The Emperor respectfully thanked him.
When Wēi arrived at Yèdū,
seeing that Héběi was in distress and impoverished,
he instructed the frontier generals to guard the borders carefully,
strengthen their defenses,
and not to launch invasions or raids.
If the Qìdān invaded,
they should solidify their defenses and clear the fields to await them.
This is what the art of war calls "first making oneself unconquerable to await the enemy's conquerability."
In the 24th year, *xīncǒu*,
an imperial edict stated:
"Defense Commissioners and Training Commissioners,
unless it is a matter of military urgency,
are not permitted to submit memorials independently.
All matters must first be reported to the Surveillance Commissioner for deliberation before being presented."
This meant that matters of military urgency requiring the court's immediate response
would not allow time to inform the Surveillance Commissioner,
and thus permission was granted to report directly to the court;
for ordinary public affairs,
they must first be reported to their respective supervisors for deliberation before being presented.
On the 25th day, *bǐngwǔ*,
the Emperor's younger brother, Chéngxūn, the Military Governor of Shānnán Xīdào, was made Governor of Kāifēng,
and additionally granted the concurrent title of Grand Counselor.
In reality, he had not yet entered the council.
He was still young
and suffered from a weak constitution.
Shānnán Xīdào was at that time part of the territory of Shǔ.
Liú Shū, the Military Governor of Pínglú,
was greedy, cruel, and tyrannical.
The imperial court wished to summon him,
fearing he might refuse the order.
Thus, using the military campaign in Yí and Mì against Táng as a pretext,
they dispatched Guō Qióng, the Prefect of Yízhōu, with troops to garrison Qīngzhōu.
Ōu Shǐ writes that Guō Huái returned after attacking Nán Táng
and garrisoned his troops in Qīngzhōu.
Liú Shū prepared a banquet and invited Qióng,
with soldiers hidden under the canopy,
intending to harm him.
Qióng, aware of his plot,
dismissed all his attendants,
and attended the meeting calmly,
showing no fear at all.
Shū dared not act.
Qióng then explained the potential consequences, good or bad,
and Shū was moved and submitted.
When the imperial edict arrived, he immediately departed.
On the *gēngxū* day,
Shū arrived at court.
On the *xīnhài* day,
Qióng was appointed Training Commissioner of Yǐngzhōu.
On the 27th day, *guǐchǒu*,
Wáng Zhāng hosted a banquet for various court dignitaries.
During the height of the drinking,
they played a hand gesture game.
Feasting and playing drinking games to enhance merriment
was a custom of the late Táng dynasty.
The *Lèishuō* says:
"Flatten its tiger's chest,"
referring to the palm.
"Bend its pine root,"
referring to the finger joints.
"Place the squatting owl beneath the tiger's chest,"
the squatting owl
is the thumb.
"Place the hooked halberd beside the jade pillar,"
the hooked halberd
is the index finger;
the jade pillar
is the middle finger.
"The hidden dragon spans three fen from the jade pillar,"
the hidden dragon
is the ring finger.
"The strange soldier spans one inch from the hidden dragon,"
the strange soldier
is the little finger.
"Kill its three *luò*,"
refers to drooping the wrist.
"Give birth to its five peaks,"
the five peaks
is a general term for the five fingers.
It was called "beckoning hand game."
Perhaps it was also a type of hand gesture game!

Zhāng's levies were harsh and exacting.
According to the old system,

called

According to the amnesty text from the fourth month of the first year of Tiānchéng of Emperor Míngzōng of Táng:
"For the summer and autumn taxes to be paid,

of one *shēng* per *dǒu*;
