Thus,
before Tiānchéng, there already was "reduced wastage" (shěnghào),
with an additional one *dǒu* paid per *hú*,

Later, when the Hàn rose,
Wáng Zhāng again ordered the payment of "reduced wastage" (shěnghào),

Zhāng initially ordered that for every eighty received,
seventy-seven were disbursed,
which was called
"reduced string" (shěngmò).
Shěn Kuò said: The current practice of calling one hundred coins a
"string" (mò)
borrows
the character
"mò"
for use,

the character
"bǎi" (hundred),
like
"shí" (ten)
and

From the time Huángfǔ Bó established the padded coin method in Táng,
up to the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng,
it was then set at eighty per string.
For even the smallest amounts,

The salt prohibition had been in place for a long time;

do not let anyone have a say!"
Yáng Bīn replied:
"Your Majesty only needs to keep silent."
"Keep silent"
means to keep one's mouth shut and not speak,
so as not to make a sound.
The Emperor had long been displeased.
His attendants then seized the opportunity to slander them to the Emperor,
saying:
"Yáng Bīn and others are autocratic and arbitrary;
eventually, they will cause trouble."
The Emperor believed them.
He once heard the sound of forging from the workshop at night.
The workshop
was where weapons and armor were made,
led by the workshop supervisor.
Forging
is pronounced Duàn.
Iron was forged to make weapons and armor.
He did not sleep until dawn.
Sīkōng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Sū Féngjí, who already had a rift with Shǐ Hóngzhào,
knew that Lǐ Yè and others resented Shǐ Hóngzhào,
and repeatedly incited them with words.
The Emperor then conspired with Lǐ Yè, Wáng Wénjìn, Wú Kuāngzàn, and Wǔ Yǔnmíng to execute Yáng Bīn and others.
Once the plan was decided,
they went to inform the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager said:
"How can such a matter be acted upon lightly!
It would be better to discuss it with the chief ministers again."
Lǐ Yè was by her side at the time,
and said:
"The late Emperor once said,
important affairs of the court should not be discussed with scholars,
as their timidity leads to error."
The Empress Dowager reiterated her concerns.
Historians say that the execution of Yáng Bīn and others was not the Empress Dowager's intention.
Fù
is pronounced Fú Yòu.
"Affairs of the state
are not something for the inner chambers to know!"
She flicked her sleeves and left.
On the Yǐhài day,
Lǐ Yè and others informed Yán Jìnqīng of their plan.
Yán Jìnqīng, fearing the plot might fail,
went to Shǐ Hóngzhào's residence intending to inform him.
Shǐ Hóngzhào declined to see him for other reasons.
If Yán Jìnqīng had been able to see Shǐ Hóngzhào,
then the death of Lǐ Yè and others
would not have awaited Guō Wēi's entry.
Heaven was about to bestow its mandate upon Guō Wēi,
so Shǐ Hóngzhào and others died first to remove obstacles to him.
How could it be merely human affairs!
On the morning of the Bǐngzǐ day,
Yáng Bīn and others entered the court.
Several tens of armored soldiers emerged from Guǎngzhèng Diàn
and killed Yáng Bīn, Shǐ Hóngzhào, and Wáng Zhāng beneath the east wing.
Wáng Wénjìn immediately summoned the chief ministers and court officials to line up in Chóngyuán Diàn,
and announced:
"Yáng Bīn and others conspired to rebel
and have already been executed.
Let us celebrate together with you, sirs."
He also summoned the generals and officers of all armies to the courtyard of Wànsuì Diàn.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: In the first year of Kāipíng of the Liáng dynasty,
Biànjīng's main audience hall was renamed Chóngyuán Diàn,
the East Hall was renamed Xuándé Diàn,
and Wànsuì Táng was renamed Wànsuì Diàn.
In the eighth month of the second year of Tiānfú of the Jìn dynasty,
Xuándé Diàn was renamed Guǎngzhèng Diàn.
Jiāng
is pronounced Jì Liàng.
Xiào
is pronounced Hù Jiào.
He further said:
"Yáng Bīn and others treated Us as a mere child.
Now We finally get to be your lord,
and you are freed from undue worries!"
They all bowed in gratitude and withdrew.
He also summoned former Jìedùshǐ and Cìshǐ to ascend the hall and instructed them.
He dispatched envoys with cavalry to arrest the relatives, partisans, and attendants of Yáng Bīn and others,
and killed them all.
Shǐ Hóngzhào had been especially generous to Wáng Yīn, the Sīwèi Bùjūn Dōuzhīhuīshǐ.
After Yáng Bīn and others died,
the Emperor sent the Gōngfèngguān Mèng Yè with secret edicts to Chánzhōu and Yèdū,
ordering Zhènníng Jìedùshǐ Lǐ Hóngyì to kill Wáng Yīn,
and also ordering Yèdū Xíngyíng Mǎjūn Dōuzhīhuīshǐ Guō Chóngwēi and Bùjūn Dōuzhīhuīshǐ Zhēndìng Cáo Wēi to kill Guō Wēi and the Jiānjūn and Xuānhuīshǐ Wáng Jùn.
Lǐ Hóngyì
was the Empress Dowager's younger brother.

He also urgently summoned Tiānpíng Jìedùshǐ Gāo Xíngzhōu, Pínglú Jìedùshǐ Fú Yànqīng, Yǒngxīng Jìedùshǐ Guō Cóngyì, Tàiníng Jìedùshǐ Mùróng Yànchāo, Kuāngguó Jìedùshǐ Xuē Huáiràng, Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐ Wú Qiányù, and Chénzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Gǔ to court.
The urgent summoning of various commanders
was intended for them to use their accompanying soldiers to guard the imperial palace.
Lǐ Gǔ was merely a Cìshǐ,
yet he was also included in the summons to court.
This must mean his intelligence and strategy were well-known at the time.
Former Pínglú Jìedùshǐ Liú Zhū was provisionally in charge of Kāifēng Fǔ.
Sīwèi Mǎjūn Dōuzhīhuīshǐ Lǐ Hóngjiàn was provisionally in charge of Sīwèi Sī affairs.
Nèishìshěngshǐ Yán Jìnqīng was provisionally Sīwèi Mǎjūn Dōuzhīhuīshǐ.
"Nèishìshěng"
should be
"Nèikèshěng".
He was Lǐ Yè's elder brother.
At that time, people both inside and outside the court were worried and alarmed.
They were alarmed by the suddenness of the upheaval and worried that disaster would strike at any moment.
Shǐ Hóngzhào had previously scolded and angered Sū Féngjí,
and wanted to kill him,
hence Sū Féngjí hated him.
È
is pronounced Wū Lù.
Upon hearing of the change, he was shocked and appalled,
and privately said to people:
"Things are too rushed.
Rushed
means hurried and not carefully considered.
It shouldn't come to this!"
Lǐ Yè and others ordered Liú Zhū to execute the families of Guō Wēi and Wáng Jùn.
Liú Zhū was extremely cruel and poisonous;
no infants or babes were spared.
Yīng
means an infant.
Zhèng Xuán said: Yīng
is like Yīmí.
Rú
means a suckling child,
a child who drinks milk.
Lǐ Hóngjiàn, however, only had people guard and watch them,
and provided them with food and drink.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
an envoy arrived at Chánzhōu.
Lǐ Hóngyì was timid and weak,
fearing that Wáng Yīn already knew about the matter.
He dared not act,
so he led Mèng Yè to meet Yīn.
Yīn imprisoned Yè,
and sent his deputy, Chén Guāngsuì, to show the secret imperial edict to Guō Wēi.
Wēi summoned the Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Wèi Rénpǔ,
showed him the imperial edict, and said:
"What should be done?"
Rénpǔ said:
"My lord,
you are a great minister of the state;
your achievements and fame are long-established.
Moreover, you command powerful forces
and hold an important strategic point.
If you are suddenly framed by petty individuals,
and disaster strikes unexpectedly,
this cannot be resolved by mere words.
Given the current situation,
you cannot just sit and wait."
He advised him to raise an army.
Ōu Shǐ says: Wēi concealed the imperial edict,
and summoned Wèi Rénpǔ, the clerk of the Bureau of Military Affairs, to discuss it in his bedchamber.
Rénpǔ advised Wēi to rebel,
used the seal of the acting governor in reverse,
and forged an imperial edict
ordering Wēi to execute his generals and officers to incite their anger.
The generals and officers all indignantly pledged their service.
I suspect Ōu Shǐ must have had a source.
What is recorded in the Tōngjiàn
must be based on the Zhōu Shǐ,
and the Zhōu ministers were concealing facts for their lord,
and moreover embellishing for Wèi Rénpǔ.
Wēi informed them of the unjust deaths of Yáng Bīn and others, and the contents of the secret edict,
and also said:
"I and you gentlemen,
cleared the thorns
and followed the late emperor to conquer the empire,
taking on the responsibility of a trusted regent for the orphaned heir.
We exerted ourselves to protect the state.
Now that you gentlemen are dead,
how can I bear to live alone!
You all should carry out the imperial edict,
take my head to report to the Son of Heaven,
so as not to implicate others."
Guō Chóngwēi and others all wept and said:
"The Son of Heaven is young and immature;
this must be the doing of the greedy and petty individuals around him.
If these people succeed,
how can the state be at peace!
Chóngwēi wishes to follow my lord to the capital to personally appeal,
to sweep away these rat-like scoundrels and clear the court.
We cannot allow ourselves to be killed by a single envoy
and bear an infamous name for a thousand years."
The Hanlin Astronomer Zhào Xiūjǐ said to Guō Wēi:
"What good would it do for my lord to die in vain!
It is better to follow the popular will
and lead the army south;
this is a divine revelation."
Zhào Xiūjǐ advised Lǐ Shǒuzhēn but encouraged Guō Wēi,
confident in his own methods.
He ordered Guō Chóngwēi to lead the cavalry as the vanguard.
On the *wùyín* day,
he personally led the main army to follow.
Mùróng Yànchāo was eating
when he received the imperial edict.
He dropped his chopsticks and went to court.
The Emperor entrusted all military affairs to him.
The Jiǔyù Zhì says: The distance from Yǎnzhōu to Dàliáng is six hundred *lǐ*.
Mùróng Yànchāo arrived in three days,
considering his kinship with the late emperor (they were of the same lineage), and was eager to rush to the capital,
but he did not realize that his talent and wisdom were insufficient to succeed.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
Wú Qiányù arrived at court.
The Jiǔyù Zhì says: The distance from Zhèngzhōu to Dàliáng is one hundred forty *lǐ*.
The Emperor heard that Guō Wēi had raised an army and was marching south,
and discussed sending troops to resist him.
Hóu Yì, the former Governor of Kāifēng, said:
"The families of the Yèdū garrison are all in the capital.
The imperial army should not be easily sent out.
It is better to close the city gates to blunt their edge,
and have their mothers and wives ascend the city walls to appeal to them.
This way, they can be subdued without battle."
Mùróng Yànchāo said:
"Hóu Yì is old and infirm;
this is merely a coward's plan."
The Emperor then dispatched Yì, along with Yán Jìnqīng, Wú Qiányù, and the former Jiedushi of Bàodà, Zhāng Yànchāo, to lead the imperial guards to Chánzhōu.
On that day,
Guō Wēi had already arrived at Chánzhōu.
From Wèizhōu south to Chánzhōu is one hundred fifty *lǐ*;
he arrived in two days,
intending to catch the Hàn unprepared.
Wáng Yīn welcomed him with tears,
and led his troops to cross the river with Guō Wēi.
The Emperor sent the eunuch Lóngtuō to spy on Guō Wēi.
Wēi captured him,
placed a memorial in Lóngtuō's collar,
and sent him back to report to the Emperor, saying:
"Yesterday, upon receiving the imperial edict,
your minister stretched his neck awaiting death.
Guō Chóngwēi and others could not bear to kill your minister,
saying that this was all due to the slander of those greedy and insatiable individuals around Your Majesty.
They compelled your minister to march south
to the capital to plead guilty.
Your minister sought death but could not obtain it,
and was powerless to control them.
Your minister will arrive at the palace in a few days.
If Your Majesty considers your minister guilty,
how would he dare to evade punishment!
If there are truly those who slandered your minister,
I beg that they be handed over to the army to satisfy the public's anger,
and your minister would then dare not but pacify the various armies
and return to Yèdū!"
On the *gēngchén* day,
Guō Wēi hastened to Huázhōu.
From Chánzhōu southwest to Huázhōu is over one hundred *lǐ*.
*Qù*
is pronounced *qīyù*.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Sòng Yánwò, the Jiedushi of Yìchéng, surrendered.
The Kǎoyì says: The Yǐndì Shílù (Veritable Records of Emperor Yǐn) states:
"In the eleventh month,
on the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Yáng and Shǐ were executed.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
Mèng Yè arrived at Chánzhōu.
Wáng Yīn imprisoned Yè and sent him to Guō Wēi,
and set off that very day.
On the *wùyín* day,
he reached the river,
and met Wáng Yīn.
On the *gēngchén* day,
he halted at Huázhōu."
The Zhōu Tàizǔ Shílù (Veritable Records of Emperor Tàizǔ of Zhōu) states:
"On the thirteenth day,
that night,
Tàizǔ dreamt of going to court for an audience.
The next morning,
he showed the dream to Jùn.
On this day,
Chén Hóngsuì arrived at Yèdū."
This was the fourteenth day, *dīngchǒu*.
The next day,
he was compelled by the crowd to set off on the road,
this was the fifteenth day, *wùyín*.
The day after that,
while on the march,
he encountered Lóngtuō.
He intended to stay at Chánzhōu,
this was the sixteenth day, *jǐmǎo*.
The text below further says:
"On the sixteenth day, he hastened to Huátái."
According to records, from Dàliáng to Chánzhōu is two hundred seventy *lǐ*,
from Chánzhōu to Yèdū is one hundred forty *lǐ*,
and to Huázhōu is one hundred twenty *lǐ*.
It is unlikely that travel back and forth would be so fast.
The Hàn and Zhōu Shílù differ on the starting date of the journey and the arrival at Huázhōu.
Probably on the sixteenth day he hastened to Huázhōu,
and on the seventeenth day he arrived at Huázhōu.
We now follow the Zhōu Tàizǔ Shílù.
Sòng Yánwò was a native of Luòyáng,
and his wife was Princess Yǒngníng, daughter of Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn.
Guō Wēi took supplies from the Huázhōu treasury to reward his officers and soldiers,
and furthermore instructed them:
"I hear that Commander Hóu has already led the armies from the south.
Hóu Yì held the concurrent title of Zhongshu Ling, hence he was called Commander.
To engage in battle would not be in accordance with the intention of coming to court,
but not to fight would lead to being slaughtered by them.
I wish to preserve your achievements and reputation.
It is better to carry out the previous imperial edict.
I would have no regrets in dying!"
Guō Wēi said this to gauge the sentiment of the crowd.
[The soldiers said:] "The state has wronged our lord,
but our lord has not wronged the state.
That is why tens of thousands are eagerly fighting,
as if seeking revenge for a private enmity.
What can people like Hóu Yì do!"
Wáng Jùn then announced to the crowd:
"I have received my lord's instruction:
once we capture the capital,
you are permitted to plunder for ten days."
Everyone rejoiced.
On the *xīnsì* day,
the *shì* (Imperial Envoy) escaped to Dàliáng.
Before this, the Emperor had deliberated on personally going to Chánzhōu,
but stopped upon hearing that Guō Wēi had already reached the Yellow River.
The Emperor showed much regret and fear,
and privately said to Dòu Zhēnggù:
"What happened just now was too hasty."
Lǐ Yè and others requested to empty the imperial treasury to reward the various armies.
Sū Yǔguī thought this was not yet advisable.
Lǐ Yè bowed to Sū Yǔguī before the Emperor,
saying:
"Chancellor, for the sake of the Son of Heaven, do not spare the treasury!"
Thereupon, the Forbidden Army soldiers were each granted twenty *mín* of cash,
while the lower army received half of that.
Soldiers who were in the north had their families provided for,
and letters were sent to their families to entice them.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Guō Wēi's army reached Fēngqiū.
The populace was alarmed and fearful.
The Empress Dowager wept, saying:
"Not listening to Lǐ Tāo's words, it is fitting that we should perish!"
Lǐ Tāo's words
can be found in the first year of the preceding volume.
He said to the Emperor:
"I view the Northern Army as mere gnats!"
The *Ěryǎ* commentary states: *mòméng*
refers to gnats born from decaying matter,
also known as *xījī* (vinegar flies).
Sūn Yán said: "These insects are tiny and fly in swarms."
The *Lièzǐ* says: "Gnawing insects are born on rotten soil,
generated by rain,
and die when they see the sun."
The *Zhuāngzǐ* calls them vinegar flies.
*Mò*
is pronounced *mò jié fān*.
*Méng*
is pronounced *mò kǒng fān*.
(Upon) retreating,
he saw Niè Wénjìn
and asked about the number of soldiers and names of generals and officers from the north.
He was quite frightened,
saying:
"These are also formidable bandits,
not to be taken lightly!"

The Emperor again dispatched Yuán Shān[AS-FBEC]yì, Commander of the Left Divine Military, and Liú Chóngjìn, former Military Governor of Wēishèng, among others, to lead the Forbidden Army and rendezvous with Hóu Yì and others to encamp at Chìgāng.
Shān[AS-FBEC]yì
was the son of Xiàngxiān.
Mùróng Yànchāo encamped a large army at Qīlǐdiàn.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
the Southern and Northern armies met at Liúzǐpó.
Liúzǐpó was south of Fēngqiū
and north of the suburbs of Biàn.
The Empress Dowager said:
"Guō Wēi is an old acquaintance of our family;
unless death is imminent,
why would he come to this point?
We should simply hold our troops and defend the city,
issue an imperial edict to persuade him,
observe his intentions and attitude.
There must be a reasonable explanation,
in which case the etiquette between ruler and minister can still be preserved.
Be careful not to lightly sally forth."
The Emperor did not comply.
If the Emperor had followed the Empress Dowager's words,
though he might not have been guaranteed to survive,
he would not have died in the wilderness.
The Empress Dowager sent an envoy to warn Niè Wénjìn, saying:
"You must be very careful!"
He replied:
"With your servant here,
even a hundred Guō Wēi's
can be captured!"
By evening,
the two armies had not fought,
and the Emperor returned to the palace.
Mùróng Yànchāo boasted loudly:
"Your Majesty, tomorrow there will be nothing to do in the palace.
I hope you will come out again to watch your servant defeat the bandits.
I don't even need to fight them;
I just need to shout at them to scatter and return to their camps!"
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
the Emperor wanted to sally forth again,
but the Empress Dowager strenuously stopped him.
He refused.
After arranging the formation,
Guō Wēi instructed his troops, saying:
"I have come to punish the wicked,
not daring to oppose the Son of Heaven.
Be careful not to make the first move."
After a long while,
Mùróng Yànchāo led light cavalry directly forward and fiercely attacked.
Guō Chóngwēi, with Lǐ Róng, former Prefect of Bózhōu, led cavalry to resist him.
Yànchāo's horse fell,
and he was nearly captured.
Yànchāo withdrew his troops,
with over a hundred of his men killed.
At this, the morale of the various armies collapsed,
and they gradually surrendered to the Northern Army.
Hóu Yì, Wú Qiányù, Zhāng Yànchāo, Yuán Shān[AS-FBEC]yì, and Liú Chóngjìn all secretly went to see Guō Wēi.
Wēi sent each of them back to their camps,
and also said to Sòng Yánwò:
"The Son of Heaven is in danger.
You are a close relative,
so you should lead your personal guards to protect the imperial carriage,
and also secretly inform His Majesty that
I hope he will take the opportunity to come to my camp early."
Sòng Yánwò
was the imperial son-in-law,
hence the mention of "close relative."
"Personal guards"
refers to the Yìchéng personal guards led by Yánwò.
"Wèi chéng"
is pronounced *shéng zhèng fān*.
"Jiàn"
is pronounced *gǔ xiàn fān*.
Disorderly troops swarmed like clouds,
not daring to advance, and then retreated.
By evening,
most of the Southern Army had defected to the North.
Mùróng Yànchāo and over ten of his cavalry fled back to Yǎnzhōu.
That night,
the Emperor alone, with the three chancellors and several dozen attendants, stayed at Qīlǐzhài.
The rest all fled and dispersed.
The three chancellors were
Dòu Zhēnggù, Sū Féngjí, and Yǔguī.
Qīlǐzhài
was the Qīlǐdiàn stockade where Mùróng Yànchāo had been stationed.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Guō Wēi saw the Emperor's banners and flags on a high slope.
He dismounted and removed his helmet to follow them,
but by the time he arrived, the Emperor had already left.
The Emperor spurred his horse, intending to return to the palace.
Upon reaching Xuánhuàmén,
Xuánhuàmén
was the first gate from the east on the northern side of Dàliáng city.
Originally named Sānzǎomén,
it was renamed Xīnghémén in the first year of Kāipíng of the Liáng Dynasty,
and then Xuánhuàmén in the third year of Tiānfú of the Jìn Dynasty.
He asked his attendants:
"Where are the troops and horses?"
He then shot his attendants.
The Emperor turned his reins
and headed northwest to Zhàocūn.
The pursuing troops had already arrived.
The Emperor dismounted and entered a commoner's house,
where he was assassinated by rogue soldiers.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* states:
"The Emperor reached Xuánhuàmén.
Liú Zhū shot the Emperor's attendants.
The Emperor turned and went northwest.
Guō Yǔnmíng followed closely with a drawn sword.
Upon reaching Zhàocūn in the northwest,
the vanguard had already caught up.
Rogue soldiers surged tumultuously.
The Emperor, afraid,
dismounted and entered a private house.
Guō Yǔnmíng, knowing that the matter was beyond help,
drew his blade, attacked the imperial carriage, and the Emperor perished."
Xuē Shǐ's hidden imperial annals state:
"Guō Yǔnmíng, knowing the matter was beyond help,
stabbed the Emperor, and he perished.
Yǔnmíng then committed suicide."
The annals of Zhōu Tàizǔ say:
"Yǔnmíng assassinated the Hàn Emperor in the northern suburbs."
Liú Shù said:
"Yǔnmíng was deeply trusted by the Emperor;
how could he commit regicide?
It was probably Guō Wēi's troops who killed the Emperor,
and after the deed was done, they concealed it,
blaming Yǔnmíng because he committed suicide."
Based on this, the one who assassinated the Emperor was not necessarily Yǔnmíng,
but since no one knows who it was,
it is simply stated as "rogue soldiers."
Niè Wénjìn fled alone,
but army soldiers pursued and decapitated him.
Lǐ Yè fled to Shǎnzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Dàliáng to Shǎnzhōu is six hundred fifty-nine *lǐ*.
Lǐ Yè wished to rely on his elder brother.
"Shǎn"
is pronounced *shī rǎn fān*.
He wished to rely on Mùróng Yànchāo.
He cried out mournfully:
"This is my old fault!"
Wēi arrived at Xuánhuàmén.
Liú Zhū fired arrows like rain outside the city.
"Fired arrows like rain"
means shooting arrows like falling rain.
He returned to his private residence,
Yíngchūnmén.
This was the first gate from the north on the eastern side of Biàn city.
Originally named Cáomén,
it was renamed Jiànyángmén in the first year of Kāipíng of the Liáng Dynasty,
and then Yíngchūnmén in the third year of Tiānfú of the Jìn Dynasty.
The various armies extensively plundered,
and smoke and fire erupted everywhere throughout the night.
The soldiers entered the residence of Bái Zàiróng, the former military governor of Yìchéng Circuit,
seized Zàiróng,
plundered all his wealth,
and then advanced and said:
"We once served under your command,
but now we have been so disrespectful as to come to this;
how can we ever face you again?"
Then they cut off his head and left.
Considering Bái Zàiróng's cruelty in Zhēndìng,
that he should now suffer this calamity
is perhaps the way of Heaven.
Wěn (刎),
pronounced Wǔ Fěn Fān.
Zhāng Yǔn, the Assistant Minister of Personnel,
had a fortune amounting to tens of thousands,
but he was stingy.
Even his wife was not entrusted with anything;
he always kept many keys tied to his clothes,
which jingled as he walked like jade pendants.
That evening,
he hid in the coffered ceiling of a Buddhist temple.
The Fēngsú Tōng states: "Hall ceilings are like the Dōngjǐng constellation,
carved with lotus and water caltrops;
lotus and water caltrops are aquatic plants,
used to suppress fire."
Dù Yòu said: "Hàn palaces and halls usually referred to the inverted roof as 'jǐng' (well),
and all were painted with water plants, lotus, and water oats to suppress fire."
Hé Yàn's Fù on the Jǐngfú Diàn states:
"Encircling with coffered ceilings,
interwoven with fine gauze."
Also, Wáng Wénkǎo's Fù on the Língguāng Diàn states:
"Round abysses and square wells,
with lotus and water weeds planted upside down."
This means a square well was made and algae painted on top of it.
Lù Diàn's Píyǎ states: "The inverted ceiling above the roof
is called a coffered ceiling (zǎojǐng)."
The plank broke and he fell.
The soldiers plundered his clothes,
and he then died of cold.
Previously,
Jiǎ Yánhuī, the Director of the Imperial Workshops, was favored by the emperor.
He was neighbors with Wèi Rénpǔ
and wished to annex Rénpǔ's residence to expand his own.

received the posthumous title Wǔmù (武穆).
All entered the barbarian settlements.
Lǐ Yànwēn (李彥溫) saw the city ablaze
and led his troops from Tuókǒu (駝口) to rescue it.
The Lǎng (朗) people had already occupied the city and resisted the attack.
Yànwēn attacked Qīngtàimén (清泰門)
but could not overcome it.
He and Liú Yànkuò (劉彥瑫) each led over a thousand men to escort Wénzhāo Wáng (文昭王) and Xīguǎng's (希廣) sons towards Yuánzhōu (袁州),
and then fled to Táng (唐).
Mǎ Xīfàn (馬希範), King of Chǔ (楚),
received the posthumous title Wénzhāo (文昭).
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* (九域志) states: "From Tánzhōu (潭州) southeast to Yuánzhōu (袁州) is 634 *lǐ*."
*Qū* (趣)
is pronounced *qīyù fān* (七喻翻).
Zhāng Huī (張暉) had previously escaped from Yìyáng (益陽) to Chángshā (長沙).
After Chángshā (長沙) fell,
he surrendered to Xī'è (希萼).
The matter of Mǎ Xīchóng (馬希崇) communicating with Xī'è (希萼) began in volume 287, Tiānfú (天福) 12th year.
*Shuài* (帥)
should be read as *lǜ* (率).
He saw Xī'è (希萼) and said:
"Unfortunately, I was misled by Xǔ Kěqióng (許可瓊).
If I die today,
I will not be ashamed before the former kings!"
Péng Shīgǎo (彭師暠) threw his spear to the ground,
shouting loudly and asking to die.
Xī'è (希萼) sighed and said:
"They are men of iron and stone!"
He did not kill any of them.
On the *yǐsì* day,
Xīchóng (希崇) welcomed Xī'è (希萼) into the residence to oversee affairs.
The city was closed.
They sent out to arrest Xīguǎng (希廣), and his Chief Secretary Lǐ Hónggāo (李弘皋), his younger brother Hóngjié (弘節), Military Judge Táng Zhāoyìn (唐昭胤), and Dèng Yìwén (鄧懿文), Yáng Dí (楊滌), etc.
All were captured.
Xī'è (希萼) said to Xīguǎng (希廣):
"When inheriting the family business of father and elder brother,
is there no order of seniority?"
Xīguǎng (希廣) replied:
"The generals and officials recommended me, and the imperial court appointed me, that is all."
Xī'è (希萼) imprisoned them all.
It turned out as Zhāng Shàodí (張少敵) and Tuòbá Héng (拓跋恆) had said.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Xī'è (希萼) ordered Liú Bīn (劉賓), Commander of Internal and External Patrols and Guards, to prohibit burning and looting.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Xī'è (希萼) proclaimed himself Celestial General-in-chief (Tiāncè Shàngjiāngjūn, 天策上將軍) and Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ, 節度使) of the Wǔ'ān (武安), Wǔpíng (武平), Jìngjiāng (靜江), and Níngyuǎn (寧遠) armies.
The Mǎ (馬) family formerly possessed the lands of these four prefectures.
At this time, the Níngyuǎn (寧遠) circuit had already fallen under the jurisdiction of Southern Hàn (南漢).
These were all the official titles of his father and elder brother.
Xī'è (希萼) claimed them himself without receiving the mandate from the central court.
This laid the groundwork for Xīchóng (希崇) to kill Xī'è (希萼).
All the positions were filled by people from Lǎng (朗).
Lǐ Hónggāo (李弘皋), Hóngjié (弘節), Táng Zhāoyìn (唐昭胤), and Yáng Dí (楊滌) were cut into pieces and eaten,
and Dèng Yìwén (鄧懿文) was executed in the marketplace.
On the *wùshēn* day,
Xī'è (希萼) said to his generals and officials:
"Xīguǎng (希廣) is a weakling,
controlled by those around him.
I wish to spare his life,
is that permissible?"
All the generals remained silent.
Zhū Jìnzhōng (朱進忠), who had once been flogged by Xīguǎng (希廣),
replied:
"Your Majesty has fought for three years with bloodshed,
only now obtaining Chángshā (長沙).
In Tiānfú (天福) 12th year,
Xī'è (希萼) and Xīguǎng (希廣) first began to contend for the state.
They engaged in battle the following year,
and it has been three years until now.
You will surely regret it later."
On the *wùshēn* day,
Xīguǎng (希廣) was granted death.
As Xīguǎng (希廣) faced execution,
he was still reciting Buddhist scriptures.
Péng Shīgǎo (彭師暠) buried him outside Liúyángmén (瀏陽門).
Liúyángmén (瀏陽門) was the east gate of Tánzhōu (潭州) city.
*Liú* (瀏)
is pronounced *liú*.
The Military Governor of Wǔníng (武寧), Yūn (贇), left Gǒng Yánměi (鞏延美), the Right Staff Supervisor, and Yáng Wēn (楊溫), the Former Chief Drill Instructor, to guard Xúzhōu (徐州).
This laid the groundwork for the two to resist Zhōu (周) with Xúzhōu (徐州).
"Gǒng Yánměi" (鞏延美),
according to the next volume and Ōu Shǐ (歐史), should be
"Gǒng Tíngměi" (鞏廷美).
Gǒng (鞏)
is a surname derived from a place name.
In the Zhōu (周) dynasty, there was the high minister Gǒng Jiǎngōng (鞏簡公),
and in the Jìn (晉) dynasty, the Grand Master Gǒng Shuò (鞏朔).
*Cóng* (從)
is pronounced *cáiyòng fān* (才用翻).
He came west from Péngchéng (彭城) to Dàliáng (大梁).
All were like kings,
and those around them shouted "Long live!"
Guō Wēi (郭威) reached Huázhōu (滑州)
and stayed for several days.
Yūn (贇) sent envoys to comfort the generals.
At the moment of receiving the mandate,
they looked at each other and did not bow,
privately saying to each other:
"We have slaughtered and captured the capital city,
our crime is great.
If the Liú (劉) family is re-established,
will our lineage even survive?"
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
Wēi (威) heard of this,
immediately led his troops to depart,
heading towards Chányáng (澶陽).
On the *xīnhài* day,
Sū Yǔguī (蘇禹珪) was dispatched to Sòngzhōu (宋州) to welcome the heir-apparent.
Xī'è (希萼), King of Chǔ (楚), appointed his son Guāngzàn (光贊) as Acting Military Governor of Wǔpíng (武平).
He appointed Hé Jìngzhēn (何敬真) as the Internal Commander of Lǎngzhōu (朗zhou),
leading troops to garrison it.
Xī'è (希萼) summoned Tuòbá Héng (拓跋恆),
wishing to employ him,
but Héng (恆) feigned illness and did not rise.
Since Xīguǎng's (希廣) enthronement, Tuòbá Héng (拓跋恆) had already closed his doors.
The matter can be found in volume 287, Tiānfú (天福) 12th year.
On the 55th day of the cyclical designations rénzǐ,
Guō Wēi crossed the Hé [Yellow River],
and was housed at Chánzhōu.
On the morning of guǐchǒu,
as he was about to depart,
several thousand officers and soldiers suddenly raised a great clamor.
Wēi ordered the gates closed,
but the officers and soldiers scaled the walls and climbed onto the roofs to enter, saying:
"The Son of Heaven must be the Shìzhōng himself.
The officers and soldiers are already enemies with the Liú clan
and cannot stand by them!"
Some tore a yellow banner and draped it over Wēi's body,
collectively supporting and embracing him,
shouting "Long live!" which shook the ground.
Thereupon, they escorted Wēi south.
Wēi then submitted a memorial to the Tàihòu [Empress Dowager],
requesting to uphold the Zōng
Miào [Ancestral Temple]
and serve the Tàihòu as his mother.
On the day of bǐngchén,
he arrived at Wéichéng.
During the Suí dynasty, Báimǎ was divided to establish Wéichéng Xiàn,
which governed the capital of the Wéi clan's state.
It was subordinate to Huázhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it is fifty *lǐ* southeast of the prefecture.
Dīng Dù said: Wéichéng Xiàn
was the ancient state of Shǐwéi.
Shàng,
pronounced *shí zhǎng fān*.
He said that since he had left the river the day before,
and had not committed any transgression on the road,
there was no need for worry or doubt.
Fearing that the gentry and common people of the capital might, due to the previous calamities of plunder,
flee and scatter in all directions,
he therefore sought to pacify them.
Lí,
pronounced *lì zhì fān*.
On the day of wǔwǔ,
Wēi arrived at Qīlǐdiàn.
Dòu Zhēnggù led the hundred officials out to welcome and pay respects,
and then encouraged him to ascend the throne.
Wēi encamped at Gāoméncūn.
Gāoméncūn
was probably outside the Gāomén.
According to records, Dàliáng City had no Gāomén.
The Shī Dàyǎ Mián chapter says: "Then they erected the Gāomén,
the Gāomén was lofty."
Máo Shì's commentary says: "The outer gate of the king's outer city wall is called Gāomén."
Zhèng Shì's commentary says: "For a feudal lord's palace,
the outer gate is called Gāomén, the court gate is called Yìngmén,
and inside there is a Lùmén."
For the Son of Heaven's palace,
Kùmén and Zhìmén
are added.
Up to the Lǐjì Míngtángwèijì, which states that Zhōu bestowed upon the Duke of Lǔ the system of the Son of Heaven,
its words are: "Kùmén is
the Son of Heaven's Gāomén;
Zhìmén is
the Son of Heaven's Yìngmén."
Zhèng's commentary also states: "The Son of Heaven has five gates:
Gāo, Kù, Zhì, Yìng, and Lù."
If Lǔ had Kù, Zhì, and Lù,
then did feudal lords have three gates?
Examining and pondering it,
the Shī commentary and Jì commentary
are slightly different.
During the Five Dynasties period,
what was called Gāoméncūn outside Biànchéng,
was probably a village outside the outer city gate,
and thus it was called Gāoméncūn,
which aligns with Máo Shì's Shī commentary.
Gāoméncūn was subordinate to Kāifēng Xiàn.
Xuē Shǐ says: Wáng Tán was buried in Gāoményuán of Kāifēng Xiàn,
and this is how it is known.
Wǔníng Jiédùshǐ Yūn had already arrived at Sòngzhōu.
Wáng Jùn and Wáng Yīn heard of the military mutiny at Chánzhōu,
and dispatched the Shìwèi Mǎjūn Dūzhīhuīshǐ Guō Chóngwēi with seven hundred cavalry to resist it,
and also sent the former Shēnzhōu Cìshǐ Mǎ Duó with troops to patrol Xǔzhōu.
Chóngwēi suddenly arrived at Sòngzhōu,
arrayed outside the prefectural gate.
Yūn was greatly alarmed,
closed the gate, and ascended the tower to question him.
To patrol Xǔzhōu
was to prepare for Liú Xìn.
From Biànjīng to Sòngzhōu was only two hundred and eighty-five *lǐ*.
Yūn did not expect his arrival,
hence his alarm and questioning.
Qī,
pronounced *qù jí fān*.
"The Chánzhōu army mutinied.
Duke Guō feared that Your Majesty was not yet aware,
and therefore sent Chóngwēi to serve as your guard.
There is no other intention."
Yūn summoned Chóngwēi,
but Chóngwēi did not dare to advance.
Féng Dào came out and spoke with Chóngwēi.
Earlier, Féng Dào had been sent to welcome Yūn,
hence Dào was with Yūn.
Yūn grasped Chóngwēi's hand and wept.
Chóngwēi comforted him with Guō Wēi's intentions.
A short while later,
Chóngwēi left.
At that time, Hùshèng Zhīhuīshǐ Zhāng Lìngchāo led his troops to serve as Yūn's guard.
According to Xuē Shǐ,
Hùshèng
was the Hàn Shìwèi Mǎjūn.
Shuài
is read as *lǜ*;
the same below.
"Observing Chóngwēi's gaze and actions,
he must have a different plot.
Everyone on the road says Guō Wēi has already become emperor,
and Your Majesty's deep penetration without stopping
will bring calamity!
Please urgently summon Zhāng Lìngchāo,
explain to him the misfortune and fortune,
and have him, at night, seize Chóngwēi with troops,
and take his soldiers.
Tomorrow,
plunder the gold and silks of Suīyáng,
recruit soldiers,
and flee north to Jìnyáng.
Sòngzhōu is
Suīyáng Jùn.
Yūn's father Chóng was stationed at Jìnyáng.
Suī,
pronounced *suī*.
Zǒu,
pronounced *zòu*.
They will not have time to pursue us.
This is the best strategy!"
Yūn hesitated and could not decide.
That evening,
Chóngwēi secretly enticed Lìngchāo,
and Lìngchāo led his followers to defect to him.
Yūn was greatly terrified.
Guō Wēi sent a letter to Yūn,
saying he was pressured by the various armies;
he summoned Féng Dào to return first,
leaving Zhào Shàngjiāo and Wáng Dù to attend him.
Dào bid farewell,
and Yūn said:
"The reason this lonely one relied on you when I came here
was because you have been a chancellor for thirty years,
hence I had no doubts."
Féng Dào became chancellor in the second year of Tiānchéng of Emperor Míngzōng of Táng,
which was twenty-four years ago by this time.
Saying thirty years
is an approximate number.
Yí,
pronounced *yú jì fān*.
"The situation is perilous.
What strategy do you have?"
Dào remained silent.
He had no answer for Yūn,
hence his silence.
Féng Dào called himself a foolish and stubborn old man,
which was truly not false.
He wanted to kill him.
Yūn said:
"You all must not be reckless.
This has nothing to do with Duke Féng."
When the Qìdān ruler entered Biàn,
he blamed Liú Jìxūn,
Jìxūn shifted the blame to Dào,
and Dào nearly died.
In the affair at Sòngzhōu,
if Liú Yūn had followed Jiǎ Zhēn's idea,
Dào would also surely have died.
Yet the Qìdān ruler considered Dào not to be meddlesome,
and Liú Yūn said it had nothing to do with Duke Féng.
Is it not because he had always maintained a calm and detached demeanor in office,
and did not contend with others,
that everyone respected his reputation and virtue?
Dào's ability to preserve himself
was indeed successful,
but what use would a state have for such a chancellor?
However, since the Tóngguāng reign of Later Táng,
the Púmìshǐ held actual power,
and the chéngxiàng merely filled the position.
Blaming others is not difficult,
but accepting blame is like flowing water;
judging by this,
Dào was not willing to accept blame.
He killed several of his close confidants, including Dǒng Yì and Jiǎ Zhēn.
On the day of jǐwèi,
the Tàihòu issued an edict,
deposing Yūn to be Xiāngyīn Gōng.
Mǎ Duó led troops into Xǔzhōu,
and Liú Xìn, in panic and confusion, committed suicide.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
the Tàihòu issued an edict,
making the Shìzhōng supervise the state.
The Tàihòu's two edicts
were both the will of Guō Wēi.
"Shìzhōng"
referred to Guō Wēi's office.
On the night of *rénxū*,
in the Jiānguó's camp, some infantry officers got drunk
and loudly declared, "Previously, the Chánzhōu cavalry supported and established (a ruler);
now, the infantry also wish to support and establish (a ruler)."
The Jiānguó beheaded them.
56 The Nánhàn Zhǔ made palace women Lú Qióngxiān and Huáng Qióngzhī Nǚ Shìzhōng,
who wore court attire, caps, and belts,
and participated in deciding government affairs.
The imperial clan and meritorious veterans
were almost entirely executed,
and only eunuchs like Lín Yányù held power.
Historians say that Nánhàn ultimately perished because of eunuchs and favored women,
but the reason the Nánhàn Zhǔ was able to rule till the end of his life
was that he was located in a remote coastal area,
and Zhōngguó had not yet found a true ruler.
